Extraction of additional fields, variants, module-level assignments, Julia generic-function containers and non-definition module-body nodes remains frontend coverage work; this step does not claim those units are implemented.
Location keys keep the existing path#kind:name/… form. Rust impl keys include self type and optional trait. Julia method keys use the whitespace-normalised complete signature (including where and return annotations), not their order among other overloads. Identical keys receive ~2, ~3, etc. A duplicate inserted before another identical signature may change its duplicate index; semantic equivalence and move tracking belong to WP-66.
Defines carries half-open UTF-8 start_byte/end_byte, 1-based start_line/end_line, and syntax_path (slash-separated child indices, including unnamed tokens, in the parsed tree). line remains on nodes for legacy consumers. Names points from a file-qualified namespace name to each definition; Julia overloads share a name node. Name nodes are metadata and excluded from the graph panel’s normal symbol filter.
Resolution is deliberately syntactic and same-file: only an unambiguous visible bare name resolves. Possible local shadows, overload dispatch, qualified/dynamic calls and external imports remain Unresolved nodes with the spelling in the label. A Calls edge also produces References. Imports retain an Imports edge to their unresolved target. An Unresolved edge additionally marks each unresolved use. No compiler, dependency loader, macro expansion, code execution, or network lookup runs.
A file represents its implicit module until explicit module/body coverage is added. Top-level uses and imports originate there; uses within explicit definitions originate in the innermost extracted item. This extends the edge table’s definition/module origins to File for implicit modules. Rust impl occurrences are likewise an explicit extension of the occurrence table.
Calls/references aggregate by (from,to,kind) with count and a ranges text property: comma-separated start:end UTF-8 ranges. start_byte/end_byte retain the first encountered occurrence. Ranges are not promised in source order. The property representation follows today’s scalar Value model; a future typed range-list value may replace it with a migration.
Provenance uses by=moonkale-index, the crate version as by_version, an input UUID-v5 digest of the exact file bytes under the index-input-v1 domain, and Unix seconds in derived_at. This input digest is independent of mtime-based source versions and is not a WP-66 content id. It is for freshness, not cryptographic authentication. Wiki-link derivatives carry the same provenance. Mirrored folder nodes and folder containment keep their source metadata.
The existing 5,000-file / 512 KiB-per-text-file walk bounds apply; the reference pass uses an explicit traversal stack. Refresh atomically replaces a file’s definitions, names, unresolved nodes and derived edges. There is no cross-file semantic resolution or persistence in this step (WP-21 remains separate).

The rename test above was corrected because location paths include names (§4); keeping both ids through a rename would contradict that definition. The implicit-module and impl-occurrence exceptions make current navigation possible without pretending L1 printing or full frontend coverage exists. Content ids (WP-66) and printing back (WP-67) are unchanged and unimplemented here.
WP-66 normalizer (v1 2026-10-16, v7 2026-10-20)
Implemented, experimental and off by default: moonkale-index/content-ids. The normal form and the hashing are their own crate, moonkale-content-id (packages/services/content-id, 2026-10-20), shared with Sophia so a definition can have one id in both (SR-116). The index adds reference resolution and the cache. The crate’s golden/ fixtures carry Moonkale’s ids and reference spans for a cross-check. v2 fixes resolution: Julia and Python parameter types and defaults (p::Point) are uses, not local names. In v1, a method typed with a same-file struct didn’t depend on it. v3: a Julia struct no longer references its own name, and a Rust struct expression’s type is a use; Sophia’s cross-check found both. v4 adds Julia’s local scopes (loops, closures, do, let, try, comprehensions), varargs, keyword parameters, destructuring and anonymous ::T parameters; real-code coverage on LinearAlgebra rose from about 69% to 99% of definitions. v5 resolves Julia references per module, as Julia does. A package is one module over its included files, found from Project.toml. A name resolves only to a unique, unimported binding in its module, and calls to a function with several methods stay unresolved (they are edges to the generic function, not part of ids). Rules agreed with Sophia in its SPEC-008. Rust and Python keep same-file resolution. v6: Julia type parameters are locals, and a callable-type or interpolated head names nothing. v7: nothing inside a Julia call is a unit, so a keyword default in @deprecate f(A; check::Bool = true) … no longer gets an id (found by Sophia against Julia’s method table). See content-id.md for the version list and rules. These are conservative syntactic identities under the rules below, not a proof of language-level equivalence. Runtime introspection, external modules, compiler flags, macro expansion and dynamic dispatch are not modeled. Files and location ids remain authoritative. No application enables the feature automatically and no UI consumer or remote query dialect is added.
Request and encoding
IndexSource::content_id(location_id) explicitly requests a definition and its reachable same-file definitions. The async API returns ContentIdentity { id, digest, normalizer_version, component_digest, component_index, component_size }; the UUID is NodeId::from_content of the full BLAKE3 member digest. The existing definition node receives content_id and the corresponding content_digest, content_normalizer, content_component, content_component_index and content_component_size properties only after the complete request succeeds. Ordinary build/search/graph queries do not compute hashes. No core kind, id encoding or source protocol changes.
Canonical fields have a little-endian u32 tag length, tag bytes, little-endian u32 payload length and payload bytes. The syntax stream includes language, normalizer version, node kinds, ordered children and leaf tokens, with explicit open/close fields. It has no path, source id, timestamp or byte position. The declaration’s own name is a dedicated empty token. Other observable names remain. Lexical value bindings use declaration slots and (scope depth, slot) references; Rust block bindings activate after the initializer and shadowing allocates a fresh slot. Python function locals are collected before body traversal. Julia positional parameters and function-local assignments use the same scheme.
References resolved by the existing conservative same-file extractor use the target’s full content digest (the information from which its content UUID is derived). Unresolved free identifiers have an explicit unresolved tag and their spelling; structured paths retain ordered syntax and name tokens. Local bindings take precedence over reference substitution. Cross-file, overload and qualified resolution are deliberately unchanged from WP-22. Reordering an unrelated top-level item does not affect the requested identity.
Observable spelling and supported syntax





























LanguageRetainedDropped or normalizedConservative failures in v1Rustliteral spelling, operators, types, generic names, lifetime names, field/member names, visibility, non-doc attributes, mutability, macro token-tree spellingcomments and doc attributes/comments; value parameter names and supported local patternsmatch/conditional/let-else binding scopes, closures, function-local imports, unsupported binding patterns, macro definitionsPythonkeyword-capable parameter names, keyword argument labels, attributes, decorators, annotations, defaults and literal contentscomments and leading function/class docstrings; positional-only parameter names; ordinary function-local assignmentsnested functions/classes inside functions, comprehensions/generators, lambdas, global/nonlocal, augmented/walrus bindings, for/with/exception/match/delete bindings and function-local importsJuliafield names, types, generic/where names, literal contents, operators and quoted syntaxcomments and attached doc strings outside occurrences; positional parameters and ordinary function-local assignmentskeyword parameter declarations, nested functions, arrow/do closures, comprehensions, explicit local declarations, for/let/catch scopes, macro definitions and unsupported patterns
Macro token trees and quoted/string data are opaque and preserve their spelling, including interior whitespace. Ordinary formatting outside opaque data is ignored. Python parameter renames that change keyword calling conventions must change the id; §9’s renamed-local test does not require them to be equal. Documentation is deliberately excluded even where introspection can observe it. Attributes/decorators and observable local spellings can therefore make two otherwise similar definitions differ. A future extension to these rules must increment the normalizer version; supported syntax must not silently become a fallback approximation.
Recursive components
Iterative SCC discovery orders components dependency-first. Within an SCC, references are ordered ports determined by the syntax stream. For each possible root, first-visit traversal assigns member indices; the lexicographically smallest complete component serialization is canonical. Its BLAKE3 digest is the component digest. A member digest hashes tagged component digest and u32 canonical index. External references include the already-computed target digest.
If several roots give the same minimal serialization, each member uses its smallest index across those roots. Automorphic, structurally indistinguishable members may share a content id. This resolves the draft’s previously unspecified symmetric-recursion tie without introducing a name/path/order dependency. Different ordered wiring remains distinguishable. Root candidates share the request work budget rather than performing unbounded graph-isomorphism search.
Cache, freshness and bounds
Parsing/hashing and optional synchronous state-store access run through a blocking worker, outside the UI input path. Memory LRU budgets are 16 MiB per index on desktop/server and 4 MiB on Android. with_content_id_store(Arc<dyn StateStore>) optionally stores rebuildable identity records in a versioned prefix of the existing INDEX table, with the same byte budget and LRU timestamps. Each record is at most 2 MiB and checksummed; malformed, incompatible or failed cache reads are misses. Records contain ids/digests and metadata, never copied source text. Full index persistence remains WP-21; platform constructors do not install this optional cache themselves.
The key includes normalizer version, exact BLAKE3 file-input hash and source/location selector. Since resolution remains same-file, that exact input covers every resolved dependency; a changed dependency cannot hit an old result. These location-scoped cache keys do not enter content hashes. Persisted cache byte enforcement is serialized within this process; separate processes may temporarily exceed the budget until a later write evicts entries. Cache failures never block recomputation.
Shared content-id limits (SR-145, 2026-10-24): 16 MiB per file, 4,096 definitions per input file, 256 MiB accumulated canonical/graph bytes, 32 million default syntax/continuation/graph steps, and a two-second parser progress deadline. Nesting has no depth cap: syntax, binding and scope passes use explicit heap stacks. The index retains its separate fetch/closure limits. These acceptance changes preserve normalizer v7 and all existing golden ids. The same-file request fetches one file, then fetches it again for freshness; the shared 16 MiB per-file limit is checked on each result. Resource exhaustion, malformed/unsupported syntax, stale input, unavailable source and failed worker produce typed errors with no partial publication.
Before computing, fetched bytes must match indexed provenance. Before publishing, bytes are fetched again, the index generation is checked, and every affected node must still exist. Refresh removes previously published identities for that file; deletion removes its definitions. No old id is published over a concurrently refreshed graph. Unrefreshed source changes can still make an already-published graph snapshot stale until the existing watcher/refresh path runs; this feature adds no new watcher guarantee.
Three-language integration fixtures cover moves/renames/trivia, body and dependency changes, recursion, unresolved references, observable spelling, lexical shadowing, optional persistent reopen, refresh/deletion, concurrent refresh and parser limits. Unit tests cover ordered wiring, disconnected components, canonicalization exhaustion, byte-budget eviction and invalid cache records. See P-200 Lazy syntactic content identities and packages/services/index/index.md.
WP-67 slices 1–5 (2026-10-16)
The native, default-off lossless-syntax feature now provides exact Rust token/trivia snapshots and pure guarded declaration-name/move plans. SourceDescriptor.truth is built with backwards-compatible Files deserialization and explicit Store metadata; existing sources remain externally authoritative. Default-off structural-edits now exposes declaration-name and same-file function moves through a revision-aware document adapter and graph preview/conflict UI. Reference-aware graph Rename now uses complete same-folder rust-analyzer plans, coordinated buffer history and explicit per-file saving; cross-file moves remain unimplemented. See Rust Lossless Syntax and Patches for the byte/trivia ownership policy, bounds, move-token conservation and the document adapter and experimental graph controls. Content identities and exact input hashes have different purposes; a doc-only change preserves the former but invalidates an old structural edit plan.

architecture/Collaboration.title: Collaboration
architecture/Collaboration.content:
Collaboration in Moonkale grows out of something that already ships: the session bus. Every window or tab of one user is a peer; a user on another machine is a peer behind the server. Same messages, different transport — so the multi-window feature built in Milestone 1 is the first, zero-latency, single-actor form of collaboration. This note extends it to many people. Related: Version Management (the entity log is the shared history), LLM and RAG (agents are peers too).
Several people and agents in one session, and what the database guarantees versus what Moonkale adds when they edit the same graph, are in Shared Work (2026-10-14).
Layers
flowchart TB
  subgraph now["shipped (Milestone 1)"]
    BUS["session bus: Hello · SourceOpened · DragStarted/Ended · Moved"]
    T1["desktop: in-process channels"] --> BUS
    T2["web: BroadcastChannel (same browser)"] --> BUS
  end
  subgraph next["presence (Phase 3)"]
    AW["awareness: cursors, selections, open documents, who is here"]
    T3["server: websocket hub per workspace, fan-out to all peers"] --> AW
  end
  subgraph later["shared editing (Phase 4–5)"]
    CRDT["text CRDT per document (Loro) + entity log for structure"]
  end
  BUS --> AW --> CRDT

1. Session bus (exists)
moonkale_ext_api::session: WindowId, SessionMessage, trait SessionBus { send }. A window announces itself (Hello), peers reply with their open sources, and documents can be dragged between windows (DragStarted → drop target in every other peer → Moved → origin closes). The transport is per platform; the messages are serde JSON so they already survive a browser hop (which is why Version is serialised as a string — 64-bit hashes don’t fit in a JavaScript number).
2. Presence / awareness
Small, frequent, ephemeral state that is never stored in the entity log: where each peer’s cursor and selection are, which document is active, a display name and colour, “is typing”. Modelled on Yjs’s awareness protocol:
Presence {
  peer: PeerId,            // (user, window) — a user with two windows is two peers
  user: UserId, name, colour,
  focus: Option<NodeId>,   // active document
  cursor: Option<{ node: NodeId, anchor: usize, head: usize }>,   // char offsets
  seen_at: Timestamp,      // peers expire when it goes stale
}

Rendering: other users’ carets and selections as decorations in the Code Editor (the decoration channel already exists for highlights/diagnostics) and as coloured dots on Explorer entries and tabs; a “who’s here” list in the status bar.
Transport: the same session bus, extended with Presence(Presence); on desktop within one process it is free, across machines it goes through the server hub.
Cost model: presence is sent on change, throttled (~20 Hz cap), last-write-wins per peer, dropped when stale. Nothing here needs consistency.

3. The server as synchronisation hub
ADR-0005 Server functions as the remote backend already makes api the place where sources live for web clients. Collaboration adds one websocket per (client, workspace):

Fan-out: every SessionMessage/Presence a client sends is relayed to the other clients of that workspace. Desktop clients connect to the same hub when they open a shared workspace (“connect to team server”), so desktop and web users share one session.
Authority: the server owns the sources (folder or database), so it is naturally the serialisation point for writes; today’s optimistic Version check becomes “the server applies transactions in arrival order and broadcasts the resulting events” — which is exactly the entity log of Version Management being appended by many actors.
Auth and rooms: workspace = room; users authenticate to the hub; permissions per source (read/write) — the same permission model extensions get (Host API Reference).
Offline/desktop-first: the local entity log keeps working without a hub; on reconnect, logs merge (structural events commute; content goes through the CRDT).

4. Shared editing
Two people typing in the same document need more than versions: a text CRDT per document (loro or automerge, both Rust; Loro’s rich-text and tree types map well onto Markdown and flow graphs). Plan:

Document.text becomes a CRDT text; the editor backend applies remote ops as setText/splices, local edits become ops. The current whole-document change events would be replaced by real splices at this point (P-037).
The entity log records a Content event per CRDT transaction — history stays one log.
Saving to a folder source writes the merged text; git sees ordinary commits.
Conflict-free structure (adds/removes) is already given by the entity log’s set semantics.

What the multi-window work decided for collaboration

Messages are typed Rust enums with serde, never ad-hoc JSON — so the server hub can be written in the same types.
A window is identified by a random WindowId, a user later by UserId; presence uses the pair. Nothing assumes one window per user.
Sources are attached by descriptor (AttachSource): a peer that learns of a source can open it without a path — the exact shape a hub needs to hand a newcomer the room’s sources.
Drag-and-drop between windows is a move (Moved closes the origin) — not a shared edit. The gesture is the workbench tab itself (already an HTML5 drag with its id as data). The OS-level drop is used where the platform delivers it; otherwise the offer persists as a banner in every other window after dragend (“README.md was dragged from another window — Move it here”), so the gesture degrades to grab-then-click instead of failing (P-044). Two windows editing the same document is deliberately unsupported until the CRDT exists; the conflict is caught by the version check on save.



                  
                  Milestone 8: presence exists — moonkale_server::presence is a hub with a room per folder id; members carry {window, name, active document}; the client publishes on every active-document change and shows others as initials badges (status bar, tabs, Explorer). No cursors yet, web only (desktop's session bus stays local). Milestone 8 - Implementation Log.
                  
                

The current move protocol reloads saved source text. Save an unsaved document before moving it: dirty tabs are not offered. If the origin receives an edit after a clean offer, the move acknowledgement leaves that origin open so the edit remains available. This can leave both windows open on the file; the source version check still governs saving. It does not provide a shared editing transport.
Open questions (→ Problem Ranking R-34, R-30)

Presence for the Graph View: show other users’ viewports/selections on the graph? Probably yes, same channel.
Should agents publish presence (“agent X is reading main.rs”)? Useful for trust; cheap.
Hub scale: one Axum task per room with a broadcast channel is enough for teams; beyond that, a message broker.

Where a shared server stands (2026-09-20)
Modes, what exists and the security model for several people on one server (accounts, roles, the terminal): Remote and Server Modes.

architecture/Core-and-Extensions.title: Core and extensions — a discussion
architecture/Core-and-Extensions.content:
Why this page: the requests keep growing. The debugger, plotting, workflows, the knowledge-graph studio, Lenticulum, a static reader, math rendering, canvas components and Unison all came in one week. Each raises “is this core?“. The Extension Catalogue has a short section on core and separate repositories (2026-10-01); this page is the longer discussion, with criteria to apply rather than taste. It is meant to be argued with. Its answers should come from Use Cases, not from preference.
Four places a thing can live






























PlaceWhat it isExample todayLibrarycrates other projects can depend on, versioned by ext-api tags, with no Moonkale UImoonkale-core, moonkale-ext-api, moonkale-graph-renderCore platformservices every extension builds on, always compiled in: the workspace, sources registry, state store, settings, secrets, policy gate, LSP and terminal services, the shellthe shell, services/*, sources/registryExtensions in this repositorybuilt and tested with the core, toggled per user: on by default (what a first-day user needs) or opt-inon: Explorer, Search, code editor, Markdown, Graph, Table, Git, History, Agent, Terminal. Opt-in: Flow editor, the Rust editor and terminalExtensions in their own repositorytheir own release cadence, toolchain or audience; compiled in behind a feature (static) or loaded (wasm)moonkale-julia (Lux, ModelingToolkit, RxInfer)
Criteria (proposed)
A thing goes to the core platform only if all four hold:

Several extensions need it, so it is a service, not a feature.
It needs no toolchain beyond Moonkale itself.
Its dependencies are light (the core must build in minutes, and on Android).
It must behave the same everywhere, so one implementation keeps every extension consistent (settings, secrets, the policy gate).

An extension in this repository if at least one of these holds:

a first-day user expects it (then on by default);
it is generic over sources or languages (the flow editor’s framework, the table, the graph);
it shares hot code with the core, so splitting would force lockstep releases.

Its own repository if at least one of these holds:

it needs a foreign toolchain to be useful (Julia, Lean, a JVM);
it serves a specialised audience;
it wraps someone else’s backend with its own release cadence;
someone else maintains it.

The library gets anything another project would reasonably reuse without Moonkale’s UI: the graph engine, the model, the extension contract, perhaps the math parser and the table grid’s arithmetic.
Open placements (proposals to discuss)











































































































ThingProposed placeWhyDoubtMath delimiters + LaTeX/Typst fallback (Math Delimiters and Renderers)the parser in the library (shared by rich, source and native preview); rendering in the Markdown extensionthree editors must agree on what is mathTypst rendering pulls the typst crate: already in the Typst preview, so no new weightCanvas component layer (WP-05)library (beside the engine)the graph view, flow editor, table schema view and a canvas view all need it—DAP service (Debugger Requirements)core platform service like LSP; the debug panel an opt-in extensionmany language extensions would use one serviceis a code debugger wanted at all, beside the model debugger?Model debugger (LT-19)the flow editor extension plus the Julia side in moonkale-juliait debugs flow models—Plot (Plotting Requirements)extension in this repository, opt-in at first, on by default once it is goodplotting query results is generic; Lenticulum needs itthe spec format may want to be library-level, shared with reader modeWorkflow runner (Workflow Automation (n8n, Windmill))opt-in extension in this repositoryit runs flows, so it is close to the flow editor and the run recordscould grow into its own repository if it gains integrationsRun records (LT-13, WF-02)core platform serviceLenticulum runs, workflow runs and debug sessions all need them—Notebooks (Notebook Editor)opt-in extension in this repository; kernels behind a featuregeneric over languages; KG Studio and Julia need it—Lenticulum library (Lenticulum Frontend Requirements)moonkale-juliaJulia toolchain, own cadenceLenticulum is the reason Moonkale exists: should its editor-side pieces (plates, typed spaces) be core flow features? Proposed yes: they are genericKnowledge Graph Studio (Knowledge Graph Studio)its own repositorywraps oxilite and tiramemsu, whose cadence is not ours; may be maintained with their author—Language-server contribution point (KG-05)core platformevery language extension—Unison source (WP-18), other code-graph sourcesown repository (moonkale-sources-extra or moonkale-codegraph)foreign toolchain (the ucm codebase format)—Datalog dialect (WP-20)library cratesources, the agent and the KG studio would share it—Declarative rendering settings (WP-30)core platform (settings schema) + the code viewevery language’s projectionfar awayStatic reader (WP-28, way later)its own build in this repositoryreuses the engine, grid and index—Postgres/Supabase source (WP-17)moonkale-sources-extraneeds a server to test—
Questions to settle

Is “on by default” decided per extension in the distribution, or per user profile (a “modeller” profile turning on the flow editor and plots)?
Should the flow editor become on by default once Lenticulum work lands? It’s the reason Moonkale exists, but most first-day users won’t need it.
Does an extension in its own repository get CI here (a check that the distribution builds with it), as moonkale-julia does today?
Who owns an extension built for someone else’s backend (the KG studio): MathStruct, the backend’s author, or both?
Which services are “core” on Android, where there are no toolchains and no PTY?

Next step: collect use cases (Use Cases), then revisit each “doubt” above against them.

architecture/Crash-Safety.title: Crash safety — what happens when an extension fails, and what comes back
architecture/Crash-Safety.content:
Question (Daniel, 2026-10-14): is Moonkale crash-safe when an extension crashes, and could it reload extensions when that happens? Partly. It depends on the kind of extension and on the platform. Since 2026-10-14 every extension panel has its own boundary with a Reload button.
Today, by kind













































KindWhat a failure doesRecovers howWasm extensions (third-party, sandboxed)a trap, an exhausted fuel budget (50 M units for the manifest, 5 G per run) or the 256 MB memory limit ends that call with an error; each call runs in a fresh store✅ the next call starts clean; nothing else is affectedOut-of-process tools: language servers, terminals, the Julia process, claudethe process dies; Moonkale sees it closed✅ language servers restart with their unsaved documents (codex’s recovery, lsp-restart.mjs); a terminal shows that it ended; a Julia run fails as a runCompiled-in Rust extensions, native desktop: a panic while a panel renderscontained since 2026-10-14: Dioxus catches render panics, and each panel now sits in an error boundary (shell.rs, guarded). The panel shows “X stopped with an error”, with the message and its location and a Reload panel button; the rest of the window keeps working. Test: shell/tests/extension_crash.rs✅ Reload re-renders the panelCompiled-in Rust, native: a panic in an event handler or a spawned tasknot caught by the render boundary; it may take the window down⚠ restart; the session comes back from the store, minus unsaved edits until ADR-0026’s recovery snapshots existCompiled-in Rust, the web clientthe client is built with panic = "abort" (for size), so any panic stops the whole page⚠ a page reload; the session comes back from the server’s storeCompiled-in Rust, the phoneas native, but Android may also kill the app under memory pressure⚠ restart restores the sessionThe server processa panic in a request handler ends that request (tokio tasks are isolated); a panic in shared state can poison it✅ mostly; ⚠ poisoned locks to review
So third-party code (wasm) and external tools are contained. The weak spot is Moonkale’s own compiled-in extensions outside render, and the web client as a whole.
The rule
A failing extension must be contained (only its panel or call fails), visible (it says what failed and where, never a blank panel), and recoverable (Reload, or a restart that loses no work). Data safety doesn’t depend on the extension: everything authored is in the state store within a second, and unsaved edits get recovery snapshots (ADR-0026 Memory and the store).
Steps

✅ A boundary per panel with the error, its location and Reload (2026-10-14).
Recovery snapshots of unsaved edits (ADR-0026, WP-56), so even a hard crash loses nothing.
Catch panics in spawned tasks and event handlers on native. Extensions spawn through a shell helper that wraps the future in catch_unwind, reports the panic to the panel’s boundary, and cancels the task instead of the app.
The web client: a global error hook shows “Moonkale stopped, Reload restores your session” instead of a frozen page. Later, if size allows, build the web client with unwinding, so panels recover there too.
Crash counting and safe mode:

An extension that fails three times in a minute is disabled for the session, with a notice and an “enable again” action.
An extension that crashes at startup twice in a row starts disabled next time.
moonkale --safe starts with core extensions only.


Reload an extension, not only its panel: for wasm modules, re-instantiate from the file (also after an update). For compiled-in ones, Reload is a remount of their panels and a restart of their services; there is no unloading of compiled code.
Third-party code defaults to isolation: an extension not built by the Moonkale project runs as wasm or as a separate process, never compiled in without the user choosing it (Extension System, Security).

Work package: WP-57 in Work Packages.

architecture/Data-Sources.title: Data Sources
architecture/Data-Sources.content:
Crates: sources (abstraction, registry, lifting, remote proxy), sources-sql, sources-graph, sources-kv, project-fs. Driver availability is in Database Backends.


                  
                  As built (2026-10-01) 
                  
                

Built: folders; SQLite, DuckDB (+ folders of CSV/TSV/Parquet), Turso, redb, RocksDB, HelixDB (embedded), LadybugDB (Linux) — all opened from a file or directory, all read-only; the remote proxy. Not built: any networked database (Postgres, Redis, TypeDB, FalkorDB), connection parameters with SecretRef, the connection state machine, SourceEvent subscriptions (sources report external changes through changes_since instead), and the shared lifting rules (sources::lift is a stub — each driver lifts its own rows and decides its own ids). Capabilities has read, write, watch, text_query only. Which file opens as which source is decided by source openers since Milestone 18 phase 2: each driver crate exports openers() (moonkale_core::SourceOpener: a name check that compiles everywhere, and an open function where the driver is built); the app assembles them into one Openers list that the Explorer, the desktop and the server all ask. Text queries are classified by the source itself (Source::classify, default rules in moonkale_core::source::risk).


Query path
sequenceDiagram
  participant E as Editor / Agent
  participant R as SourceRegistry
  participant S as Source (e.g. Postgres)
  participant L as lift
  E->>R: query(Query::Neighbours{node, depth:1})
  R->>S: structured → SQL (FK joins)
  S-->>L: rows
  L-->>R: nodes + edges (ids derived from PKs)
  R-->>E: GraphView (paged, with watermark)
  S-)R: SourceEvent::NodeChanged (LISTEN/NOTIFY)
  R-)E: invalidate above watermark

Families















































FamilyNode kindsEdge kindsText dialectNotesFolderDirectory, FileContains—all platforms; backends differSQLTable, Column, RowContains, ForeignKeySQLrows lifted lazily; PK → idGraphVertex, typed1:1 relationsCypher / TypeQL / HelixQLthe natural fitKVsynthetic hierarchy + KeyContainsraw commandskey patterns make it navigableRemoteanyanyanyproxy to api; the only source on web
Lifting rules (sources::lift)

Tables without a primary key get unstable ids (ctid/rowid/hash) and the descriptor flags them; editors show a warning and disable inline edit.
Foreign keys become edges on demand (neighbour queries), never eagerly.
Schema is a graph too: Table/Column nodes with Contains, ForeignKey edges between tables — so the schema view is the graph view.
KV patterns: user:{id}:{field} → user → 42 → profile, configurable per source, auto-detected by sampling.
TypeDB: attributes → properties; roles → Custom edge kinds carrying the role name.

Capabilities, not brands
Capabilities { READ, WRITE, WATCH, TEXT_QUERY(dialect), FULLTEXT, VECTOR, TRANSACTIONS }. Editors and the LLM policy feature-detect. A read-only DuckDB file says !WRITE; a Redis without keyspace notifications says !WATCH; a Postgres with pgvector says VECTOR.
Connections and secrets
ConnectParams are persisted with a SecretRef name, never a password. Resolution per platform: keychain (desktop), server env (web), Keystore (mobile). The connection state machine (Connecting → Ready ↔ Degraded → Closed) feeds the status bar dot.
Remote source (ADR-0005 Server functions as the remote backend)
api exposes query/fetch/apply as server functions and (later) subscribe as a websocket, per SourceId. The web/mobile builds have one factory: moonkale_server::RemoteSource. The desktop build has it too (“connect to a team server”).
As built (Milestone 1): RemoteSource lives in the api crate, not sources, to avoid a dependency cycle (it calls api’s server functions; api holds the registry). The server confines open_folder to MOONKALE_ROOT; there is no auth yet. Errors are nested Result<Result<T, SourceError>, ServerFnError> so a remote Conflict is a local Conflict.
Order of implementation (from Roadmap), with where each stands

✅ Folder (native) — everything else needs files.
✅ SQLite + DuckDB — embedded, no server; DuckDB also gives “folder of CSV/parquet as tables”.
✅ Remote proxy — web parity.
◐ Turso ✅ (embedded, Milestone 17) · Postgres/Supabase ○.
◐ LadybugDB ✅ (embedded; Linux only, P-144) · FalkorDB ○.
◐ redb, RocksDB ✅ (embedded key/value, Milestone 17, not in the original list) · Redis/Dragonfly ○.
◐ HelixDB ✅ (embedded, git dependency, Milestone 17) · TypeDB ○.
○ Writes (OLTP) for every database source — the next step announced after Milestone 17.

Projects
Several sources open at once, grouped into a saved project with a selector, per-source colour and read-only, suspended sources, an open report and sync: Projects and Sources (desired behaviour, 2026-09-19).
Open questions

Supabase’s REST/RPC layer would allow a browser-direct source. Deferred; treat as Postgres for now.
Should IndexSource (derived data) be allowed to write back (e.g. materialise embeddings into pgvector)? Leaning yes, behind Capabilities::VECTOR.

Driver designs not built yet
Until Milestone 18 these lived as comment-only files in the driver crates; they were removed in phase 1 so the workspace compiles only real code (Milestone 18 - Implementation Log).

Connection lifecycle (sources/connect.rs): ConnectParams → SourceFactory::connect → ConnectionState (Connecting → Ready ↔ Degraded → Closed) with backoff; the UI draws the status dot from it. Today every source is a file opened synchronously that never reconnects.
Credentials (sources/credentials.rs): SecretRef names are persisted, values resolved at connect time — desktop from the OS keychain (keyring), web never in the browser, mobile from Keychain/Keystore.
Lifting (sources/lift.rs): the shared rules of the section above; folder lifting is trivial and lives in project-fs.
SQL — schema (sources-sql/schema.rs): information_schema / PRAGMA table_info / duckdb_tables() → a schema cached per connection, invalidated on SchemaChanged. Structured queries (structured.rs): Query → SQL, conservative — paginated SELECT with keyset pagination, FK-based neighbour expansion, LIKE/FTS for text search, dialect-specific vector ops (pgvector, sqlite-vec, DuckDB array_cosine_similarity) when the capability is there. Postgres/Supabase (postgres.rs): LISTEN/NOTIFY for change events when the user opts in (needs a trigger; offer to install it).
Graph — dialects (sources-graph/dialect.rs): GraphDialect::{Cypher, TypeQl, HelixQl} with per-dialect decoding into nodes / edges / paths / scalars. Structured queries (structured.rs): Query → Cypher / TypeQL / HelixQL — neighbourhood expansion, path queries, kind filters, SKIP/LIMIT or cursor pagination. Schema (schema.rs): TypeDB match $t sub thing;; property graphs list labels and relationship types plus sampled property keys. FalkorDB (falkor.rs): the falkordb crate over RESP, Cypher, sharing connection plumbing with Redis. TypeDB (typedb.rs): typedb-driver; a strongly typed schema, explicit read/write/schema transactions that map well onto core::Transaction.
Key/value — Redis (sources-kv/redis.rs): a connection pool, SCAN with cursor pagination, keyspace-notification subscription, raw commands through Query::Text. Values (values.rs): strings as text/blob, hashes as property maps, lists/sets/zsets as rows, streams as paginated rows, RedisJSON as nested values. Key patterns (patterns.rs): user:{id}:{field} → a synthetic hierarchy, editable per source, auto-detected by splitting on : / / and sampling.

architecture/Debugging-and-Logging.title: Debugging and Logging
architecture/Debugging-and-Logging.content:
“In a browser I hit F12. When this is compiled, how do I see what went wrong?” — Per platform, per build type. Verified against Dioxus 0.7.10 sources on 2026-09-17.


                  
                  Still open (P-032, checked 2026-10-01) 
                  
                

None of the release-build measures below exist yet: no log file, no panic hook or dialog, no JavaScript console forwarding, no Diagnostics panel. An installed desktop build still has to be started from a terminal to see its output.


The mental model
There are two worlds in a Dioxus app and they log to different places:
flowchart LR
  subgraph Rust["Rust world"]
    T[tracing::info! / error!]
    PANIC[panic!]
  end
  subgraph JS["webview / browser world"]
    C[console.log from JS packages]
    JSERR[uncaught JS errors]
  end
  T -->|web| BC[browser console F12]
  T -->|desktop| TERM[terminal that launched the app]
  T -->|desktop, release| FILE[(log file — we must add this)]
  T -->|android| LOGCAT[adb logcat]
  T -->|ios| XC[Xcode console]
  T -->|server| STDOUT[server stdout / journald]
  C & JSERR -->|web| BC
  C & JSERR -->|desktop| INSP[WebKit/WebView2 inspector]

dioxus::launch calls dioxus::logger::initialize_default() for you (DEBUG level in debug builds, INFO in release) — so tracing::info! works out of the box, and the destination is chosen per platform by dioxus-logger: browser console on wasm, stdout on desktop/server, logcat on Android.
Web

F12 works exactly as you expect. Rust tracing lines show in the console (with level colours); panics show as panicked at … with a wasm stack trace — in debug builds the frames have Rust function names.
dx serve also mirrors the console into its own TUI (v toggles verbose).
Release: the same, minus symbol names unless you keep debug info (dx build --release --debug-symbols true).

Desktop, debug build (dx serve --platform desktop)

Rust side → the terminal running dx serve (the dx TUI shows app stdout/stderr; scroll with the keys it lists).
JS side / DOM → the webview inspector. Debug builds compile it in: use the app menu Toggle Developer Tools (Dioxus adds it under the app menu in debug builds) or right-click → Inspect Element (WebKitGTK / WebView2 context menu, unless with_disable_context_menu(true)). Console, Elements, Network — everything a browser F12 has, because it is WebKit’s/Chromium’s inspector.
Panics: printed to the terminal; set RUST_BACKTRACE=1 for the stack. A panic in a component handler tears down the app, so you’ll see the window close and the trace in the terminal.

Desktop, release build (the compiled binary a user runs)
There is no inspector unless we enable wry’s devtools feature (macOS uses private APIs, so don’t ship it enabled), and stdout goes nowhere when launched from a desktop icon. This is the gap we must close in the desktop crate:

Log to a file: install a tracing_subscriber with tracing_appender::rolling::daily(log_dir, "moonkale.log") before dioxus::launch (the auto-initialiser won’t replace a subscriber you set first). log_dir = dirs::data_local_dir()/moonkale/logs. Keep the stdout layer too for terminal launches.
Panic hook: std::panic::set_hook → write the panic + backtrace to the same file, then show a native dialog (rfd) with the path.
Capture the JS console: install window.onerror / console.error overrides in the interop bundles that forward to Rust via the same CustomEvent path (JS Interop Boundary), so JS errors land in the log file. Cheap and invaluable.
Diagnostics panel in the app: OS, webview engine + version, GPU/WebGPU probe result (Linux Desktop Setup), log path, “copy last 200 lines”.
Env overrides: RUST_LOG=moonkale_graph=trace style filters via EnvFilter; MOONKALE_DEVTOOLS=1 to open the inspector in builds compiled with devtools.

Until (1)–(4) exist, a user with a broken release build can still run it from a terminal (./moonkale or RUST_LOG=debug ./moonkale) and read stdout.
Server (api, fullstack)
dx serve shows server logs in the same TUI as the client (INFO Registering: POST /api/echo etc.). Deployed: stdout → whatever runs it (journald: journalctl -u moonkale -f). Server-function errors surface on the client as ServerFnError values — log them on both ends.
Mobile

Android: adb logcat -s RustStdoutStderr (dioxus-logger routes to logcat); Chrome chrome://inspect can attach to the WebView for the JS side in debuggable builds.
iOS: Xcode console; Safari → Develop menu → device → the WKWebView for the JS side.

Debugging technique, by symptom

































symptomlook atblank/black window on Linuxterminal for WebKit warnings; try WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1 (Linux Desktop Setup)UI renders but a button does nothinginspector console (JS error?) then Rust log (handler panicked? signal write while borrowed?)“already borrowed” / write-while-readclippy.toml in the repo flags holding Read/Write guards across .await; search for .read() inside async moveserver fn returns error on web onlyserver log; CORS/auth; the same function works on desktop because it’s called in-processhot reload stopped applyingdx serve log, press r to force rebuildgraph canvas emptyDiagnostics panel: which surface was chosen, WebGPU probe; WGPU_BACKEND=…
What to add to the skeleton (tracked)

desktop: file logging + panic hook + Diagnostics panel — Phase 1, cheap.
packages/js/*: console/error forwarding — part of the protocol spec.
Logged as P-032 in Problem Log.

architecture/Extension-System.title: Extension System
architecture/Extension-System.content:
Crates: ext-api (the contract), ext-host (the implementation). The user-facing guide is Writing an Extension.


                  
                  As built (2026-10-01) — read this before the principles 
                  
                


Static extensions implement moonkale_ext_api::Extension: manifest() (a Rust Manifest { id, name, description, optional, default_enabled, permissions }), panels(), render(), on_panel_closed(), commands()/run_command(), claims() (which documents it is the editor of, and how strongly — Milestone 18), flow_libraries(), settings(). They are listed in moonkale_shell::default_extensions(), enabled per tier in the Extensions panel. Since Milestone 18 an extension can also put file marks on Explorer rows and tabs (Workspace::contrib.file_marks, git’s status letters), and the platform hands the workspace its services in five groups (WorkspaceConfig { folders, processes, persistence, network, runtimes }).
Wasm extensions use the JSON ABI v1 (ADR-0013 JSON ABI before components): commands and agent tools only.
Not built: the moonkale.toml manifest, the lifecycle below (every static extension is constructed at start; there is no lazy activation), activation events, when clauses, the Host handle with kv_get/notify/ask, moonkale_shell::Tree panels, WIT, contribution points other than panels, commands, settings and flow libraries. Those parts of this page, Contribution Points, Manifest Reference and Host API Reference are the target design.



Principles

No privileged path. Built-in editors are static extensions using only ext-api. If they need something the API lacks, the API grows.
Declarative first. Manifests describe panels, commands, languages, keybindings, themes and renderers so the shell can build UI before activating code. Activation is lazy.
Capabilities are explicit. The manifest requests; the user grants; the Host checks on every call. Static extensions are checked too.
Two runtimes, one API. Static (Rust crate, linked in, full Dioxus) and WASM component (sandboxed, portable). See ADR-0004 WASM components for extensions.

Lifecycle
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Discovered: manifest found
  Discovered --> Registered: manifest valid, contributions indexed
  Registered --> Activating: activation event fires
  Activating --> Active: activate() ok
  Activating --> Failed: error → diagnostics panel
  Active --> Registered: deactivate() / disable
  Registered --> [*]: uninstall

Contributions (panels, commands, …) are available in the Registered state — a command can appear in the palette for an extension that has never run; running it triggers activation.
Catalogue
What exists and what is planned, with tiers and platform fit: Extension Catalogue — keep it current when an extension is added, moved or retiered.
Runtimes by platform



































staticwasmtimebrowserdesktop✅✅—web✅—✅ (Worker + wasm_component_layer)mobile✅❌ (JIT; wasmi would fit)planned: the same Worker runtime inside the WebView, see Android Extensions and Bundlingserver✅✅—


                  
                  Status after Milestone 6 ( Milestone 6 - Implementation Log)
                  
                

Milestone 8: the browser runtime exists for the JSON ABI: packages/js/wasm-host runs the module in a Worker and serves its synchronous call import through a SharedArrayBuffer mailbox that the main thread (the client Workspace) answers with the same three host calls and permission check; the server sends COOP/COEP so the page is cross-origin isolated; /api/ext/module/{id} serves the bytes. The server runtime remains the fallback and the only runtime on desktop.
Static extensions are the catalog in moonkale_shell::default_extensions(); each Manifest is core / optional / opt_in with declared permissions, and Settings.extensions (user ← workspace) decides what is enabled and granted — Settings → Extensions. wasmtime runs on desktop and on the web server (moonkale-ext-host, feature wasmtime) with a JSON ABI v1 over core wasm modules — exports alloc / manifest / run, imports moonkale.log / moonkale.call (list_sources, query, fetch_text), permissions checked per call — instead of the component model described below, which stays the target (the manifest shape is the same). Modules are discovered in ~/.config/moonkale/extensions/ and <folder>/.moonkale/extensions/; their llm_tool commands become agent tools (policy Mutating). The browser runtime and the moonkale_shell::Tree panels are not built yet: wasm extensions contribute commands, not panels, in v1. Example: packages/extensions/wordcount.


WASM panels render through a small retained-mode moonkale_shell::Tree (rows, columns, text, inputs, lists, tables, Embed(view)), diffed and rendered by the shell. It is less expressive than Dioxus on purpose: portable, sandboxable, and cheap over a Worker boundary. Static extensions may return real Elements.
The WIT world
ext-api’s Rust types are the source of truth; wit/moonkale.wit is generated from them so the two can’t drift. Extension authors in Rust use moonkale-ext-api directly and compile with cargo component; other languages use the WIT.
Hot topics

Hot reload of a wasm component during development (watch .wasm, re-instantiate, replay activation) — wanted, not designed.
Renderer contributions must stay declarative for wasm extensions (colours, glyphs, popup templates) because the GPU renderer batches them; custom wgpu passes are static-only.
Conflicts (two extensions, one command id) are reported, not resolved.

architecture/Graph-Native-Model.title: Graph-Native Model
architecture/Graph-Native-Model.content:
Crate: packages/core. The model is the contract between sources, editors, the index, extensions and agents.


                  
                  As built (Milestone 18 phase 6.2, 2026-10-03) 
                  
                

The design and the code agree since ADR-0015 The core model: nodes and edges carry props (Properties, sorted typed values); GraphView and subscribe left the design (editors hold QueryResults; sources report changes through the changes_since long poll); ids are derived from (SourceId, native key), or content-addressed with NodeId::from_content(digest). Not built: fetch(NodeId) -> Content (it is fetch_text / fetch_bytes), ContentRef::{Rows, Nested}, Custom(ExtensionId, String) kinds (they are Custom(String)). The entity log (graph::history) is in Version Management.


Entities
classDiagram
  class Node {
    NodeId id
    SourceId source
    NodeKind kind
    String label
    String native_key
    ContentRef? content
    Version version
    Properties props
  }
  class Edge {
    SourceId source
    NodeId from
    NodeId to
    EdgeKind kind
    Properties props
  }
  class Source {
    <<trait>>
    descriptor()
    query(Query) QueryResult
    fetch_text(NodeId) / fetch_bytes(NodeId)
    apply(Transaction) Applied
    changes_since(seq) Changes
  }
  Node "1" --> "*" Edge : from/to
  Source --> Node : owns

Design choices
Open enums for kinds. NodeKind and EdgeKind have well-known variants editors can match on (File, Row, Vertex, Page, Symbol, Block; Contains, References, Links, ForeignKey) plus Custom(ExtensionId, String). Extensions add kinds without touching core; editors advertise which kinds they open (Contribution Points).
Content is a reference, not bytes. ContentRef::{Text, Blob, Rows, Nested} describes shape and size; Source::fetch gets the body. This is what makes “open a 10 GB folder” or “open a billion-row table” an open, not a load. It also mirrors the old README’s “discourage very large files”.
Deterministic ids for sourced entities. A file’s NodeId is derived from (SourceId, relative path); a row’s from (SourceId, table, primary key). Re-opening yields the same ids with no lookup table, so saved layouts, links and agent citations survive restarts.
Queries, not views. Editors hold the QueryResult of a query and re-run it when the source reports a change (changes_since). The graph editor, the table editor and an LLM tool call all run queries — “display a subgraph” is just “run a narrower query”. (A GraphView with a version watermark was the design until ADR-0015 The core model dropped it.)
Identity: derived, or content-addressed. By default an id is derived from (SourceId, native key). A source whose entities are their structure (Sophia’s declarations and proofs) uses NodeId::from_content(digest): the same structure is the same node everywhere, and names become edges to it.
Two query levels. A structured Query IR every source must support (listing, neighbourhoods, paging, search) so every editor works with every source; and TextQuery { dialect, text } for raw SQL/Cypher/TypeQL. Results from text queries are lifted into nodes/edges using rules the source provides (Data Sources).
Writes are transactions of ops with expected versions. Optimistic concurrency, undo/redo by replay, partial success with Unsupported reasons. Text edits are patches (ADR-0009 Patches not snapshots).
Cross-source edges are owned by the source that stores them; the target may be foreign. This enables “wiki page links to a database row” and is the trickiest consistency problem in the project — see Problem Ranking (R-16).
What the model is not

Not a database. Nothing is persisted by core; sources and the index persist.
Not a CRDT. Versions + patches leave the door open (ADR-0009 Patches not snapshots).
Not yet versioned. Version is a change marker; the append-only entity log that gives nodes and edges a history (added/removed by UUID, with timestamps) is designed in Version Management / ADR-0012 Two histories.
Not typed beyond kinds. Schema (TypeDB types, SQL columns) is exposed as a schema graph in SourceDescriptor, not enforced by core.

Worked example: a Rust crate in a folder













































ThingNode kindEdge to parentsrc/DirectoryContains from crate rootsrc/main.rsFile{Text, lang: rust}Containsfn mainSymbol (from index)Defines from fileApp used in main—References from main symbol to App symboldocs/arch.md with [[main.rs]]PageLinks from page to filea users table in PostgresTableContains from schemathe page also says [[users]]—Links page → table (cross-source)
All of that is one graph; the Graph View draws it, the Table Editor pages through users, and an agent can walk from the doc to the code to the data.

architecture/Indexing.title: Indexing
architecture/Indexing.content:
Crate: index. The index turns files and rows into a graph by deriving what sources don’t know: symbols, links, outlines, embeddings, stack frames. It is exposed as IndexSource, so its output is just more nodes and edges.


                  
                  Index rechecked 2026-10-24 (WP-21/WP-65/WP-22/WP-66) 
                  
                


Extractors: wiki-links and tree-sitter definitions for Rust, Julia and Python. The three languages run through the same dispatch. Definitions have location ids, names, ranged occurrences, lexical containment and provenance; syntactic calls/references/imports resolve unique same-file names and preserve other targets as Unresolved. See Code Graph Schema for exact coverage and limitations. No headings/front matter nodes yet.
Parsing is native tree-sitter through arborium (shared with the Rust code editor, P-113) — not .wasm grammars; the index runs on desktop and the server, and the web/phone query the server’s.
Default storage is memory: graph, BM25 postings (search.rs) and embeddings (brute-force cosine, reciprocal-rank fusion) rebuild on open. Default-off sophia now adds a derived SQLite code store per folder, reused on reopen (below; ADR-0029). No tantivy, usearch or recoco dependency.
Content identities: experimental moonkale-index/content-ids, off by default. Explicit async requests hash normalized Rust/Julia/Python syntax and same-file recursive dependencies; a bounded memory cache and optional state-store adapter are available. Unsupported syntax fails explicitly. No eager workspace hashing or UI activation. See Code Graph Schema for normalizer v7 and its conservative syntax subset.
Rust L1 foundation: default-off lossless-syntax snapshots preserve exact bytes/trivia and return guarded pure patch plans. The separate default-off structural-edits host feature now connects these plans to revision-aware document buffers and graph preview/conflict controls on desktop/web, plus complete same-folder reference-aware Rename via the existing LSP manager (coordinated buffer history, separate per-file saves); see Rust Lossless Syntax and Patches.
LSP as a second extractor and the precision field are not built.
Stack traces live in their own crate, moonkale-trace (TraceSource), not in index::trace.



Sophia folder cache (WP-21, implemented 2026-10-24)
With the default-off sophia feature, opening a folder writes the index’s code
records into .moonkale/code.sophia (SQLite, enforced derived mode). The existing
in-memory index and its search remain available. The extra Sophia Source offers
names, definitions, references, generic Calls, SQL and Sophia queries to the
graph view and agent. It is read-only and declares file truth (ADR-0029).
Only the index’s admitted Rust/Julia/Python code enters it: not hidden or
ignored, under 512 KiB per file; 5,000 walked files and 64 MiB aggregate bound.
Metadata files are read only for naming, never copied into the store. The walk
explicitly excludes .moonkale/; the cache adds its own ignore file.
Reopen hashes text against manifests and skips unchanged code without parsing
or ingesting it. Julia uses the shared module/include resolver; its dependants
are recomputed when needed and only changed manifests are written. Rust uses
nearest Cargo package names and conventional file modules; Python uses package
roots. Nonstandard Rust #[path] / custom target module trees are not inferred
by this first writer. Shared naming and content-id limits remain authoritative.
One watcher debounce window crosses Source::refresh_batch and the server
proxy intact, then becomes one replace_files transaction, including both
sides of a rename. Structured name conflicts add owners with a 16-owner bound;
empty/repeated owners fail visibly. Normalizer mismatch rebuilds the derived
cache. Removing it loses no authored content. Sophia manifest @1 owns facts
and their per-file reference counts, including atomic rollback.
The adapter checks current file hashes on text fetch. Matching definitions use
exact source spans; stale spans fall back to the current whole file and mark
the path stale. No reprinted code is written back. A derived reader reopens
its cache connection per call so it can follow cache recreation. Rebuilding
preserves definition content ids and names; generic nominal ids are allocated
by Sophia and may change. This does not yet make Sophia the default backend
or complete ADR-0029’s release/default gates.
Rust acceptance tests live in packages/services/index/tests/folder_store.rs;
producer/mapping details in packages/services/index/index.md, reader details
in packages/sources/sophia/sources-sophia.md. Reproduce the repository
measurement with cargo run -p moonkale-index --example folder_store --features sophia -- . (native debug; reads current working-tree code).
flowchart LR
  EV[SourceEvent] --> P[pipeline: debounce, prioritise visible]
  P --> PA[parse: tree-sitter wasm grammars]
  PA --> X1[Symbols]
  PA --> X2[WikiLinks]
  PA --> X3[Headings / Frontmatter]
  P --> X4[Imports]
  P --> X5[Embeddings via llm::embed]
  LSP[lsp::graph] --> ST
  X1 & X2 & X3 & X4 & X5 --> ST[(in-memory index)]
  X1 --> SC[(optional Sophia folder cache)]
  SC --> SS[Sophia Source]
  ST --> IS[IndexSource → GraphView]

Decisions

tree-sitter grammars as .wasm — one artefact for desktop, web and mobile; contributed by language extensions (Contribution Points).
Two symbol extractors: tree-sitter (fast, always available, approximate) and LSP (precise, needs a server). Derived edges carry precision; views prefer LSP when both exist.
Incremental by node: a change re-runs extractors for that node only and re-links only its edges. Priority goes to nodes that are visible in some editor.
Storage is native/server: tantivy + usearch don’t target the browser; the web build queries the server’s index. Parsing still runs client-side for highlighting.
Sophia is the persisted code graph and query engine (ADR-0029). Recoco/Thread remain requirements prior art, not pipeline dependencies.

Stack traces and ASTs
index::trace parses rustc/Julia/Go/Python trace formats into Frame nodes with Calls edges, linked to Symbol nodes. A panic in the Terminal becomes a clickable subgraph in the Graph View with a hierarchical layout. Function ASTs are the tree-sitter tree exposed as a GraphView (nodes = syntax nodes) — free once parsing exists.
Embeddings and RAG
See LLM and RAG. Chunking is per symbol / heading / row; vectors are stored locally (usearch) or in the source when it has VECTOR (pgvector, HelixDB). Hybrid search = BM25 (tantivy) ∪ vector, fused.
WP-21 repository measurement (2026-10-24)
Measured on this Linux worktree at master 9bedc5ab plus WP-21, native debug
build, Sophia c3c48e02, fresh cache, owned target/slot and shared benchmark lock. The example reopens the
folder Source and rereads code on both passes; these are folder-store times,
not full UI startup times. Browser servers were stopped for the measurement.





























passtotalwalk/read snapshothash/produce/storestore sizeparsed / replaced / skippedcold build8.830 s0.729 s8.101 s36,704,256 bytes478 / 478 / 0reopen0.664 s0.635 s0.030 s36,704,256 bytes0 / 0 / 478
The snapshot was 6,111,526 source bytes. The cold pass added 4,962 distinct
records, 5,552 names, 3,740 memberships and three generic-call facts. It refused
2,787 definitions outside the conservative normal form and reported 12 ambiguous
named bindings (including conditional SERVICES definitions). Ambiguous names
are omitted rather than arbitrarily choosing a conditional branch; records
remain available. folder_store_report and the index root’s
sophia_refused / sophia_naming_diagnostics properties report such partial
coverage. Timing columns are rounded independently. These are observations, not performance assertions or proof of full
repository/compiler coverage. Evidence: target/next17-measured-final.log.
Verification: all 18 mandatory/feature gate commands passed in
target/next17-verified-gates.log (826 workspace tests, seven ignored;
73 feature-focused tests, including ten folder-store regressions). Browser
sophia-folder, graph, watch and search-trace pass with the feature enabled
on owned port 8117; the renderer suites use Chromium/SwiftShader.
ADR-0029 gate 4: history replay (2026-10-24)
Rerun with the P-231 fix: clean. Sophia 77f5c1c9 (master; the v0.1.1 tag
waits for Daniel) fixes both causes of P-231: duplicate old member ids, and
names changing kind. With the same tool, checker full-digest-v1 and debug
build, both histories show 0 differences at every checkpoint, with no write
or fresh-build errors and no retries:





























repositorycommitsbatch median / p95sum of batch timesfinal store bytesrecords / live factsmoonkale (→ edcf3c86)469122.1 / 932.9 ms119.6 s92,475,39211,536 / 3lenticulum (→ 488ce636)130187.3 / 1089.2 ms49.3 s20,258,8162,775 / 408
Final-checkpoint reads (median / p95 ms): Moonkale lookup 0.009 / 0.010,
text_source 4.78 / 5.95, All(1000) 6180 / 6226; Lenticulum lookup 0.006 / 0.007,
text_source 1.37 / 1.46, All(1000) 128.0 / 128.7. The All(1000) growth is
unchanged by the fix and still unprofiled. Raw reports:
packages/services/index/measurements/history-2026-10-24-{moonkale,lenticulum}-77f5c1c9.jsonl.
The run header now names the Sophia source from Cargo.lock.
The v0.1.0 run below is kept as the evidence for P-231.
First run, Sophia v0.1.0
The opt-in history_replay example runs behind sophia; its shared test helper
also drives the hermetic five-commit CI test. Both real repositories were read
through Git blobs, without checkout or writes to either repository or Sophia’s
checkout. Owned scratch/target directories, the heavy slot and the shared bench
lock were used. Native debug build, Sophia v0.1.0 (c3c48e02), normalizer v7,
Linux, Rust 1.98.1. These are observed timings, not performance assertions.
Compilation/checks were excluded from the measured runs.
Each adjacent tree in reverse topological order is one watcher-shaped
sync_selected window, using the production replace_files/NameClaimed
retry path. The full eligible snapshot supplies dependency/owner recovery.
Only regular Rust/Julia/Python blobs and naming/ignore metadata are materialized;
the ordinary ignore-aware Source walk selects the code. Limits remain 512 KiB
per file, 5,000 walked files and 64 MiB admitted code. Unsupported/hidden/ignored
files, symlinks and internal cache/build directories do not enter the store.
This measures the folder writer, not OS event delivery or full app startup.
Equivalence checks consistency within today’s conservative producer, not full
compiler-level definition/extraction coverage.
At every 50 commits and the end, a separate snapshot/store is built fresh.
Comparison covers full content ids/canonical bytes, actual names, text-source
pointers, file manifests, live generic memberships (including orphan relations),
and facts even on historical record subjects. Immutable historical records,
logs, randomly allocated nominal ids and first-writer display labels are
excluded from equivalence. Record counts below include retained history;
fact counts count actual live facts, not manifest claims. Differences are
reported without repairing or resynchronizing the incremental store.
