kindwhat it isplatformswritestatusFoldera directory on this machine (desktop) or under MOONKALE_ROOT on the server (web)allyes(exists), several at once (exists)Remote foldera directory on another machine reached over SSH, the way Zed does it: Moonkale starts (or connects to) its own server on the remote host and uses it through RemoteSource — so LSP, terminal, git and the index run there, not over sftpdesktop, web (server → server)yesnew; the transport is ssh -L/ssh host moonkale-server + the existing web protocol (ADR-0005 Server functions as the remote backend)Git-host repositoryGitHub / GitLab / Codeberg (Forgejo) by URL. Two levels: browse through the host’s REST API (tree, blobs, commits, issues and PRs as nodes — read-only, no clone), or check out into a cache folder (~/.cache/moonkale/repos/<host>/<owner>/<repo>) which is then a Folder source with git, writable if the token allows pushall (API browse works from the browser too)browse: no; checkout: if permittednew; token is a SecretRefDatabaseSQLite, DuckDB, LadybugDB files (exist); Postgres, Turso, Redis, TypeDB, Helix by connection (stubs)native + via serverper driver and per user choice(exists) for filesAPIinformation behind a REST/GraphQL endpoint — an OpenAPI/GraphQL description lifted into nodes (resources → Table-like nodes, items → rows)allrarelynew; realistically an extension contribution (source in the manifest, see Example - Data Source) with a generic OpenAPI one built in laterIndexderived over the others (exists)allno(exists), spans all open sources
Read-only is a property of the pair (source, project)
Three layers, any of which can say no:

the driver (capabilities.write == false: a DuckDB file, an API browse) (exists);
the credentials (a GitHub token without push, a DB user without INSERT) — reported by the driver at connect time as write: false with a reason;
the user, per project: “treat this source as read-only here” (a production database you only want to look at; someone else’s repository). Stored in the project, shown as a lock, enforced in the editor (no edits, Save disabled), in file operations, and in the agent’s policy (writes refused before they reach the gate).

Explorer roots, tabs and the status bar show the lock; the reason is in the tooltip (“read-only: token has no push permission”).
Open and close individually

Every source can be opened into the project and closed from it without touching the others: Explorer root context menu → Close source; commands source.open.folder, source.open.remote, source.open.repo, source.open.database, source.open.api, source.close (palette (exists)).
Closing a source closes its documents (asking about unsaved ones), drops it from the index and the graph, and — this is the difference from today — keeps it in the project as suspended: listed greyed in the Explorer, reopened with one click, not connected. Remove from project is a second, explicit action. A laptop away from the office keeps its database sources in the project without trying to connect.
The Index always spans exactly the open sources; links across sources resolve (a note in one folder can [[link]] to a file in another, and the Links panel says which source the target is in).

Colours
Each source in a project has an accent colour: chosen by the user or assigned deterministically from a palette (hash of the source id, so it is stable across machines). It appears as a stripe on the Explorer root, on the tab of every document from that source, in the editor’s header line, as a tint on the source’s nodes in the graph, and next to the file name in the status bar. Themes define the palette (eight colours that work on both dark and light backgrounds); the colour never carries meaning beyond “this source” — read-only is the lock, not a colour.
Large roots: a drive, the home folder, /
Someone on Windows opened the whole of E: (P-195). Opening a very large root has to work, but cheaply and honestly:

What stays cheap by design: the Explorer lists one directory at a time; the index stops at 5 000 files; the watcher uses one native recursive watch on Windows and macOS, and has a directory budget elsewhere (past it the source is unwatched, with ↻).
To build:

when the root is a drive root, the filesystem root, or the home folder (or the first listing finds more than a threshold), the Sources panel shows a notice: “a very large folder: the index covers the first 5 000 files, watching is off; open a subfolder for everything”;
per source, an “index this subtree” action for the part someone actually works in;
system folders ($RECYCLE.BIN, System Volume Information) are always skipped.



Projects
What a project stores
// ~/.config/moonkale/projects/<id>.json   (desktop; server: per user under MOONKALE_CONFIG_DIR; mobile: files/projects/)
{
  "version": 1,
  "id": "9f2c…",                       // stable uuid; the file name
  "name": "Moonkale",                  // shown in the selector
  "created": "2026-09-19T20:00:00Z",
  "updated": "2026-09-19T21:10:00Z",
  "origin": "daniel-laptop",           // machine that wrote `updated` (for sync)
  "sources": [
    { "kind": "folder",   "id": "src:folder:…", "path": "${HOME}/Code/Moonkale", "open": true,  "color": "#5b8def", "read_only": false },
    { "kind": "remote",   "id": "…", "host": "build-box", "path": "/srv/moonkale", "open": false, "color": "#e0a84a" },
    { "kind": "repo",     "id": "…", "url": "github.com/DioxusLabs/dioxus", "mode": "browse", "token": { "secret": "github-daniel" }, "read_only": true },
    { "kind": "database", "id": "…", "driver": "postgres", "params": { "host": "db.local", "db": "app", "user": "ro" }, "secret": "pg-app-ro", "open": true, "read_only": true }
  ],
  "layout": "…PanelLayout::encode()…",  // moves here from .moonkale/settings.json
  "open_documents": ["src:folder:…/packages/shell/src/frame.rs"],
  "active_document": "…",
  "settings": { "llm": { "provider": "mistral" } }   // project-scope overrides, same SettingsFile shape
}

Never a secret in the file — SecretRef names only, resolved by the platform keychain/secrets.json/env (exists). Importing a project on another machine therefore asks for the secrets it names, once.
Paths are portable where they can be: ${HOME} and named roots ("roots": { "code": "/home/daniel/Code" } per machine in the user settings, "path": "${code}/Moonkale" in the project). A project written on one machine opens on another after the roots are mapped; unmapped roots are reported, not guessed.
Settings scopes become user < project < folder: the folder’s .moonkale/settings.json (exists) keeps folder-bound things (git, extension permissions granted for that repo); layout and open documents move up to the project, because they describe the set, not one folder. The Default project keeps writing them to the folder so today’s files stay valid.
Window state (size, position) is not project state; presence rooms are per source, as now.

The selector

Titlebar: the project name is a dropdown left of the window title (Moonkale — vault today) listing the projects, most recently used first, with New project…, Import…, Manage…. Palette: project.switch, project.new, project.rename, project.duplicate, project.delete, project.export, project.import. Phone shell: the same list under the Files tile’s header.
Switching saves the current project (layout, documents, source state), closes its sources, opens the target’s, restores its layout. Unsaved documents block the switch with the usual prompt. A window shows exactly one project; a second window may show another (the session channel (exists) keeps them apart by WindowId).
New project starts empty, or from the current sources (“save these as a project”), or from a folder (the folder becomes its first source and the project takes its name).
Manage is a Settings tab: rename, colour per source, read-only toggles, remove, the roots map, and the failures of the last open (below).

Failures are reported, never hidden
Opening a project opens every source marked open and produces a report, one line per source:








































statewhenoffered actionsokconnected—missingfolder or file does not exist (moved, other machine, USB drive)Locate… (rewrites the path, offers to add a root), Suspend (keep in the project, don’t try), RemoveunreachableSSH host, database or API not answeringRetry, SuspendunauthorisedSecretRef not present on this machine, or rejectedEnter secret…, Suspendunsupported herea remote folder on the web client, a native driver on mobileSuspend (it stays for the machines that can)read-only nowconnected, but with fewer rights than the project expectsnone needed — the lock shows, tooltip says why
The project opens with whatever succeeded; the report is a notice in the status bar with Details → the Manage tab, and it is written into the project file as last_open (so the sync target also knows). Nothing is removed from a project by a failure — only the user removes.
Import, export and synchronisation

Export writes the project file as <name>.moonkale-project.json (secrets stripped by construction, paths with ${roots}); import reads one, assigns a new id if it collides, maps roots, asks for the secrets it names, and runs the open report. Drag a project file onto the window or moonkale --project file.json on the command line.
Sync, three tiers, all using the same file:

A synced folder — set projects_dir in user settings to a directory Syncthing/Nextcloud/git already carries. Zero infrastructure. Conflict rule: last updated wins, per file; the loser is kept as <id>.conflict-<origin>.json and the selector shows a conflict badge with a side-by-side (sources added/removed, layout differs).
The hub — the same server that does presence (exists) stores projects per user (/api/projects, bearer token (exists)); the desktop pulls on start and pushes on save; the web client uses it as its only store. Same conflict rule, resolved on the client.
A git repository of projects — tier 1 with history; nothing to build.


What syncs and what does not: the project file syncs; the sources’ data does not (a folder stays on its machine — that is what remote folders and repositories are for); secrets do not; per-machine roots do not; last_open reports carry origin so a stale “missing” from another machine is shown as such.

How this maps onto what exists

Workspace.sources: Signal<Vec<SourceHandle>> (exists) is already the open set; open_folder, attach_source (exist); the Explorer already draws several roots. Missing: close_source, suspended entries, per-source color/read_only, the project file, the selector, the report, the remote/repo/API kinds.
SettingsFile (exists) gains a project scope and the roots map; recent_folders becomes the Default project’s source list.
RemoteSource + the web server (exist) are the remote-folder backend; the new part is launching/tunnelling the server over SSH and treating that connection as a source rather than as “the” server.
Capabilities.write (exists); a read_only override is one field on the handle, checked where Ops are applied (exists) and in the agent policy (exists).
Presence rooms are per folder id (exists) — per source id after this, unchanged in spirit.

The remote-folder source, the desktop as a client of a server, and what each means for credentials and isolation: Remote and Server Modes.
Open questions (to decide in the implementation plan)

Does the Default project write layout to the folder forever, or migrate once a second project exists? (Leaning: write both while Default is the only project.)
Remote folders: start the remote server by SSH (ssh host moonkale --server --stdio) or require it to run already? Zed starts it and installs the binary if missing; that is the better experience and the bigger job.
Git-host browse: which objects become nodes beyond files — issues and PRs are useful for the graph and the agent, but every host API differs; start with the tree and commits.
One index across sources with different ids: the IndexSource already resolves by key; cross-source [[links]] need a precedence rule (same source first, then by project order).
Colour on the phone: a stripe on the tile header is all the room there is.

Not in scope
Real-time merging of edits across machines (CRDT — Collaboration), syncing source contents, a hosted project store beyond the hub, per-project extension installation.

architecture/Publishing-Sources.title: Publishing sources — reader mode, not a static site
architecture/Publishing-Sources.content:
From Prompt18 (2026-09-20), corrected the same day.
The decision
A static Moonkale export (a Quartz-like site of pre-rendered files) is dropped as a goal. Daniel’s argument: replacing Quartz is pointless unless the result does something Quartz cannot — being queryable. Think of someone going through proteomics/metabolomics sources and asking for a lot of data: a static site cannot answer SQL, cannot run a graph query over a database, cannot search anything that was not pre-scored. For text vaults Quartz is already fine and stays. So the value is entirely in the live half, and that half exists: the web server.
What is worth having: reader mode
The web build already is “Moonkale on a website”: the wasm client plus the server holding the sources under MOONKALE_ROOT, with token auth and the jail (Milestone 7 - Implementation Log). Publishing a source means running that server read-only for visitors:

moonkale serve --reader (or MOONKALE_READER=1): every source is opened read_only; no terminal, LSP, agent, git operations, file ops or presence; no login required (or a token for a private audience); the same client in the reader-mode shell (no Save, no write rail entries — 009).
What visitors get that a static site never could: SQL and graph queries against the published SQLite/DuckDB/LadybugDB/Postgres sources (read-only, statement-classified, row/byte caps per request — the existing policy machinery), the graph view over the live index, search (BM25 + embeddings if configured), backlinks, the History panel over the entity log and git history, and — later — plots over any query result. A DuckDB data folder of CSV/Parquet is exactly the proteomics/metabolomics case: visitors query it, they do not download it.
Deep links: /doc/<key>, /node/<id>, /query?… open the corresponding tab; per-visitor layout in localStorage.
Costs and limits, stated: it is a process, not files — hosting, caps per visitor (rows, bytes, query time, concurrent connections), and rate limiting (present for /login, to be generalised). Crawlability: an optional per-document HTML fallback for search engines is the only piece of the static idea worth keeping, and it is small.

Revisited 2026-10-14: a light static reader (way later)


                  
                  Status: an idea for much later, not scheduled 
                  
                

Daniel, 2026-10-14: the full web version stays the web target. A stripped-down web version is wanted, but only way later. Quartz stays for publishing the vault until then. Nothing below is planned work. It records the shape so the idea isn’t lost.


Daniel asked for a lightweight, wiki-like way to browse a GitHub repository or a knowledge graph on a website, read-only, “like Quartz but with some more features reasonable for this deployment”. This would reopen one sentence of the 2026-09-20 decision above: “a static Moonkale export … is dropped as a goal”. The rest of that decision (the full web client, reader mode as the server-backed way to publish) is untouched. The objection then was that a static site cannot answer queries. Two things have changed: the graph engine and the table grid are Rust/wasm components that run in a browser on their own, and small published data can be queried in the browser. So the proposal is two tiers, not one:








































Static reader (new)Reader mode (above)Hostingfiles: GitHub Pages, any CDNa moonkale-server processBuilt bymoonkale publish <source> <out>, run locally or in a GitHub Action—Pagesone pre-rendered HTML page per document, code file and graph node; works without JS, crawlable, fastthe full wasm clientInteractive partsa small wasm reader client, loaded on demandeverything read-onlyQueriesin the browser over published small files (SQLite and DuckDB/Parquet files, the index)any source, any size, with visitor capsLive, private or large data, graph-DB queries, agentsnoyes
What the static reader gives beyond Quartz

Code, not just notes. Every source file is highlighted with the same tree-sitter grammars as the editor. Symbols become anchors, and go-to-definition, references and a per-symbol call graph come from the index built at publish time. A repository reads like a wiki of its own code.
One graph for notes and code, in Moonkale’s engine: the page’s local graph in the sidebar, the whole graph on its own page, and the engine’s layers (folders, kinds, languages) as toggles. The engine scales past where Quartz’s graph view slows down.
Knowledge graphs as pages. A graph source (a LadybugDB, HelixDB or TypeDB export) publishes one page per node: properties, typed edges grouped by kind, and neighbours. Backlinks work across notes, code and nodes.
Tables you can query. A published SQLite or DuckDB file opens in the virtualised grid, with sort and filter, and a SQL box that runs in the browser. It needs a wasm SQL engine (a Rust one to evaluate first: Turso/limbo compiles to wasm; DuckDB’s is JS-wrapped). Big files stay with reader mode.
Diagrams as diagrams: .flow.json files render through the engine with their symbols. Typst, KaTeX and TikZ render to SVG at publish time.
History: per-page “last changed”, and recent commits and authors from git, without a server.
Search: a BM25 index sharded at publish time, loaded on the first query.
Small extras:

deep links to an anchor or a node;
“Open in Moonkale” (moonkale:// or the web app) for readers who want to edit;
English, German and Chinese UI;
light and dark themes.



Weight
The point is lightness.

A page is HTML and one shared CSS file.
The reader client is a separate, small wasm build, with no editors, terminal, agent, LSP or sources, loaded only when the reader opens the graph, a table, or search. The engine’s wasm is about 2.7 MB today; the budget for the whole reader client is a few MB, split so the graph and SQL parts load separately.

Steps, if it is ever scheduled

moonkale publish for a folder: Markdown and code pages, backlinks, the index as JSON, search shards, git metadata.
The reader wasm client: graph view (local and global) and search.
Code navigation from the index (definitions, references, call graph).
Graph-source pages and the table grid with in-browser SQL (after a wasm SQL engine is chosen).
A GitHub Action that publishes a repository to Pages. Whether it could one day replace Quartz for this vault is a question for then; until then the vault stays on Quartz.

Plots and time series in a window (later)
A Plot panel: line / scatter / bar / histogram over a data frame from a query (SQL/DuckDB result, a CSV view, a graph.query result) or a live source (the Lenticulum viewer’s beliefs over time — Julia and Lenticulum). Rendered in Rust (plotters → SVG/canvas in wasm; no JS charting library — JS Interop Boundary). In the app: open a table → Plot…; in reader mode the same panel over the visitor’s query. Time axis, range selector, follow mode for live data.
Steps (when scheduled)

Reader mode flag: read-only sources, capabilities stripped from WorkspaceConfig, reader-mode shell.
Visitor caps and rate limits on /api/* query endpoints; anonymous access option.
Deep links and per-visitor layout.
Optional HTML fallback per document for crawlers.
Plot panel.

architecture/Remote-and-Server-Modes.title: Remote and server modes — SSH, a Moonkale server, collaboration
architecture/Remote-and-Server-Modes.content:
From Daniel’s question (2026-09-20): he works in a browser against code-server on another PC and asks whether Moonkale can do the same — open a remote folder and terminal over SSH like Zed, or run a Moonkale server reached from the desktop app or the web — and what the security considerations are, given an SSH key in ~/.ssh and/or a password for the remote machine. Related: Projects and Sources (remote folder as a source kind), Publishing Sources (reader mode), Collaboration, Milestone 7 - Implementation Log (token auth).
What exists today









































piecestateMoonkale server + web client (the code-server model)✅ packages/web: the client is served by the same process that holds the sources; terminal (PTY), LSP, git, Typst, the agent and wasm extensions run on the server; MOONKALE_ROOT jails every path; MOONKALE_TOKEN gates every request (HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie from /login, or Authorization: Bearer; Secure when behind an HTTPS proxy); /login rate-limited (10/min per address); every /api/* and /mcp request writes an audit line; the server refuses to bind a non-loopback address without a token (guard_bind); COOP/COEP headers for the browser wasm runtimeTLS✅ built in since Milestone 11: MOONKALE_TLS_CERT + MOONKALE_TLS_KEY (PEM, rustls); off loopback the server refuses plain HTTP unless MOONKALE_INSECURE_HTTP=1 says a reverse proxy terminates TLSOrigins and proxiessince 2026-10-07 (audit 7): every /api, /mcp and websocket request from a page must come from this server’s origin — host and port; a reverse proxy whose public origin differs (TLS on 443 in front of :8080) lists it in MOONKALE_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=moon.example. Dev mode (no token) answers only to loopback host names (DNS rebinding). X-Forwarded-For counts only from proxies listed in MOONKALE_TRUSTED_PROXIES (their socket addresses). The cookie is Secure when the server serves TLS or MOONKALE_INSECURE_HTTP=1user accounts / roles❌ one token = one identity; presence names are self-declared (Settings → You)Desktop app as a client of a remote server✅ Milestone 11: MOONKALE_REMOTE=http://host:port + MOONKALE_TOKEN (or a session’s forwarded port) makes the desktop a client of that server for sources, terminal, LSP, git, Typst and wasm extensions (moonkale_server::client); the LLM provider stays localRemote folder over SSH (Zed model)✅ Milestone 11: File → Open Remote Folder… (moonkale-remote) — the system ssh in a terminal tab, the server uploaded once per version into ~/.local/share/moonkale/server/<version>/, started on loopback with a per-session token over stdin, port forwarded, closed with the source. Details in Milestone 11 - Implementation LogStandalone server binary + hardening✅ moonkale-server --port --bind --root --token-stdin --version; MOONKALE_TERMINAL=0 switches the terminal off; cross-origin websocket upgrades refusedCollaborationpresence only (who is here, which file, which line — Milestone 8 - Implementation Log, Milestone 9 - Implementation Log); no shared editing (CRDT deferred, Collaboration)
Usable right now (Milestone 11): File → Open Remote Folder… in the desktop app, or moonkale --ssh "[VAR=v] [ssh options] host:/path" — the host field takes everything you would type after ssh (-p 443, -i key, SSH_AUTH_SOCK=0, aliases). By hand, with nothing but ssh: on the remote machine run the server on loopback (MOONKALE_ROOT=/home/me/Code MOONKALE_TOKEN=… ./moonkale-server --port 8080 — or dx serve --port 8080 in packages/web), then from the laptop ssh -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 host and open http://127.0.0.1:8080. The only credential in play is the SSH key or password already in use; the token is a second lock on the tunnel’s local end. This is exactly the code-server situation, with the same trust model.
The three modes
1. Remote folder and terminal over SSH (Zed’s model) — recommended for one person, two machines
Moonkale on the laptop starts (or connects to) its own server on the remote host through SSH and treats that connection as a source: the folder, the index, LSP, git and the terminal run there, the editor and the UI run here. The desktop app speaks the same server-function protocol it would speak to any Moonkale server, over a port forwarded inside the SSH session.
How it would work:

Transport: the system ssh binary, never a re-implementation. ssh -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -L <local>:127.0.0.1:<remote> host moonkale-server --stdio-or-port …. This inherits ~/.ssh/config (aliases, ProxyJump, IdentityFile), the agent, known_hosts, and password prompts. Moonkale runs ssh in a PTY it owns — the terminal panel already does that — so a passphrase or password prompt appears in Moonkale and is typed by the user; Moonkale never reads, stores or forwards the secret.
The remote binary: Moonkale checks for ~/.local/share/moonkale/server/<version>/moonkale-server on the host, and if missing offers to upload the matching release (checksum verified against the version the desktop was built with — never curl | sh). Zed does the same. The binary runs as the SSH user, binds 127.0.0.1 only, with MOONKALE_ROOT = the chosen folder, and dies with the SSH session.
Identity inside the session: the forwarded port is reachable only from the laptop’s own loopback, but any local process could reach it — so the server still requires a token: Moonkale generates one per session (random, 32 bytes), passes it to the remote through the SSH channel’s environment or stdin (never a command-line argument, which ps shows), and uses it as the bearer. Nothing is written to disk on either side.
What runs where: sources, index, LSP, git, terminal PTY, wasm extensions (wasmtime) — remote. The LLM provider stays local: the agent’s model calls go from the laptop with the laptop’s keys, and its tools reach the remote sources through the source proxy, so API keys never leave the machine that owns them. (A remote-side provider would be a per-source choice, off by default.)
The terminal is a PTY on the remote host as the SSH user — the same shell you would get with plain ssh host, inside Moonkale’s terminal panel; the trace-to-graph feature works unchanged.

Security considerations, specific to this mode:

Credentials: keys stay in ~/.ssh and the agent; a password is typed into the ssh prompt in Moonkale’s PTY and goes straight to ssh. Moonkale adds no credential store for SSH and must not (a stored password in a settings file would be the weakest link on the machine). Recommend keys + agent; passwords work but are typed every time.
Host keys: first connect to an unknown host shows ssh’s own fingerprint prompt in the PTY; Moonkale never passes StrictHostKeyChecking=no. A changed host key is a hard stop, as with plain ssh.
Agent forwarding is not needed and must not be enabled by default (a compromised remote could use the agent).
The remote binary is the trust boundary: it has the SSH user’s rights on that host. Uploading it means running code there — the same trust as pip install on that machine; verify the checksum, keep the version pinned to the desktop’s, keep it under the user’s own home.
Local exposure: the forwarded port on the laptop is loopback-only and token-gated; other users on a shared laptop cannot use the session.
Blast radius: if the laptop is compromised, the attacker has what the SSH user has on the remote — identical to plain SSH; Moonkale does not widen it. If the remote is compromised, the laptop’s secrets (LLM keys, secrets.json) are not on it; only the session token, which dies with the session.
Logging: the remote server’s audit log records the session’s requests; Moonkale’s history (the entity log) lives with the folder, on the remote: in the remote server’s state.sqlite (Persistence::host, Milestone 18 phase 5.10; before that .moonkale/history.jsonl).

2. A Moonkale server on the network (code-server’s model)
The server runs permanently on a host and is reached over the network from a browser (today) or the desktop app (soon). Same process as mode 1, but exposed rather than tunnelled — which is where every consideration comes from:

TLS is mandatory for anything but loopback: the token travels in a cookie/bearer header; without TLS it is readable on the wire. Today: a reverse proxy (Caddy does automatic certificates; nginx with certbot) in front, with X-Forwarded-Proto: https so the cookie gets Secure. Planned: built-in MOONKALE_TLS_CERT / MOONKALE_TLS_KEY (rustls) and a refusal to bind a non-loopback address without either TLS or an explicit MOONKALE_INSECURE_HTTP=1 — the token check alone is not enough.
The token is a shell: whoever has MOONKALE_TOKEN gets the terminal, i.e. a shell as the server’s Unix user, plus every file under MOONKALE_ROOT. Treat it like an SSH private key: ≥ 32 random bytes, never in a URL, never in a shared settings file, rotated if leaked (restart with a new value — sessions are cookies of the token itself, so rotation logs everyone out). A MOONKALE_TERMINAL=0 switch (planned) turns the shell off for servers that are only meant for editing.
Network placement beats every other control: keep the server on a private network — WireGuard or Tailscale between your machines — or behind the SSH tunnel of mode 1. Exposing it to the Internet is possible with TLS + token but is the least defensible option because rate-limited login is the only brute-force protection and there is no lockout, no 2FA, no accounts.
Isolation: one server = one Unix user. Run it under a dedicated user with only the folders it should see (MOONKALE_ROOT), not your login user; systemd ProtectSystem=strict, ProtectHome=tmpfs + BindPaths for the root, NoNewPrivileges, a memory limit, and a private MOONKALE_CONFIG_DIR so extension modules and secrets are separate. Several people → several servers (or mode 3 with accounts).
Secrets on the server: LLM keys live in <config>/secrets.json (0600) or the environment, never in settings.json; the agent’s tool calls run under the policy gate with the audit log; wasm extensions run in wasmtime with per-call permissions. The MCP endpoint has its own token (MOONKALE_MCP_TOKEN) so an external agent’s credential is not the human’s.
Browser hardening already in place: SameSite=Strict + HttpOnly cookie (no CSRF from other sites, no script access), COOP/COEP (isolation), Origin checks on the websocket to add (planned: reject cross-origin Upgrades explicitly).
What the desktop-as-client adds: the desktop app connects with the bearer token stored in the OS keychain (SecretRef, as for LLM keys), pins the server’s certificate on first use (TOFU, shown to the user), and then offers the same panels over the remote sources; its terminal panel is the server’s PTY. The local LLM-keys rule of mode 1 applies.

3. A shared server for several people (what Daniel first imagined)
Several people connect to one server, see each other (presence exists), and eventually edit together. Everything in mode 2 applies, plus the parts that only matter with more than one identity:

Accounts: a users.toml (name, token hash — argon2 — role) under the config dir, or OIDC later for a team that already has an identity provider; /login takes name + token; presence, history (actor), annotations (Annotations) and the audit log carry the authenticated name, not a self-declared one.
Roles: reader (sources, search, graph, history), editor (+ save, file ops, agent under policy), admin (+ terminal, settings, extensions). The terminal is admin-only on a shared server — a shell as the server user is not something to hand to a group.
Per-user policy and secrets: each account’s LLM provider and policy (or none — a shared provider with a shared budget is an admin decision); each account’s approval prompts are its own.
Shared editing: presence today; next the entity log relayed through the hub (every save is an event other windows apply — last writer wins, with the conflict surfaced), then CRDT text merge for simultaneous typing (Collaboration). None of this changes the security model: the hub relays what the roles allow.
Rooms are folders: a user sees the folders their role grants; MOONKALE_ROOT stays the outer jail.

Recommendation

Now (built in Milestone 11): mode 1 — File → Open Remote Folder…; the remote-folder session over the system ssh, the server uploaded once per version, a per-session token, LLM keys local. Mode 2 with the desktop app or a browser behind SSH port forwarding / WireGuard / built-in TLS also works.
Then: accounts + roles — what makes mode 3 exposable. Collaboration proper (shared history, CRDT) after that.

Decided in Milestone 11
The desktop uploads the server binary (Zed’s way; no install step on the host), over the same multiplexed ssh connection; the token travels over stdin (--token-stdin), typed into the PTY with echo off — SendEnv needs AcceptEnv on the host’s sshd, which most hosts do not allow. Still open: the account store format (users.toml vs OIDC first); a checksum on the uploaded binary once releases are signed.

architecture/Rust-Lossless-Syntax-and-Pa.title: Rust Lossless Syntax and Patches
architecture/Rust-Lossless-Syntax-and-Pa.content:
Built, experimental and off by default, 2026-10-16: WP-67 slices 1–5. Implements the foundation of ADR-0028 Files or the graph option B through opt-in graph actions. See Code Graph Schema, Indexing and P-202 Lossless edits must conserve syntax tokens.
Source truth is metadata, not permission
SourceDescriptor.truth: SourceTruth declares Files or Store, serialized as "files"/"store". Missing fields on old descriptors deserialize to Files. Existing source constructors explicitly retain that default, including databases whose external source remains authoritative. Remote descriptors preserve the received value. Store grants no write permission; capabilities.write and the server’s ordinary authority still apply. No existing source is converted to graph-owned storage. Rust callers constructing descriptors must add truth: Default::default(); the library changelog records this breaking struct-literal addition, and no tag is cut here.
Exact syntax snapshot
Native moonkale-index/lossless-syntax is a separate default-off Cargo feature. It reuses the already-added optional BLAKE3 dependency, independently of content-ids. RustSyntaxSnapshot::parse(&str) owns exact source bytes, the tree-sitter tree, full input hash, token ranges, leading-trivia ranges, EOF trivia and top-level function metadata. Comments are trivia rather than lost text. No whitespace, CRLF, BOM, literal spelling or Unicode normalization occurs. print_original() reconstructs bytes from token/trivia partitions, not a pretty-printer.
Every source byte belongs to a token or a trivia gap. Trivia precedes its next token; the final gap belongs to EOF. Function move ownership starts at the previous non-comment top-level item’s end (or after the protected file prefix), so adjacent leading comments and blank lines travel with the function. The syntax range already contains attached doc comments/attributes. A same-line trailing comment and its line terminator also travel. File BOM, shebang and inner attributes stay protected; standalone final comments/whitespace remain file-owned EOF trivia. This is an explicit v1 ownership policy, not an inferred statement about which prose the author intended to move.
The snapshot is an explicit owned working value, not a global cache or persisted copy. Callers schedule parsing outside the UI input path and release snapshots when no longer needed. Input/output are capped at 512 KiB; tree walking is capped at 200,000 nodes and depth 128, with a two-second parser progress deadline. Parsing errors or limit exhaustion are typed failures.
Pure plans
use moonkale_index::lossless::RustSyntaxSnapshot;
let syntax = RustSyntaxSnapshot::parse(text)?;
let rename = syntax.plan_declaration_rename(0, "new_name")?;
let proposed = rename.apply_to(text)?;
let move_before_first = syntax.plan_move_function(1, Some(0))?;

Declaration rename changes exactly the selected top-level function’s name token. It does not update calls, imports, macro text or other files, and must not be presented as semantic Rename. Names are checked with a parser probe and the Rust Reference’s strict/reserved/raw restrictions; the conservative policy rejects reserved words from every edition. Source spelling and normalization are retained. Name requests are at most 256 UTF-8 bytes. See keywords and identifiers.
Move function reorders a top-level function before another function’s owned range, or before file-owned EOF trivia with before=None. It produces a deletion and insertion against the original byte coordinates, without adding separators or formatting. No-ops return an empty plan. Cross-file moves, nested item moves, reference updates and compiler semantic checks are not implemented.
RustEditPlan exposes read-only input_hash() and edits(). Each RustTextEdit has a UTF-8 byte range, expected removed text and inserted text. Its apply_to(current) checks the exact input hash, all boundaries, expected text, overlap and final size before constructing output right-to-left. Stale text is rejected, not rebased automatically. Output limits count the final size, so an equal-size move at the cap is valid.
Planned output is reparsed and must retain the function count. Moves additionally preserve the complete multiset of terminal token kind/spelling pairs. Grammar validity alone is insufficient: an unterminated EOF line comment can swallow another item while leaving a valid parse. Such placements return InvalidPlacement. No unsafe partial plan is returned.

Neither planning nor apply_to writes a file, edits a Workspace buffer, changes revisions/history, saves or refreshes the index. The returned String is a proposed result; the explicit document adapter below performs the separate in-memory commit. SyntaxEditError distinguishes invalid names/functions/ranges, overlap, stale input, invalid placement, malformed syntax and limits.
Revision-aware document adapter
Workspace::document_edit_base(node) captures an already-open document’s unsaved text, editor revision, source version, generational document/session handles and source instance. It supports writable Files sources only; Store ownership is not implemented by this adapter. A stale editor mirror returns Changed instead of overwriting the canonical buffer. Capture on the UI thread, clone the snapshot text for background syntax planning, then return byte edits to the UI thread:
let base = ws.document_edit_base(node)?;
let syntax = RustSyntaxSnapshot::parse(&base.snapshot().text)?;
let plan = syntax.plan_declaration_rename(0, "new_name")?;
plan.apply_to(&base.snapshot().text)?; // verify the syntax plan's exact input
let proposal = base.propose(plan.edits().iter().map(|edit| TextChange {
    range: edit.range.clone(),
    removed_text: edit.removed_text.clone(),
    inserted_text: edit.inserted_text.clone(),
}).collect())?;
// Present proposal.base().text and proposal.preview() as plain data.
let committed = proposal.apply(ws)?; // no save
workspace::proposals is engine-neutral; it depends on the existing TextChange/EditBatch contract, not the index/parser. A native-only development dependency tests this exact bridge with real Rust plans. Normal builds and wasm do not acquire the parser dependency through ext-api.
propose validates ranges, expected removed bytes, UTF-8 and overlap in a disposable editor session before exposing a preview. Base/output are capped at 512 KiB, edits at 4,096, and total removed/inserted payload at 1 MiB. apply rechecks source instance and Files/write capability, document/session identity, source version, editor revision, canonical text and editor text before a synchronous commit. Even a close/reopen or edit/undo returning identical bytes cannot accept the old proposal. Invalid or conflicting application changes no buffer/history. A successful edit is one ordinary undo entry, retains current live selection rebased in UTF-16, and marks the document dirty through the existing text/saved comparison. A no-op creates no history entry. Other editor views observe the same session and canonical document.
Conflicts are typed (Closed, UnsupportedSource, Changed, LimitExceeded, Invalid). apply(&self, ...) retains the base and preview on failure: a consumer can compare those with the current document, discard the proposal by dropping it, or capture a new base and rerun the planner. Old ranges are never automatically rebased. The backing source is not fetched or written during application; external file changes remain the responsibility of the ordinary version-checked Workspace::save. Its SourceError::Conflict leaves the proposed buffer dirty and undoable. The optional graph UI below consumes this contract.
Evidence and the next slice
Tests cover byte-exact Rust corpus reconstruction (including real project source), Unicode/CRLF name-token edits, leading docs/attributes and trailing comment ownership, file-prefix protection, no-ops, stale input, invalid UTF-8 and overlapping edits, invalid names, deep/oversized inputs, a near-limit backward move, and EOF-comment token loss. Descriptor tests cover legacy JSON defaults, both values and remote Store preservation without write capability.
CI runs both experimental index features alongside the feature-off workspace checks. The final handoff records the exact gate/browser evidence. No new dependency or graph-render bundle change is introduced by this slice.
WP-67 remains conservative and experimental. Graph controls and explicit conflict presentation are now implemented behind structural-edits; reference-aware rename now uses complete same-folder rust-analyzer plans with coordinated buffer history and explicit per-file saves; cross-file move remains unimplemented. Source transactions permit partial success, so saving is never a disk-wide transaction. No autosave, mode/default flip, multi-file atomicity or semantic-equivalence guarantee is claimed here.
Document-adapter integration tests additionally cover real Rust declaration edits and moves, exact Unicode/CRLF output, live selection, one-step undo/redo, revision ABA, close/reopen ABA, source replacement, permission/truth changes, canonical-buffer drift, source-version changes, malformed/overlapping edits, bounds, no-op history and a failed save followed by explicit recomputation. See P-204 Structural proposals must retain document identity.
Experimental graph controls (slice 3)
Build desktop or web with --features structural-edits (web’s server and wasm client must both enable it). The feature is forwarded through distribution to the graph panel and through the app to the planner service. Default builds expose neither controls nor planner endpoint. No renderer bundle changes or new default setting are required; dragging remains graph layout only.
Select one Rust function definition in the graph and choose Edit Rust function (experimental). The panel offers Change declaration name, Rename with references and Move function, with a same-file Move before selector or End of file. The declaration-name action changes only a declaration token; the separate Rename action uses the language server. The source file is resolved using the selected node’s own index and Defines edge, then loaded in the background without replacing unsaved edits. Old index provenance/ranges preselect a function only when they match the captured input; otherwise choose a function from the freshly parsed snapshot. Only top-level functions returned by the planner can be edited.
Preview renders original/proposed text as plain escaped source with exact replacement ranges highlighted. Apply uses the existing proposal adapter, creates one undo entry and leaves the buffer unsaved. Open its normal source tab to undo/redo or save. Discard drops review state without changing a document. Conflict retains original/proposed text alongside current text, disables Apply and requires Recompute followed by an explicit fresh function/destination choice and another preview. Completed review state survives panel remounts in Workspace-owned signals. Selection changes or dismissal invalidate pending work; snapshot validation rejects responses after document edits, session replacement or closure.
ext-api::structural defines the pure protocol and optional StructuralPlanner service. Function handles include the entire input digest and syntax range; they cannot be reused on another snapshot. Desktop uses local blocking workers; web uses POST /api/structural/plan behind the existing auth/origin gate. The endpoint is content-only: no paths, source lookup, code execution or file writes. The auth middleware caps the request body at 4 MiB before deserialization; decoded source is at most 512 KiB, functions/edits at most 4096, combined edit payload at most 1 MiB, and at most two parser jobs run per process with immediate Busy rejection. Existing tree-sitter size/depth/work/time limits apply. UI errors are localized categories rather than raw source/parser output.
See P-205 Graph previews must reject stale asynchronous results. The browser suite structural-edits requires the feature-enabled server/client build and exercises the real graph renderer, remote planner and native editor together.
CodeMirror retains its own undo stack. When it emits a change, any existing Rust
revision mirror adopts the canonical text, invalidating outstanding proposals;
an unchanged echo of an applied Workspace edit preserves the Rust history.
Both backends are exercised by the structural browser workflow. Save completion
records exactly the submitted snapshot, so later edits remain dirty while the
source write is pending (P-206 Save completion must acknowledge submitted text).
The Graph review remains visible after attaching a previously unopened source tab.
CodeMirror Workspace replacements use isolated undo boundaries and widen their
common-prefix/suffix diff over complete UTF-16 surrogate pairs and CRLF.
Protocol probes cover both surrogate boundaries, and the graph workflow renames
supplementary-plane Rust identifiers end to end (P-207 CodeMirror external edits must preserve UTF-16 boundaries).
Reference-aware graph rename (slices 4–5)
Rename with references uses the shared rust-analyzer connection on desktop
and web. The pure lossless planner first validates the snapshot-bound function
and requested identifier. Code-view converts the declaration byte offset to
UTF-16 and synchronizes open unsaved buffers. A discovery request identifies
files; targets load in the background without replacing unsaved buffers or
changing focus. A second authoritative request runs against captured bases. A
new target in that response requires Recompute, never a partial application.
Startup retains the manager’s 30-second timeout; each rename request is limited
to five seconds. Resource operations and targets outside the originating writable
folder source are refused in full. This is rename under the server’s current
project configuration, not proof of completeness across generated/disabled code.
Every target uses the existing Unicode/CRLF-safe range converter and checks
source/document/session identity, exact text/revision and backing version. Open
resolver buffers and the language-server connection/version remain guarded
through preview and Apply. Duplicate path aliases, overlaps and malformed
ranges are refused. Limits are 64 files, 4096 edits, 4 MiB aggregate edit
payload and 8 MiB combined original/proposed text, with the existing per-file
512 KiB input/output and 1 MiB edit payload limits. No new dependency, server
endpoint or compiler launcher is introduced.
MultiDocumentEditProposal composes immutable per-file proposals. Preview shows
each file’s original/proposed text and retains it on conflict. Apply prepares
CodeMirror views under a five-second barrier, then validates and stages all
buffer/history results before one synchronous commit. There are no awaits or
fallible edits between canonical assignments. Apply never writes a source.
Cancellation, input revision/sequence stamps and held views prevent queued input
from overwriting the committed group.
Undo rename / Redo rename, keyboard Ctrl+Z/Y and the Edit menu use the same
coordinator in both editors. Any newer edit in any participant blocks the whole
group until that local history is restored. No inverse patch is rebased over
newer work. CodeMirror history, including opaque group effects, survives panel
remounts for the open document’s lifetime; closing/reopening or switching editor
implementation retires affected groups. The coordinator retains at most 32
groups / 32 MiB. Unknown/retired markers block instead of falling back to a
single-file undo. Lost commit acknowledgements retire history and resynchronize
held views to canonical buffers; already committed buffers remain complete.
Save affected files is separate: it uses normal Workspace saves for only the
reviewed text, skips newer buffers, continues after failures and reports Saved,
Already saved, Changed, Closed, Read only, Conflict or Failed per file. Successful
writes are never automatically rolled back. Group undo/redo always changes
buffers only, including after partial saving; dirty flags compare against each
file’s actual saved text. No cross-file move or disk-wide atomicity is claimed.
graph-rename runs against a real Rust crate and rust-analyzer in both editors:
unsaved calls, recursion, comments, shadowing, exact CRLF, two-file preview,
Apply, separate saves, newer-edit blocking and undo from either document. Injected responses verify that a new authoritative target or an outside-folder target refuses the whole plan.
group-history verifies CodeMirror’s public protocol against the committed
bundle: non-mutating history probes, menu/keyboard routing, retained group
effects across remounts, held input, token isolation and redo. Core tests cover
all-buffer refusal, guarded history and partial-save behavior.
See P-208 Graph rename must refuse incomplete file subsets and
P-210 Multi-document rename needs coordinated history.

architecture/Security.title: Security — the trust model and the security document
architecture/Security.content:
Purpose (Daniel, 2026-10-14): much of Moonkale runs internally today, so security isn’t the priority yet. But a document should lay out the security of the whole project (how secrets are managed, whether it is safe from exploits and prompt injection, whether its connections are safe), and Moonkale should never reach the point where a large share of its issues are security issues. So this page is two things:

the skeleton of that document, filled in where the facts exist and marked to write where they don’t;
the rules every change follows from now on (at the end), so the debt doesn’t grow while the document waits.

The pieces are described where they were built (Remote and Server Modes, LLM and RAG, Extension System, Agent Sessions and Profiles); this page puts them side by side. The open findings of the external audit are in Audit 2026-09-23.


                  
                  State on 2026-10-01 
                  
                

Moonkale is a prototype. Eleven of the twenty audit issues are security findings; the structural part of #1, #4 and #8 is fixed on the refactor branch (Milestone 18 phase 4.5: the server and the user decide, not a client or a folder), the rest are open. Run a server only on loopback, behind SSH, or on a private network (WireGuard, Tailscale) until they are fixed.


Boundaries

































































boundarywhat is trustedenforced bywhere in the codeServer ↔ browser/desktop clientwhoever holds MOONKALE_TOKEN gets every file under MOONKALE_ROOT and, unless MOONKALE_TERMINAL=0, a shell as the server’s usercookie (HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict) or Authorization: Bearer; /login rate-limited; non-loopback bind refused without a token (guard_bind); TLS built in (MOONKALE_TLS_CERT/_KEY), plain HTTP off loopback refused unless MOONKALE_INSECURE_HTTP=1; Origin check on websocket upgrades; COOP/COEPserver/src/auth.rs, web/src/main.rsExternal agents (MCP)a separate bearer, MOONKALE_MCP_TOKENserver/src/mcp.rs—Pathseverything below MOONKALE_ROOT (server) or the opened folder (desktop)canonicalisation in moonkale_server::open_any, relative keys in project-fssymlinks and Windows paths escape it (#5)Secretsnames in settings, values neverresolved from MOONKALE_SECRET_<NAME>, the provider’s usual variable, or <config>/moonkale/secrets.json (mode 600); web clients never see a valuellm/src/secrets.rs; an OS keychain (keyring) is planned, not builtThe agenta model that may propose any tool callthe policy gate: reads allowed, writes ask, destructive always ask; SQL statements classified; every call in the audit logllm/src/policy.rs, core/src/source/risk.rs (Source::classify, overridable per source since Milestone 18); Cypher is a keyword scan, and LadybugDB runs any statement on its read-only database (#9)Extensions (wasm)a module with the permissions the user grantedJSON ABI v1: every host call checked against the grant; grants come from the user scope only (a folder cannot grant, Milestone 18 phase 4.5); an id belongs to the file that loaded it first, so a folder’s module cannot squat a user-installed module’s id and grantsext-host; fuel per call (50 M for the manifest, 5 G per command run) and 256 MB of linear memory per instance, each call in a fresh store (audit #4)Extensions (static)compiled in; trusted like the rest of the binarythe tier (core/optional/opt_in) only decides what is on; the distribution’s Cargo features decide what is in the binarymoonkale_distribution::default_extensions()A folder’s own settings.moonkale/settings.json of a folder you open — data, not authority (Milestone 18 phase 4.5)SettingsFile::without_authority before the merge: no language model or agent, no auto-approved writes, no embeddings switched on, no grants, no shell, no SSH hosts; it may switch things off and deny tools (added to the user’s denials). Settings shows what was ignoredext-api/src/settings.rs; test a_folder_has_no_authoritySSH remote foldersthe system ssh and the user’s keys; Moonkale never sees a passwordthe server binary uploaded per version, a per-session token typed over stdin with echo off, loopback-only portremote/src/session.rs; temp names and the control socket (#18); the remote server is not checksummed yet
Assets and adversaries (to write in full)


What is worth protecting:

the user’s files and databases (confidentiality and integrity);
secrets (API keys, database passwords, SSH keys, which Moonkale never holds, and tokens);
the machine itself, since a terminal, LSP or agent can run code;
the user’s session state and history;
licensed data (market data, whose republishing Trading with Databento rules out).



Who might attack:

a file or repository the user opens: malicious content, settings or extensions;
content an agent reads: prompt injection;
a network peer: the server’s clients, an SSH host, a presence hub, an MCP client;
a dependency or a release artefact: the supply chain;
a co-tenant on a shared server.

Not in scope: an attacker with the user’s own OS account.


Secrets
Today:

Only names are in settings, sessions and documents, never values.
Values come from the environment (MOONKALE_SECRET_<NAME>, a provider’s usual variable) or <config>/moonkale/secrets.json (mode 600).
Web clients never see a value; the server resolves names for them, and only toward allowed endpoints (the LLM relay below).

To build:

the OS keychain (keyring): Secret Service, Keychain, Credential Manager; Android Keystore;
secrets scoped to a source or a session, not only global;
redaction of secret values in logs, transcripts and history;
a rotation story.

To write: a diagram of where each kind of secret lives on each platform.
Connections













































ConnectionTodayGapsClient ↔ server (web, desktop as client, phone)a token as an HttpOnly cookie or bearer; TLS built in; plain HTTP off loopback refused; /login rate-limitedaccounts and roles; a CSP; generalised rate limits; #20 (the batch of low findings)Desktop ↔ remote folder (SSH)the system ssh and the user’s keys; a per-session token over stdin; a loopback-only port#18: control socket in shared /tmp, port hijack, fixed upload temp name, unchecksummed server binaryMoonkale ↔ databasesdrivers in-process; read-only opens; statement classificationper-source credentials through secrets; TLS for remote databases (Postgres, D1, Databento) checked, not optionalMoonkale ↔ LLM providersthe server decides endpoints (MOONKALE_LLM_ENDPOINTS); the client sends only namesprovider TLS pinning not planned; request logging must redactExternal agents ↔ Moonkale (MCP)a separate bearer (MOONKALE_MCP_TOKEN)scopes per token (read-only, one source)Presence hub—#20 (presence impersonation)Language servers, adapters, toolchainsspawned from discovery, never from a client valuethe planned language-server and debug-adapter contribution points (KG-05, DBG) must keep that rule
Prompt injection
The threat: an agent reads files, web pages, database rows, issue text and tool output. Any of it can contain instructions (“ignore your rules, run this”). Models follow such text sometimes, so content can never be trusted to stay data.
Today:

The policy gate: reads are allowed, writes ask, destructive calls always ask, and SQL statements are classified.
A folder can’t grant permissions: it cannot switch on an agent, auto-approve writes or name a shell.
Every tool call is in the audit log.

To build:

Provenance in the context: tool output and file content enter the model’s context marked as data from , never as instructions, and the UI shows which part of a proposal came from where.
Egress control: an agent cannot send content to a URL it found in content without the user seeing the destination.
No chaining past the gate: a read result can’t trigger a write that skips approval, even through an MCP tool.
Separate trust for external MCP servers’ tools, by default lower than built-in ones.
A test suite of injection fixtures (files, rows and pages carrying instructions) that the agent must not follow.

Untrusted content and exploits
Moonkale renders and parses what it opens: Markdown (HTML inside it, KaTeX, Typst, Mermaid, TikZ), images and SVG, notebooks, flow documents, database files, RDF, DBN. Today:


path jail (#5 open for symlinks and Windows paths);


link-scheme allow-list (#10);


bounded buffers (#14);


folder settings without authority.


Built — fuzzing (WP-47, 2026-10-17): fuzz/ compiles the production math range parser and Flow::parse directly. Separate nightly CI jobs run each for 60 seconds with 64 KiB inputs, a 10-second per-input timeout and 2 GiB RSS limit; failures are non-blocking and crash inputs are uploaded for regression tests. The planned WP-36 delimiter normaliser does not exist yet; it and the wasm ABI JSON still need targets;


Parser crash containment (P-212, 2026-10-17): Markdown presentation rejects NUL, vertical tab and form feed before pulldown-cmark construction, retaining original source on desktop and abort-profile wasm. Unwind builds also catch complete parse failures and discard partial results. Diagnostics are fixed, content-free text; rejected controls log once per process. Stable regressions exercise math, block/list/table/callout/image preview, wiki projection/hover/heading lookup, native front matter, documentation and agent messages; four corpus seeds retain the first CI crash and minimized variants. No parser upgrade is available; upstream #1129 remains open. This prevents the known crash family on abort builds, not arbitrary future parser panics. See P-212 Markdown offset iterator can panic.


To build:

a Content-Security-Policy for the web client and the webviews;
HTML sanitising in the Markdown renderers, one allow-list;
SVG sanitising (no scripts, no external references);
resource limits for every renderer (Typst compile time, image size, Mermaid in a worker);
#15 (project-fs races: data loss).

Extensions and the supply chain
Extensions:

Static ones are compiled in and trusted like the binary. The distribution’s features decide what’s included.
Wasm modules get only the permissions the user granted, and grants come from the user scope only. They run with fuel (50 M units for the manifest, 5 G per command run) and 256 MB of linear memory per instance, each call in a fresh store, so a trap or an exhausted budget is an error for that call only. (This page said otherwise until 2026-10-14; ext-host/src/runtime.rs has had the limits since audit #4.) To build: a signed manifest for “Install from URL”.

Dependencies:

Enforced in CI (WP-47, 2026-10-17): tools/check-security.py rust runs pinned cargo-deny 0.20.2 (all workspace features/platforms, licences, RustSec, sources; duplicate versions warn) and cargo-audit 0.22.2 against Cargo.lock. New vulnerabilities, informational advisories and yanked crates fail the job. Both read one dated exception list in deny.toml: 25 existing vulnerabilities, 12 informational advisories and yanked yoke-derive 0.8.3 are deferred for Daniel’s upgrade decision, not fixed. No dependency versions were changed. The HelixDB helix-metrics AGPL-3.0 exception records existing licence obligations; it does not approve adding AGPL code. Missing HelixDB crate licence metadata is clarified from its pinned root Apache-2.0 LICENSE; local Moonkale crate metadata inherits the existing MIT workspace licence.
JS: tools/check-security.py js discovers every tracked npm/pnpm/yarn lockfile (and unignored local additions), audits npm production dependencies without installs/scripts, and fails on new high/critical advisories or registry errors. An unsupported lockfile format fails pending a pinned auditor. Six npm lockfiles are covered: CodeMirror, KaTeX, Milkdown, wasm-host, xterm and Quartz. tools/npm-audit-exceptions.json records 53 existing package/advisory pairs in Milkdown and Quartz with URLs, exact locked versions, dates and reasons; lower severities are reported too. The e2e environment has no committed lockfile: its existing runtime-created npm lock is audited immediately after installation. That install remains unpinned and needs a separately reviewed lockfile; no versions were upgraded in this work.
Vendored bytes: tools/check-vendored.py is an offline blocking check of all 63 files under packages/ext-api/assets/katex/ and any vendor/ directory. tools/vendored-assets.json records SHA-256 per file, upstream versions/URLs and local patch provenance; additions, removals and changes fail until explicitly reviewed. KaTeX 0.18.7’s 20 woff2 fonts match upstream, and its CSS matches after removing unused woff/truetype fallback URLs. The upstream tarball SHA-256 is recorded. The Rust forks intentionally include the patches documented beside them, so their reviewed local hashes are not represented as pristine upstream hashes. CI does not download vendored assets.
Local checks: python3 tools/check-security.py rust (install the pinned tools first), python3 tools/check-security.py js, python3 tools/check-vendored.py, python3 tools/test-security.py. A writable RustSec cache can be supplied with --db-root <directory>; registry/advisory fetch failures fail closed. Only the checksum check and gate regression tests are fully offline. Updating a dependency requires revisiting its exceptions; never regenerate a baseline to hide a new finding.

Releases:

To build: signed artefacts and published checksums, and a checksum for the server binary the SSH path uploads (#18).

Data at rest

What is stored: the state store (state.sqlite: settings, sessions (ADR-0025), layouts, the entity log, agent transcripts), caches (.moonkale/cache/, downloaded market data), and the index.
To decide:

encryption at rest for transcripts and history (they may hold pasted secrets: redaction first);
file permissions on every platform;
what export and session bundles may contain (never secrets, never licensed data marked non-redistributable).



The LLM relay (server)
Since Milestone 18 phase 4.5 the server decides what a client’s provider settings may make it do (moonkale_server::llm::server_side, audit #1): the client picks the kind, the model and the secret’s name; a secret goes only to the provider’s built-in endpoint or one the operator listed in MOONKALE_LLM_ENDPOINTS (comma-separated URL prefixes), and claude-code runs MOONKALE_CLAUDE_BIN or claude on the server’s PATH, never a path from the client. A refusal reaches the client as an error, not a silent fallback.
Rules that follow from the audit

The server decides. Anything that turns into a process, a network request with a secret, or a permission is resolved from the server’s own settings, never from a value the client sends (#1, #4, #8). This is the main design input to phase 4 of Milestone 18 - Library Refactor.
The workspace scope is data, not authority. A folder may choose a theme, a layout or an editor; it may not name a command to run, grant a permission or point a secret at an endpoint (#8).
Read-only means read-only for the engine too. A driver opened “read-only” must also be unable to read outside its file (#2: DuckDB’s read_csv, glob).
Every buffer has a bound (#14), every path goes through one jail function (#5), every link scheme through one allow-list (#10).

Status by area (to keep current)


















































AreaStateOpenServer boundary◐ token, TLS, loopback guardaccounts, CSP, #20Secrets◐ names only, env and filekeychain, redactionSSH remote◐#18Agent and prompt injection◐ gate, classification, audit logprovenance, egress, injection testsUntrusted content◐ jail, link allow-list, bounds; P-218 Rich images share native-preview source scoping, image limits and bounded cache, with display-only URLs and blocked remote/escaping destinations; default-off content normalizer has byte/work/parser limits; the Rust lossless planner also retains its depth limit, exact-input guards and move-token checks; single-document proposals recheck Files/write capability, source/session identity, backing version and exact live revision/text before one bounded in-memory batch (WP-66/67); content caches are bounded/checksummed; opt-in structural planning is pure, authenticated on web, capped at 4 MiB raw/512 KiB decoded input, two non-queued workers, and existing parser limits; source bytes are never logged or rendered as HTML; graph Rename reuses the existing LSP connection, rejects cross-source/resource operations and incomplete plans; two-pass target preparation, 64-file/4096-edit/4-MiB-payload/8-MiB-text caps, all-buffer staging and held/stamped editor input guard grouped history; explicit per-file saves report partial success; validates URI/range/version bounds and live identities before preview#5, sanitising, CSP, fuzzing, #15Wasm extensions◐ permissions, fuel, memory limitssigningSupply chain and releases◐ WP-47: blocking Rust/npm audits with dated baseline exceptions, offline vendored hashes; non-blocking parser fuzz smoke jobsdependency upgrades, signing, release/SSH server checksums, wasm ABI fuzzingData at rest○redaction, encryption decision
Legend: ◐ partly, ○ not started. Open GitHub issues today: #15, #18, #20.
Rules for every change (from 2026-10-14)
They keep the debt from growing until the full document and a review exist. Each is one line in a review:

The server decides what becomes a process, a network request with a secret, or a permission (rule 1 above), and so do new contribution points (language servers, debug adapters, runners).
No secret values in settings, sessions, documents, logs, transcripts, test fixtures or error messages; names only.
Content is data: anything read from a file, a row, a page or tool output never becomes an instruction, a command line, a URL with a secret, or an approval.
Every parser of untrusted input has a bound (size, time, depth), and every new one gets a fuzz target before it ships enabled by default. WP-47 adds the first two nightly CI smoke targets with resource limits; this does not establish production bounds for every existing parser. Retain each crash as a regression in its normal crate tests before fixing it (How to Write Tests).
Every new connection has TLS off loopback, authenticates, and says in this page’s table what it trusts.
Every new dependency passes the blocking Rust/JS security jobs above and has a reason in its commit. New CI tool installs have pinned versions; new actions have reviewed commit SHAs. Exceptions need an advisory ID (or exact yanked crate/version), date and reason; upgrades and licence decisions stay with Daniel.
A security-relevant change updates this page (the table above), and a found weakness is a GitHub issue labelled security, never only a comment.

Not built
Accounts and roles for a shared server (design in Remote and Server Modes); a Content-Security-Policy; signed releases and a checksum for the uploaded remote server; an OS keychain.
Browser CI startup diagnostics contain only the owned process group’s executable names, process state, disk availability and progress timestamps. No environment or process argument dump is taken. Servers launch in a dedicated session; cleanup checks the recorded PID birth identity and signals only that process group, including orphaned descendants (P-209). Build logs/screenshots are retained for seven days.
WP-69 preview performance fixes retain at most three folding parser/tree/source entries per thread (one latest document per supported grammar). Incremental edits align byte endpoints to UTF-8 boundaries; switching documents is diffed against the exact retained source. The cache is derived editor state and adds no evaluation, file access, network authority, dependency or persistence.
Markdown highlighting may reuse captures for ASCII alphanumeric appends at EOF only when the unchanged prefix matches exactly, the last nonempty line is bounded to 4096 bytes of plain ASCII prose, and no retained capture touches that tail. Other edits parse normally, including syntax changes after retained appends. Canonical source always updates; parser/structure providers still receive it. Fresh-parser comparisons cover syntax, Unicode and earlier edits after a retained tail.
WP-23 (2026-10-17, review corrected) separates cheap folder query metadata hints from content save preconditions. Listings (Children, ls, Node, path, Neighbours) never open file contents; Unix hints include device/inode/ctime as well as mtime/length. Only content reads and known written text produce BLAKE3-based Version(u64) tokens, which are opaque and not cryptographic identities. Workspace state/history/settings writes fetch first and refuse failed reads; document/proposal preconditions already come from fetched text. Image freshness compares query hints with query hints. Fetch/save reads remain capped for growing files, special-file content is refused, and neighbourhoods cap nodes, entry collection and depth. Native rename exclusion on Linux/Android/macOS/Windows refuses unsupported operations; other platforms retain check-then-rename. Saves hold an OS file lock through handle revalidation and pathname identity checks. Unix writers ignoring advisory locks can still race after the final check (#15); parent/symlink swaps remain #5. No security issue is declared closed. Existing transitive BLAKE3 and same-file become direct dependencies for content hashes and portable identity checks. Index failures publish only a fixed content-free file diagnostic and clear stale derived/search data; no contents or OS error text are logged.
WP-18 Unison (2026-10-17), default-off: only the operator’s MOONKALE_UCM/PATH selects an executable. A direct argument-vector spawn owns a loopback-only UCM 1.5 HTTP server with a fresh random token; proxying and redirects are disabled, no remote endpoints/Share commands or shell are exposed, and no token/process output is logged. Hash-only definition display avoids UCM’s named attached-documentation evaluation path. The source submits only fixed read API routes. UCM itself may acquire its codebase lock and perform migrations/maintenance; Moonkale’s read-only capabilities do not make UCM a read-only SQLite engine. Snapshot limits are 4,096 nodes / 65,536 edges / 64 namespace levels / 16 MiB aggregate successful API bytes / 16,384 requests / 60 seconds overall / five seconds per request / ten seconds startup, with serde_json recursion limits. An RAII guard kills/reaps UCM on completion/error; cancellation’s blocking task remains bounded. Branch hash changes reject publication. No source text becomes HTML, a command or a URL authority. Existing reqwest (blocking, no default/TLS features), serde_json, Tokio and UUID crates provide loopback reads, bounded parsing, worker isolation and random tokens. Tests create bundled-only transcript fixtures and stop their own UCMs. See packages/sources/unison/sources-unison.md for limits and the per-branch snapshot/port-reservation limitations.
Pre-existing symlinks in .unison, v2 and UCM’s SQLite/lock files are refused. This is a pre-spawn check, not OS process confinement: concurrent pathname replacement remains the existing #5 boundary.
WP-26 portable CI (2026-10-17) uses SHA-pinned actions, read-only repository
permissions, OS/architecture-specific Rust caches and a 45-minute job timeout.
Windows/macOS tests start advisory; the existing blocking security gates remain
in force. No secrets, publishing or deployment permissions are supplied. Native
symlink fixture coverage remains Unix-only; Windows path jail checks run without
requiring elevated symlink privileges. See How to Write Tests for coverage.
P-224 graph transport keeps the existing serde JSON parser/wire format: the
panel sends its graph as a serde-escaped string through Eval::send, and the
view passes the string directly to the renderer. No graph text becomes script,
HTML or a URL. Numeric load profiling records timings only, never node contents.
The two renderer regression suites serve only the two committed engine files
from an ephemeral loopback test server with exact route matching and cleanup;
no production connection, dependency or parser is added.
P-218 Rich images reuse native-preview source resolution, path normalization,
image classification, byte/pixel limits, freshness checks, a two-reader queue
and bounded workspace cache. Display-only data URLs never replace document
paths. Node views request at most 128 images per mount, with 4096-byte paths;
remote destinations and source escapes receive no URL. Stale backend responses
are discarded. No new dependency, network fetch or parser is introduced.
WP-04/05 canvas components (2026-10-22) add numeric camera reports and a host-only
Dioxus component layer. Node content remains escaped Dioxus text/attributes;
embed does not introduce HTML, scripts or extension authority. Pointer capture
uses a fixed eval script with a serialized element id and pointer number. Bounds
reject non-finite camera/geometry data, and invisible/small cards unmount. The
shared crate reuses existing Dioxus/serde dependencies; no external connection,
parser, persistence or extension contribution point is introduced.
P-227 flow code generation now uses the fetched content version and text length together for replacements, and refuses failed reads. Query metadata versions never authorize generated-file overwrites; optimistic conflict checks remain enforced by the source.
WP-07 e-graph paste (2026-10-23) reuses serde JSON with its default recursion
limit and caps input at 4 MiB, 4096 nodes, 32768 edges and 4096 groups before
projection. Unique node/edge/group identities, member ownership, representatives
and child endpoints are validated. Rewrite walks use visited ids and adjacency
lists, including cycles. JSON text goes through Eval::send as data; labels
remain canvas/Dioxus text. There is no evaluation, connection, new dependency or
persistence. The fuzz workspace’s egraph target exercises parsing, ancestry,
collapse and expansion, seeded by the synthetic snapshot. It is available for
local fuzzing; the existing two-target nightly jobs are unchanged.
WP-06 hierarchy projection (2026-10-23) reuses the structured serde query
protocol and existing source reads. It fetches no content bodies and adds no
connection, dependency or authority. The snapshot fallback refuses incomplete
results, duplicate ids, cycles and multiple parents of equal precedence; it caps input at two
million nodes/eight million edges, requested level at 64 and output at 100,000
nodes. Traversal is iterative, including malformed cyclic input. These are
projection bounds after source enumeration, not new limits on source-internal
allocation. Source-native cached cuts and end-to-end performance remain open.
WP-06 region navigation sends source query results as escaped JSON strings
through the existing Eval channel. The static controller never interpolates
labels into script or HTML. Source membership and complete-source counts stay
source-owned; only numeric placement, pinning, groups and boundary proxies are
computed in the host. The combined visible cut/region refuses more than 100k
nodes. Generation checks discard replies after source replacement. The lazy
million-node test source lives only in a separate fixture crate. No new
production parser, connection, permission or dependency is introduced.
P-229: Sophia coarse queries use namespace/name/definition-ID/indexed-reference
metadata instead of Interface::all’s definition/Calls traversal, after the latter
exhausted a worker stack on the large local copy. Metadata limits remain two
million nodes/eight million edges, and log-position checks reject changes during
listing. No term decoder is added. This avoids that traversal in coarse queries;
existing All/neighbour/body traversal is not declared fixed or bounded by it.
WP-11/15 (2026-10-23): symbol paths are data parsed by Path2D, capped at 64 KiB
and 256 closed-region fills per draw. Grid drawing caps rows/columns and skips
distant zoom. Core date parsing caps text at 128 bytes and validates offset and
timestamp ranges. Numeric vectors cap at 4096 finite samples during construction
and streaming deserialization; DuckDB inspects borrowed list lengths before
allocating. Sparkline coordinates are normalized against extreme magnitudes.
Ref targets come from source-known NodeIds, never guessed UUID text or URLs;
opening reuses workspace source/editor behavior. New direct chrono dependency
reuses the locked version with std/serde only, no clock or connection.
The typed_cells and symbol_paths fuzz targets exercise production serde/date
and closed-region parsing with 64 KiB inputs; no new network, process or permission authority is added.
WP-21 naming prerequisite (2026-10-23) adds pure metadata extraction over the
existing bounded content-id syntax trees, with the same file/definition/byte
limits and request budget. Package discovery and file reads stay with callers.
Names with empty segments, whitespace, controls or backquotes bind nothing and
are reported; formatting never removes offending bytes. Store paths remain data,
with independent Sophia path-validation regression checks. Conflicting imports
are unresolved independent of read order; named collisions are explicit errors.
No normalizer/id change, dependency, evaluation, persistence or connection is added.
SR-145 content identities (2026-10-24): nesting has no depth cap. Explicit heap
stacks cover normalization, patterns, type parameters and Julia scope
continuations. Requests instead cap source bytes (16 MiB/file), definitions
(4,096/file), work (32 million default visits) and accumulated canonical/graph
bytes (256 MiB, charged before field allocation); parser progress still has a
two-second deadline. Julia modules retain their aggregate source/work budgets.
No dependency, code execution or new authority is added. See
packages/services/content-id/content-id.md for the full budget contract and
256 KiB-stack depth-100,000 regression coverage.
