Large single atomic widgets still require their full content and geometry when visible; links/wiki links, images, tables, mathematics and callouts remain further provider work. Milkdown stays available as Rich mode.
Lists and tasks (2026-10-13)
CommonMark list items now produce independent source replacements: bullet and ordered markers, nested indentation, checked/unchecked task status, decoded text, inline emphasis/code, and wrapped single-paragraph bodies. A parent’s preview stops before its nested children so each item reveals locally. The canonical Markdown remains editable, copyable and undoable; task state changes by editing its source marker. Items containing links/wiki links, images, quotes, code blocks or multiple paragraphs retain source until those providers support the complete construct.
Unchanged block keys/decorations and list fragment payloads are shared across revisions to avoid repeated allocation. Replacement offsets use one byte-to-scalar index per changed block, and overlap checks use sorted item ranges. Presentation filters collapsed folds once rather than scanning every expanded heading/list fold for every replacement. The long-note gate includes hundreds of list/task items and checks deep list previews while retaining its existing latency limits. Rich mode stays available; links/wiki links, images, tables, math and callouts remain next.
Link preview and navigation (2026-10-13)
CommonMark inline/reference/autolinks and wiki-links now share structured inline fragments in paragraphs, headings and supported list/task items. Wiki aliases are literal text; their temporary CommonMark projection retains a byte-boundary map to canonical source. Escaped wiki syntax, embeds, code, images, HTML and metadata remain source. Reference definitions still select the conservative document-wide semantic parse.
Ordinary clicks reveal the enclosing source replacement. Ctrl/Cmd-click follows only a measured link glyph rectangle, including wrapped fragments inside an atomic heading/list widget. The existing narrow geometry bridge reports identifiers and rectangles; Rust validates identifiers and retains destinations. Revision, font epoch, viewport and presentation identity reject stale measurements.
File links resolve relative to the origin within its source, with normalized paths and one percent-decoding pass; missing regular files are not created. Wiki links retain guarded resolve/create behavior and explicit .md suffixes. Same-note and cross-note fragments use canonical unsaved text, rendered heading slugs with duplicate suffixes, or case-insensitive heading text. A missing heading opens the target at the top and reports a localized status. Background loading does not activate a document; origin revision/selection and target text guards protect the eventual reveal.
ExternalLinkOpener is a workspace service. Web calls Window.open synchronously during the gesture with _blank and noopener,noreferrer; desktop/mobile use the platform browser opener. Only HTTP, HTTPS and mailto destinations are accepted. Hover previews, link completion, images/embeds and Rich-mode replacement remain later work.
Wiki resolution invalidates on the origin node, unique page targets and index epoch, rather than offsets or unrelated edits. Same-note headings remain resolved immediately. Visible row lookups reuse fold visibility from the engine row index. The long-note fixture turns its existing bold fragments into external links and adds wiki aliases inside existing list items, preserving comparable widget counts while testing 480 links.
Replacement validation converts requested scalar endpoints to bytes in one pass and asks GraphemeCursor about those boundaries only. It avoids materializing every plain-source grapheme boundary; comparison tests retain the full-segmentation oracle for CRLF, ZWJ emoji, regional indicators, combining marks and Indic clusters.
The derived-fold refresh keeps the row prefix index while collapsed ranges are unchanged. Wiki span cache identity includes normalized scalar positions as well as raw byte ranges, so equal-byte Unicode edits still move source marks correctly. CRLF counting uses substring matches rather than an allocated byte-window walk.
The deferred structural pair pass classifies parser spans only at bracket characters, while retaining Unicode scalar offsets and line counts across prose. Performance measurements wait for pending network/font/save work before timing either mode; the fixture keeps the preceding byte budget by replacing plain filler with link syntax, while preserving every section and list/task item.
Measured proportional runs may reuse geometry across revisions only when their source, marks, tags, replacement payloads, model/row/source start, viewport width, font epoch and presentation identity match exactly. The result is rebound to the current revision and republished to the height index. Request sequence numbers still cancel pending old responses; resize clears the cache, and font/viewport/presentation changes force measurement.
Source-backed image blocks
Standalone top-level Markdown images (including references) and wiki image embeds render through the originating Source. Relative paths decode once and stay within that source; wiki resolution prefers the same directory, then root, then complete filename matches with shortest-path/lexical ordering. Mixed paragraphs, containers, sizing modifiers, note embeds and remote/data input URLs retain source. Alt text and titles remain literal. Plain click reveals the full canonical paragraph at its start; Ctrl/Cmd-click opens the asset through guarded navigation.
The shared workspace cache coalesces fetches, allows two active byte reads and retains at most 64 MiB of encoded payload. Versioned keys refresh when the asset version changes; unversioned keys follow the graph epoch. Metadata and actual bytes enforce 24 MiB, and known raster headers enforce 100 megapixels. SVG is loaded as an image data URL, never injected as markup. Visible blocks load lazily; loading/error placeholders are localized. Images preserve aspect ratio without upscaling, with 640 px width and 320 px height caps.
Opaque image identities retain exact canonical source ownership in the geometry bridge. Loading, decode, error and version transitions invalidate measured geometry and pending requests, including when the dimensions happen to match. Shared format helpers live in moonkale_ext_api::media::image; the image editor keeps its existing public reexports.
Source-owned tables
Top-level pipe tables render as a single replacement owning the complete original table, including its delimiter row. CommonMark’s table extension supplies cell boundaries, escaped pipes, entities and column alignment. Headers and cells use semantic table/row/columnheader/cell roles with an equal-column grid, wrapped text and theme borders. Inline emphasis, strong text, code, ordinary links and wiki aliases use the existing literal fragment renderer and guarded navigation. HTML and Markdown images inside cells, and tables inside lists or quotes, retain source.
The caret or an intersecting selection reveals the whole table locally. Plain pointer hits use the existing atomic source boundaries; modified link clicks use measured fragment identities. Continuation source rows collapse into the table’s measured height, while adjacent blank rows remain source. The geometry bridge still validates exact concatenated cell text and canonical ownership; no new JS parsing or model/history contract is introduced. Shared table payloads participate in block reuse and revision/font/viewport/presentation guards.
Source-owned math
Rust enables the CommonMark math extension and retains exact scalar ownership for inline dollar expressions and standalone display paragraphs. Code, metadata, escaped/unmatched delimiters and mixed display text retain source. Closing inline delimiters followed by digits remain literal currency. Inline fragments carry typed math payloads through headings, lists, table cells and link labels; wiki projection never enters TeX. Paragraph formulas reveal independently; existing atomic headings/list items/tables reveal their enclosing source, and display paragraphs reveal their complete delimiters/body.
An isolated, locally bundled KaTeX 0.18.7 renderer accepts TeX/display/macros and returns HTML/MathML or failure. Markdown parsing, macro lookup, cache ownership and navigation remain Rust. CSS/fonts are shared through ext-api::media::math with Rich mode. Visible widgets read saved .moonkale/katex.json through their originating Source; configuration is coalesced per source/graph epoch, and source refresh re-reads it. Missing config uses defaults; invalid/oversized config reports localized status. Macros are cloned per render, so definitions do not leak.
The renderer disables trusted commands, caps expansions at 1000 and requested sizes at 20 em, bounds TeX at 16 KiB and returned markup at 1 MiB. Rust bounds config at 64 KiB and retained markup at 8 MiB/256 entries. Keys include source, TeX, mode and macro fingerprint. Errors remain literal canonical text with a localized indication. Stale responses cannot paint changed/disposed widgets; unchanged prose does not restart rendering.
Geometry validates math owner identities and projects their canonical labels while checking surrounding text exactly. Render/config/error/font transitions invalidate pending measurements even when dimensions match. Display equations scroll independently: scrolling does not reach the editor viewport, and measured scrollbar areas retain native interaction. Display content uses a guarded owner-relative pointer path to canonical source; inline/link hits retain existing navigation. No document/history/LSP contract changes.
Source-owned callouts
Root blockquotes beginning with [!type] render as a whole source-owned callout. Types are case-insensitive ASCII identifiers; custom types use the same layout. A custom title supports inline emphasis, code, links/wiki links and math. An omitted title uses the type. Bodies support paragraphs (including lazy continuations), headings, lists/task lists, nested quotes, and the same inline fragments. HTML, images, tables, fenced code and display math inside a callout keep the whole quote as source; callouts inside lists/other quotes and inline title spans crossing into the body also retain source.
A trailing - initially folds the body; + initially opens it. A separate native button toggles presentation with pointer, Enter or Space without moving the editor caret or changing source/history. Its expanded state is local to the mounted source range; it is not saved to the document. Title/body clicks continue to reveal the enclosing source range, while modified link clicks follow the existing revision-checked routing. Selections and composition use canonical text.
Geometry validates every literal fragment and math owner even while folded, measures the enclosing block’s current bounds, and ignores hidden math hit rectangles. Folding invalidates geometry and the row-height index; asynchronous math and font changes use the existing guarded invalidation. The long-note fixture includes callouts beyond the old 4096-character prefix and retains its existing typing-latency bounds.
Callout acceptance (2026-10-14): the 247,882-byte CRLF note retains 240 sections, 720 list items, 480 links, three tables, four images and three display equations, and adds three source-owned callouts at sections 60, 180 and 239. With both dev server and Firefox restricted to two cores, software rendering, three warmups and seven samples, preview typing measured 249 ms median / 279 ms p95 against the 3 MB Source baseline’s 539 / 544 ms. These are dev-build harness measurements for the existing relative acceptance bound, not release-build latency estimates; the 25% median / 50% p95 limits are unchanged.
Wiki-link hover excerpts
The native editor previews wiki targets through a view-local controller, without loading the target into Workspace or changing activation, selection, history or canonical text. Rendered links supply the semantic target from revision-checked geometry, including aliases inside headings, lists, tables and callouts. Source links use the actual character under the pointer, independently of the LSP caret-boundary hover position. Code, embeds, escapes, math, HTML containers and leading front matter are excluded. Source tokens are cached by canonical revision and parsed lazily while source text is hovered; the disabled branch reads no document signals during typing.
After a 250 ms dwell, the controller uses Workspace’s existing wiki resolver, then reads the open target’s live text or fetches text directly from its Source. Same-note and heading targets share the navigation heading resolver and duplicate-slug rules. Heading excerpts stop at the next peer/higher heading. Excerpts omit front matter and HTML, project wiki aliases to literal text, and render plain CommonMark text without media or nested popups. Returned text is limited to 1200 scalars and 14 lines, scanned from at most 4096 source scalars. Advertised sizes above 256 KiB are rejected before fetching; unknown-size Sources still use their whole-text API and are checked after fetching. Resolution/fetching has a five-second timeout, with localized loading, missing, unavailable, oversized and missing-heading states.
Requests/results retain origin node, canonical revision, target identity and source epoch. Origin edits, navigation, scrolling, composition and leaving the link dismiss the popup; a 200 ms close grace lets the pointer enter it for reading. Open target edits update the excerpt, and discarding/closing an unsaved target invalidates its cached excerpt and re-fetches saved text. Popups have independent view state and clamp to the browser viewport. Pointer, clipboard and keyboard events stay inside the read-only popup; Escape restores the editor input focus. Existing LSP hover remains separate, with the wiki popup taking precedence while displayed.
Wiki-hover acceptance (2026-10-14): with dev server and Firefox on two cores, the unchanged 247,882-byte fixture measured 253 ms median / 282 ms p95 against the 3 MB Source baseline’s 539 / 549 ms. The existing 25% median / 50% p95 bounds remain unchanged. Native checks also copy the popup’s DOM-selected excerpt while the editor has its full source selected, proving clipboard ownership stays separate.
Front-matter properties
Native Markdown live preview now has a collapsed Properties bar above the document. It summarizes the first three top-level YAML keys; expanding it opens a plain YAML draft with Apply and Cancel. Notes without metadata show “none” and can add a block. Empty applied YAML removes the block. This matches Rich’s YAML-oriented interface while keeping the canonical document in the editor session; Rich remains available.
Recognition follows Rich’s conservative leading-only block rules: an exact opening delimiter and closing delimiter, with property/list/indented/comment/blank lines in between and no leading blank line. Ordinary thematic-break prose, incomplete blocks and later delimiters retain source. This is a recognition guard, not a complete YAML schema validator. Drafts cannot inject closing delimiters or unstructured top-level prose. Arbitrary keys and nested YAML remain literal text; there is no value deserialization or reserialization.
The leading prefix uses a source-owned hidden replacement. Its complete rows collapse, including the first row, through the existing presentation height index. Caret/selection/search reveals expose the original prefix; Preview off always shows the complete source. Zero-height rows do not mount interactive source runs. Body bytes and canonical coordinates remain untouched by presentation.
Apply emits one revision- and node-checked prefix EditBatch through the existing session history. Original opening/closing delimiters, closing whitespace, trailing blank YAML lines and EOF convention remain intact; edited textarea newlines use the opening delimiter’s LF/CRLF convention (new blocks use the document convention). An unchanged draft performs no edit. Body text is never reconstructed. Body selections shift by the UTF-16 prefix delta; undo/redo restores source and selection. Save applies a current draft before saving; stale or unsafe drafts retain their text and report a localized error instead of overwriting newer content.
Draft/focus/composition state belongs to the mounted document view. Cancel/Escape restores editor input focus; disabling preview or reloading cancels the draft and clears composition state. Textarea clipboard, typing, composition and local undo remain separate from the editor engine. Apply/Save defer during composition. The properties memo reads only the leading prefix while preview is enabled and never clones the body.
Properties acceptance (2026-10-14): all 626 workspace tests pass; native and full-app tests cover draft save/cancel, stale rejection, source reveal, clipboard/composition isolation and byte-preserving edits. The 247,882-byte note retains the same content/widget budget. With dev server and Firefox restricted to two cores, software rendering, three warmups and seven samples, preview typing measured 257 ms median / 547 ms p95 against the 3 MB Source baseline’s 529 / 534 ms. The unchanged 25% median / 50% p95 limits pass; these are dev-harness measurements, not release latency estimates. Widget checks scroll at most one viewport to mount adjacent blocks below the pinned Properties bar.
Documentation comments in code
Rust, Python and Julia expose a separate Doc preview toggle, persisted as editor.doc_comment_preview and disabled by default. It is independent of Markdown Preview and code wrapping. Only documentation rows use reader typography and wrapping; surrounding code retains its monospace grid and the existing Wrap preference.
A per-document incremental syntax tree recognizes Rust outer/inner line and block doc comments, Python’s first literal module/class/function statement, and immediately attached Julia declaration/assignment docstrings or explicit literal @doc. Whole-line ownership includes indentation and exact delimiters in canonical source. Incomplete, interpolated, escape-dependent, ambiguous and code-sharing strings retain source. Documentation is never evaluated or rewritten.
Each recognized block is atomic for presentation: caret, selection and search reveal its complete canonical source. The renderer supports headings, paragraphs, emphasis, inline/fenced code, lists, blockquotes, tables and ordinary external or explicit file-path links. Images, math, wiki syntax, HTML and unresolved Rustdoc-style symbol links remain literal. No language interpreter, HTML execution, media fetch or Rustdoc resolution participates.
Local normalized edits update the syntax tree’s byte points and line-start index. Rendered bodies and mounted code examples retain document-owned caches. Rust edits after the last owner can retain existing ranges only when neither the old nor new complete tail contains any documentation token; the syntax tree still parses incrementally. Other changes reclassify syntax, and replacements or unsupported batches take a fresh snapshot. Visible widgets alone mount. Unwrapped owner rows avoid repeated fold/coordinate queries; retained heights require the same payload identity, range, row, width, font and visible owner. Revision-only height rebinding does not invalidate the whole viewport. Switching a reused public panel to another document remounts its keyed hook state.
Acceptance so far (2026-10-14): 642 workspace tests; fmt, clippy, wasm, minimal builds, public docs and dependency/colour/string checks; nine native browser suites; twelve full-app suites including lsp2 and exact CRLF save/history for all three languages. All 16 Source corpus files round-trip byte-exact. The 263,574-byte same-file fixture passes the unchanged two-core dev latency gate: Source 89/98 ms median/p95, Doc preview 106/107 ms, with three warmups and seven samples. These numbers do not establish release-build 60 FPS acceptance. CED-R22 web/desktop frame measurements remain outstanding; the standalone editor-fps.mjs reports them independently of run-all.

decisions/ADR-0018-One-frontend-graph-en.title: ADR-0018 — One frontend graph engine: the flow editor moves onto graph-render
decisions/ADR-0018-One-frontend-graph-en.content:
Status: accepted 2026-10-08 (Daniel’s decision, given with spec 031). Related: ADR-0011 Desktop graph surface strategy, ADR-0016 Freya is a reference, not a target, dioxus-flow, Flow Editor, Frontend Graph Engine Mapping.
Context
The flow editor’s canvas is dioxus-flow 0.1.2 — a third-party crate (~8.3k lines, one author, crates.io) adopted in Milestone 6 after dioxus-flow recommended it for drag-and-drop flows at ~1 000 nodes, with the wgpu graph view kept as a separate surface. Spec 031 now asks for the opposite end state: graph exploration and flow/canvas editing as distinct interaction modes over one renderer (§5), with ports as independent hit targets, orthogonal routes, layers, LOD discipline and 100k-scale behaviour (§2–§6).

We do not own dioxus-flow. The substantial changes the spec needs cannot be contributed upstream at our pace, and a fork of a 0.1.x DOM/SVG canvas buys none of the instanced-WebGL scale that §6 exists for. Its DOM rendering caps it near a thousand nodes (its own roadmap; the flow editor is fine today, but spec 031’s domains — factor graphs, hardware layouts — are not).
Only the canvas depends on it. The flow model already lives frontend-free in ext-api::flow (FlowLibrary, PortType/unify, validate, codegen); panel.rs converts between it and dioxus_flow::{Node, Edge} at every sync, so the renderer swap is confined to that conversion.
Lenticulum.jl and ModelingToolkit.jl integration must stay mostly frontend-agnostic (Daniel): block libraries, port types, validation and codegen are extensions’ contributions over ext-api::flow, whatever draws them — the same headless-model rule as ADR-0016’s editor.

Decision

One engine. moonkale-graph-render grows an edit mode (spec 031 §5: ports, typed wiring, orthogonal routes) and the flow editor moves onto it. dioxus-flow is gradually replaced by our own flow editor extension, per stage 7 of Frontend Graph Engine Mapping, gated on a parity checklist (ports, typed validation hooks, layered layout, undo, parameter editing).
The model stays frontend-agnostic. ext-api::flow keeps no renderer types; Lenticulum/MTK libraries never learn which canvas drew them. Validation and simulation stay outside the renderer, as the spec demands.
No fork of dioxus-flow and no upstream work on it. It stays until stage 7 retires it; dioxus-flow remains the record of why it was the right choice at Milestone 6 scale.

decisions/ADR-0019-Extension-coordinates.filePath: decisions/ADR-0019 Extension coordinates and block addressing.md
decisions/ADR-0019-Extension-coordinates.title: ADR-0019 — Extension coordinates and block addressing
decisions/ADR-0019-Extension-coordinates.content:
Status: proposed. Written by Claude after reviewing the editor-extensibility RFC (2026-10-11), which asked which decisions are hard to reverse and should be settled while Moonkale is small. Daniel decides. Related: ADR-0008 Rust owns the document, JS is a view, ADR-0009 Patches not snapshots, ADR-0013 JSON ABI before components, ADR-0015 The core model, ADR-0017 Markdown live preview on the code editor.
Context
Two things every editor extension will bake in, and that are expensive to change once extensions exist: which unit a text position is in, and how a piece of a document (a block) is named when it is not a whole file.
Positions. Moonkale already uses four units:

UTF-8 bytes: ext-api::editor::EditBatch (on codex), wiki::WikiSpan, and the byte ranges pulldown-cmark and tree-sitter return;
UTF-16 code units: LSP, CodeMirror’s splices (code-view/src/backend), Utf16Selection and Utf16Position in ext-api::editor, DOM ranges;
Unicode scalars (chars): core::Splice (the source-level patch), editor-core’s offsets and the native decorations (native_decorations.rs);
graphemes: the boundaries a replacement must respect (valid_replacements).

Each boundary converts. Extensions would add a fifth party, and an extension that guesses the wrong unit is correct on ASCII and wrong on 😀 or 猫.
Revisions. There are two counters, and they mean different things. core::Version is the source’s version of a node: it changes on save and is used for conflict detection. DocumentRevision (on codex) is the live editor session’s revision: it changes on every keystroke.
Blocks. Nothing names a block today. NodeKind::Block exists and nothing produces it. Headings and paragraphs are not in the graph. Symbols are, and since ccb7d90 their native keys are paths (src/lib.rs#impl:A/fn:new, ~n for repeats) that survive edits above them. Before that they ended in @<line>. Wiki links already address headings ([[Page#heading|Heading]]; WikiSpan::heading) but never resolve them. The RFC wants to open a block, show it in several contexts, and embed one block in another. All of that needs a name for a block that survives edits.
Decision
1. One external unit: UTF-8 byte offsets into the text the extension was given

Every range an extension receives or returns is a half-open start..end of UTF-8 byte offsets into the snapshot text it received, tagged with that snapshot’s DocumentRevision.
The host validates every incoming range: within the text, on str::is_char_boundary, and for replacements on a grapheme boundary. An invalid range is rejected with a diagnostic, never clamped.
UTF-16 stays where it is native: LSP, CodeMirror and the DOM. Scalars stay inside editor-core and in core::Splice, which extensions never build (the host turns sessions into transactions, decision 2). Conversions live in one module per boundary (code-view owns UTF-16↔bytes and scalars↔bytes). Extensions never see either unit.
Lines and columns are for display only. When an extension needs one, the host gives a 0-based line and a byte column.

Why bytes: they are what Rust &str slicing, tree-sitter, pulldown-cmark, EditBatch and WikiSpan already use. A wasm module receives UTF-8 JSON strings, so bytes are its native unit too. Validation is O(1). UTF-16 would favour only JavaScript, which is not an extension language here (ADR-0013). Scalars make every slice O(n).
2. Results are tied to a revision and mapped, never applied blindly

An extension’s output (decorations, widgets, diagnostics) carries the DocumentRevision it was computed against.
If the document has moved on, the host maps the ranges through the EditBatches since that revision, or drops the ones an edit touched. It never applies old offsets to new text. This replaces today’s rule of dropping every stale batch, which makes asynchronous providers flicker.
Edits from extensions are EditBatches against a base revision, with today’s BatchRejected semantics: stale means rejected plus the canonical snapshot.
Extensions never see core::Version. Turning a session into a core::Transaction on save is the host’s job.

3. A block is (file, anchor), and the anchor is text
A block is addressed as the file’s NodeId plus an anchor, resolved against the current text whenever it is used:



































anchorwritten asresolves tosurvivessymbol#impl:A/fn:new (the symbol’s native key after #)the index’s Symbol node, then its definition rangeedits elsewhere; not a renameheading#Decision/Consequences (heading path; ~n for the n-th repeat, as for symbols)the section under that headingedits elsewhere; not a heading renameblock id#^theorem-3 (an explicit ^id marker, Obsidian’s syntax)the paragraph or block carrying the markerrenames and moves within the filerangestart..end@revisionitselfnothing: never persisted

The persisted form is a string, <file key>#<anchor>. It is the same string a wiki link uses ([[Page#heading|Heading]], [[Page#^id|^id]]) and, for symbols, the same as the native key. One syntax names a block in links, in layouts and in the graph.
Resolution parses the current text, independently per consumer, as the RFC’s D1 suggests. An anchor that no longer resolves is shown as unresolved. It is never guessed by position.
Blocks are not graph nodes. Headings and paragraphs are not persisted in the index, and NodeKind::Block stays unused until a source owns blocks as data. Content ids (NodeId::from_content, ADR-0015) are for identity across files and machines, not for paragraphs.

4. An occurrence is view state
Where a block is shown (which panel, beside what, in what order) belongs to the layout. It is persisted with the layout in the state store (ADR-0014 One store for internal state), if at all. It is never written into a source or into the graph, and changing a layout never changes text.
Consequences

Built: path keys for symbols (ccb7d90, the index crate note). Byte ranges already exist in EditBatch and WikiSpan.
To build, when the first consumer needs it:

heading-path and ^id resolution, shared by the wiki-link extractor and the editors;
mapping decoration ranges through edit batches in the native compositor (native_decorations.rs);
one conversion module per boundary in code-view;
reveal state keyed by decoration identity instead of its position in a bitmask.


Cost of reversal: low today, since nothing outside the host consumes these units. After the first extension ships it means a versioned ABI change.
ext-api::editor’s UTF-16 Utf16Selection/Utf16Position stay as the view↔Workspace contract (they match LSP and the browser). They are not part of the extension surface; an extension asking for the selection gets bytes.
Heading anchors break when a heading is renamed, as in Obsidian. Rename refactoring (like spec 012’s rename rewriting for wiki links) can follow later.
Not decided here: the decoration vocabulary and the provider interface (the RFC’s seams 1–2). They should be decided after experiment E1, using the units fixed here.

decisions/ADR-0020-Undirected-pins-in-th.filePath: decisions/ADR-0020 Undirected pins in the flow model.md
decisions/ADR-0020-Undirected-pins-in-th.title: ADR-0020 — Undirected pins in the flow model: the ladder toward ModelingToolkit
decisions/ADR-0020-Undirected-pins-in-th.content:
Status: proposed 2026-10-12 (Daniel’s direction: Lux.jl → ModelingToolkit.jl → RxInfer.jl → Lenticulum.jl, “so the graph engine displays actual projects”). Related: ADR-0018 One frontend graph engine, Flow Editor, Julia and Lenticulum, Frontend Graph Engine Mapping.
Context
The flow editor models a directed dataflow: BlockKind has inputs and outputs, a Wire goes from an output to an input, validate type-checks that direction, refuses unconnected required inputs and reports cycles, and codegen walks the topological order. That is Lux.jl’s shape (a DAG of layers).
The next rung of the ladder is ModelingToolkit.jl — acausal components whose connect is symmetric (no direction), systems nest, and loops are normal (algebraic loops, feedback) — and beyond it RxInfer/Lenticulum’s factor graphs, which are also undirected and bipartite. Julia and Lenticulum names exactly this: “undirected ports, bipartite constraints and nested subgraphs are what the ModelingToolkit editor needs”.
The engine side is already in place: InPort.direction has a Both variant (its default), ports draw by colour, the wire gesture starts from any port, and InEdge.directed = false draws no arrowhead. What is missing is the model and the panel.
Decision

BlockKind gains connections: Vec<Port> — undirected pins, #[serde(default)], so every existing flow and library parses unchanged. A pin’s PortType names the domain both ends must share: Named { name: "electrical" }, “mechanical”, … — unify already requires name equality for Named, which is exactly MTK’s domain rule. A directed library (Lux) simply has no pins.
A wire between two pins is an equation, not dataflow. It is accepted in either drag order; a pin may carry several wires (a bus — connect(p, n, q)); it is exempt from the cycle check (Flow::topological_skipping ignores pin wires; topological() itself keeps its meaning — the directed dataflow order the Lux codegen walks); and its type check is symmetric (unify both ways). Required pins must be wired in at least one direction.
The panel draws pins on the block’s top edge with direction: "both" — the engine’s own default — and pins’ wires as directed: false edges. Port names must be unique across a kind’s inputs, outputs and connections; the panel resolves a wire by trying the directed interpretation first, then the pin one.
Staging toward the goal. This ADR covers the pin half; the rungs after it, in order:

Nested subflows (double-click into a subsystem, the parent drawing it as one block with boundary ports — the engine’s group machinery is the basis) — its own design pass before implementation;
the ModelingToolkit library in MathStruct/moonkale-julia: components with unit parameters, @named + connect codegen, structural_simplify as the run hint, and an e2e that builds a real RC circuit;
RxInfer: bipartite constraints (a library-level rule: variable and factor kinds refuse same-kind wires) and per-run channel polarity;
Lenticulum: the factor-graph editor and its live half — a Moonkale.jl companion streaming beliefs and energies into a live graph source.
Alongside: the Julia depot source (Project.toml/Manifest.toml as a read-only source with using edges) so the graph engine shows real code projects.



Consequences

.flow.json stays the document; a pin wire is the same Wire shape (its from/to are just the two ends; codegen decides what a wire means — layers or connect equations — by looking at the ports).
The Lux codegen (moonkale-julia) is untouched: it walks topological(), which never sees pins.
The engine needed no change for this stage; the acausal drawing rules (pins on the top edge) are the panel’s conversion, like every other shape decision (ADR-0018 §2).
What we deliberately do not decide here: subflow document structure, the bipartite rule’s error surface, and polarity’s representation — each gets its own pass at the rung that needs it.

decisions/ADR-0021-Subflows.title: ADR-0021 — Subflows: a subsystem is one block whose ports the subflow declares
decisions/ADR-0021-Subflows.content:
Status: accepted 2026-10-12 (Daniel; Claude’s review folded in — per-instance naming and the ext-api tag). Related: ADR-0020 Undirected pins in the flow model, ADR-0018 One frontend graph engine, Flow Editor, Julia and Lenticulum.
Context
ModelingToolkit systems nest (compose), and the MTK library (ADR-0020’s first consumer, in moonkale-julia) proved the pins model end to end — but every circuit is still one flat sheet. The ModelingToolkit editor needs hierarchy, and so does Lenticulum (a sub-graph as one factor). Claude’s review order put the MTK library first precisely so this design knows what nesting really needs.
What building the library taught: the panel already owns every shape decision (ADR-0018 §2) — the engine never learned what a “pin” or a “block kind” is; it draws nodes, ports and edges. That is the lever for hierarchy: the engine needs nothing at all.
Decision

One document, nested. A subflow lives in the same .flow.json — Flow gains subflows: Vec<Subflow> (#[serde(default)], non-breaking like every field since the pins review), where Subflow { id, name, blocks, wires, inputs, outputs, connections } reuses the ordinary Block/Wire/Port shapes. (Amended 2026-10-13, in stage A’s implementation: the sketch had one ports field, but §2 already says a boundary port is a directed input, an output or a domain-typed pin — the declaration mirrors a BlockKind’s three port lists, so the shape carries which.) A parent block references one by Block.subflow: Option<String> (also defaulted). Not a referenced file: the document stays one unit for git, diff, agents and undo — the founding rule (“a diagram stays a diagram”; the file is the serialisation, the editor is the interface).
Boundary ports are declared, and they are the parent block’s ports. Subflow’s boundary declaration — inputs/outputs/connections, the same Port type a BlockKind uses, so a boundary port is a directed input, an output or a domain-typed pin exactly as before. The panel’s to_scene draws the subsystem block like any other, with its ports resolved from the subflow’s declaration instead of a library kind; wire() resolves a subflow block’s ports the same way. Wires to the subsystem are ordinary wires; nothing about validation’s shape changes (the resolution source grows by one case).
Inside, a boundary port is a pseudo-block. Within the subflow’s own blocks, a port appears as a block with a reserved kind (boundary/…, one per port, placed at the canvas edge and locked there). Inner wires attach to it like any block. The panel owns the illusion; the engine draws a node.
Editing is a scope stack in the panel. Double-click a subsystem block enters its subflow (the scene swaps — a plain set_graph, the same as any document change); a breadcrumb (parent / sub_1) and Escape or an empty-canvas click pop out. Undo needs nothing new: a snapshot is the whole document, so an edit inside a subflow restores with the parent intact. The palette, toolbar and status bar serve whichever scope is open; the engine never knows a “level” exists.
No engine change; no group machinery. The parent view draws the subsystem as one block — not a hull, not a group. The engine’s groups and hulls stay what they are: graph-exploration devices (spec 031 §4). A subsystem that is closed stays closed; “entering” is a scene swap, not a zoom into a region.
Codegen flattens, with per-instance names. An MTK subsystem inlines into the parent circuit: its components and nets join the parent’s, and each boundary pin’s inner net merges with whatever the parent wires to it (a boundary pin is just a net continuation — connect never cared where a component came from). Two blocks may reference the same subflow, so every inner component carries a per-instance prefix in MTK’s own ₊ style (rc_1₊resistor_1) — the second instance must not collide with the first. (Amended 2026-10-13, in stage C’s implementation: the separator is _ — rc_filter_1_resistor_1 — not ₊. ModelingToolkit reads ₊ in a component’s name as its own namespace separator at runtime and looks for a system rc_filter_1 that does not exist; the prefix is still per instance, which is the point.) A Lux subflow is a sub-Chain: the inner layer path splices between the boundary input and output. Nothing generates a nested Julia structure; structural_simplify flattens anyway.

Stages

A. Model + parent view: Subflow, the Block.subflow reference, boundary ports on the parent block, validation of the boundary wiring. Native tests; a subflow block visible with its declared pins in the browser.
B. Editing: the scope stack, boundary pseudo-blocks inside, undo across levels, the breadcrumb. The palette can create a subflow (a “Subsystem” block whose empty subflow you enter and fill).
C. Codegen + e2e: MTK flattening and the Lux splice in moonkale-julia (its v0.3.0, the same tag ladder); mtk.mjs grows an RC whose RC-filter is one subsystem — golden generation and the same 99.3 % simulation, proving the flatten merges nets correctly.

Consequences

The document schema grows two defaulted fields — old files parse; source compatibility is a separate question: Block.subflow is a new field on Block, and Block { … } literals that list every field break. Stage A therefore ships with a new ext-api-YYYY-MM-DD tag and its CHANGELOG entry, like the pins did (Block: Default covers only literals finished with ..Default::default()).
Subflows compose: a subflow may reference a subflow (the scope stack is a stack; flattening recurses). Depth is bounded by sense, not by the model.
What we do not decide here: cross-subflow references between documents (Lenticulum’s “a sub-graph as one factor” may want a referenced subflow later — the model leaves room: Block.subflow names an id, today always in the same document), and the palette/UX of editing boundary declarations (a small editor on the subsystem block, like the parameter editor).

decisions/ADR-0022-Bipartite-factor-grap.title: ADR-0022 — Bipartite factor graphs: variables and factors as block roles
decisions/ADR-0022-Bipartite-factor-grap.content:
Status: accepted 2026-10-13 (Daniel; written by Claude, covering Mistral’s rung while Mistral is out). Related: ADR-0020 Undirected pins in the flow model (§4 names this rung and leaves “the bipartite rule’s error surface, and polarity’s representation” to it), ADR-0021 Subflows, Julia and Lenticulum, Flow Editor.
Context
RxInfer and Lenticulum models are factor graphs: bipartite and undirected, cycles allowed. Variables have no behaviour of their own. Factors are everything with content: priors, likelihoods, losses, data. Lenticulum’s own model (lib/Mycelium.jl, graph.jl) settles the shape:
VariableNode(id, name, space)        -- a wire; no behaviour
FactorNode(id, name, factor)
Edge(factor, channel, variable, direction, coupling)


An edge joins one named factor channel to one variable.
“A channel is a port, not a bus”: connect! refuses a second edge on the same (factor, channel). Fan-out goes through a variable, and a variable of degree d is a copier.
Polarity (Observed / Unobserved / Latent) is resolved per message at run time from which channels carry messages. It is not authored per wire. What is authored is the edge’s direction (Emitting, Absorbing or bidirectional) and, per run, which variables are observed (the data).

RxInfer (GraphPPL) has the same bipartite shape: random variables and factor nodes with named interfaces (out, μ, σ², …), and data variables bound at inference time.
The flow model already has what this needs:

undirected pins (BlockKind.connections, ADR-0020): a pin wire’s ends are just its two ends;
subflows (ADR-0021): “a sub-graph as one factor” later.

What is missing is the rule that a wire joins one variable and one factor.
Decision


Variables are blocks, not wires. A flow Wire joins exactly two ends, and a variable joins any number of factors. So a variable is a block with one pin of any degree, drawn as a circle (factors stay boxes, as on paper). Mycelium’s “a variable is a wire” is the semantics; on the canvas, the variable node is that wire’s junction.


BlockKind.role: Option<Role>, with Role::{Variable, Factor} (#[serde(default)]; kinds finished with ..Default::default() keep compiling). This is a library-level property, as ADR-0020 §4 sketched: an RxInfer or Lenticulum library marks its kinds, and every library before it (Lux, ModelingToolkit) has no role and is outside the rule. BlockPorts.role carries it through Flow::ports_of. A subflow block and a boundary pseudo-block have no role yet; whether a subsystem is one factor is stage C’s question.


The rule, and where it is enforced. Between two pin ends that both have a role:

Two of a kind are refused: “factors connect to variables, not to factors” (and the same for variables).
A factor’s channel carries one wire: “a channel is a port, not a bus”. A variable carries any number.
Ends without a role are not checked.

This is the error surface ADR-0020 left open. It has two sites with one wording, through the shared flow::bipartite_refusal and flow::channel_refusal:

the panel’s wire gesture refuses the wire, so a wrong wire is never stored;
validate reports what a file brings in (a hand-edited or agent-written .flow.json), about the wire or the factor, at the root and inside subflows.



Polarity is not a wire property (stage B, proposed here, not built). The authored part is per run: a variable is observed (bound to data) or not, plus, for Lenticulum, an edge direction where a factor is used one way only. The proposal:

a variable block carries its data, and a variable with data is observed, so RxInfer’s data variables are simply observed variables. (Amended 2026-10-13, in stage B: the sketch had a separate observed flag, but a flag without data, or data without the flag, would only be two more ways to be wrong.)
Lenticulum’s edge direction waits for its library, because Mycelium’s Bidirectional is the default and the only one RxInfer needs.



Stages.

A (built, 2026-10-13): the role, the rule at both sites, variables drawn as circles.
B (built, 2026-10-13, moonkale-julia v0.4.0): an RxInfer library in moonkale-julia: a variable kind, and Beta, Bernoulli, Normal (variance or precision), Gamma and Poisson as factors. @model codegen takes the observed variables as the model’s data arguments, writes one ~ per factor in graph order (a data vector is i.i.d., in a loop), and an unwired parameter channel takes its constant. Inference is exact message passing, and mean-field variational (with initial marginals and 30 iterations) only when a factor has two latent inputs. An e2e infers a coin’s bias: Beta(9, 10), the exact conjugate posterior. The engine learned sized circles (InNode.width now sets a circle’s radius too), so a variable stays a click target beside the blocks.
C: a subsystem as one factor (a role on Subflow), and Lenticulum’s edge directions once its library exists.



Consequences

The change is additive. BlockKind gains a defaulted field. BlockPorts gains role too: a caller that builds BlockPorts literally must add role: None. Inside Moonkale only the flow panel does that, and moonkale-julia doesn’t. It rides under the CHANGELOG’s Unreleased section, and the next ext-api tag carries it.
Codegen doesn’t change for existing libraries. Lux and ModelingToolkit have no roles, and their files validate as before.
Not decided here: the variable’s space (Mycelium’s type of the wire, so the pin’s PortType is Any for now); schedules (an overlay, not a node, per Julia and Lenticulum); and whether “observed” belongs to the document or to a run configuration beside it.

decisions/ADR-0023-Native-editor-frame-m.title: ADR-0023 Native editor frame measurements
decisions/ADR-0023-Native-editor-frame-m.content:
Status
Accepted measurement design, 2026-10-14. Desktop release acceptance remains open.
Context
Code Editor Requirements CED-R22 requires p95 frame intervals at most 16.7 ms and no frame over 50 ms during typing, held arrows, scrolling, selection dragging and caret movement. It applies to highlighted source and spec 018’s 3 MB document, on release web and desktop builds. Input latency alone does not expose renderer stalls.
Decision
editor-fps.mjs is a standalone Playwright suite. It records RAF callback intervals, p50/p95/max, supported long-animation-frame/longtask observations, actual build labels and browser version. It measures all seven gesture variants on the same 5000-line Rust file with documentation previews off/on, and on the 3 MB text file. Scroll and selection checks reject gestures that do not interact with the editor. Development recordings are diagnostic evidence; strict acceptance requires a release build. The 16.7/50 ms limits remain unchanged.
Desktop uses the production native panel in the release WebView fixture. MOONKALE_FPS_SOURCE supplies the same corpus file and MOONKALE_FPS_REPORT enables a manual recorder. It observes trusted input and RAF intervals for five seconds from the first intended gesture, records WebView/viewport metadata, and writes bounded JSON samples. It injects no input. Missing/insufficient gestures and development builds cannot pass. The private-display harness may supply compositor input through tools/headless.sh; the recorder itself only observes events. Daniel tests real input on his own desktop.
Run performance acceptance separately from builds and other browser work. Retain the raw report outside the repository and record its aggregate results in Rust Code Editor Roadmap. Keep correctness, byte-exact round trips and the existing same-file relative latency checks alongside the frame gate. The standalone suite stays outside run-all.sh’s strict list until both platform gates have evidence.
Consequences and evidence
The initial release web run exposed 233 ms p95 typing in the 3 MB file, up to 83 ms p95 preview scrolling and a 117 ms held-arrow stall. Profiling found an unbounded cursor-word status display, fractional scroll snapping, repeated height notifications and source-cell DOM churn. A full-sequence Chrome timeline identified 62 ms garbage collection after scrolling.
Bounded engine-owned word slices, retained fractional offsets, coalesced height updates, keyed virtual rows and same-presentation ASCII text runs address those costs. Text runs split at Unicode/tabs, wiki, caret, search and other presentation boundaries; Rust still owns exact scalar hit testing and selection. The release web rerun passed all 21 cases, each at about 16.67 ms p95, with a longest frame of 33.33 ms. This is web evidence only; desktop acceptance remains unmeasured.
Measurement amendment — 2026-10-15
The v4 headless desktop report contains integer-millisecond rAF deltas: 15 of 21 cases fail, including otherwise steady cases with p95 = 17 ms. A 60 Hz interval is 16.666… ms, so the rounded rAF argument cannot resolve the 16.7 ms gate. Desktop now measures unrounded performance.now() deltas at callback entry and retains the original rAF deltas as rafIntervals, with clock: "performance.now" in the report. Web keeps its existing sub-millisecond rAF timestamps. Callback-entry spacing includes callback scheduling delay; it must not be confused with physical presentation timestamps. The p95 ≤ 16.7 ms and max ≤ 50 ms limits are unchanged; no refresh-relative relaxation or rounding of measured intervals is applied. If the WebView also quantizes performance.now(), those measurements remain inconclusive and need another clock or a separately agreed refresh-based gate.
The old report still identifies likely real CPU-side misses: typing p95 20 ms (Source) and 23 ms (documentation preview), with maxima 24/27 ms; preview wheel max 23 ms and scrollbar-drag max 21 ms. Do not reclassify these old samples as passing under the new clock. Rerun and profile before changing the renderer.
Headless sway uses pixman and Mesa software GL because the NVIDIA WebKit path crashes in libnvidia-eglcore. These runs measure CPU-side Rust, DOM and layout costs, not hardware GPU compositing. Passing them is necessary, not sufficient; Daniel’s real-desktop release check remains the final acceptance. The amended recorder has not yet been validated in the desktop WebView: the private runtime fix from master now permits display startup, and the repository gates and release desktop rebuild pass; Git staging still reports a read-only index, and the required ~/.cache/moonkale-bench.lock cannot be created in this sandbox. The recorder transport check passes, but timing acceptance and profiling remain pending. WP-02 and WP-03 remain open.
Quantized-clock fallback — 2026-10-15
A locked, quiet-machine release desktop rerun of all 21 cases confirms that both public clocks produce integer-millisecond intervals. Switching to performance.now() alone does not resolve the gate. This agrees with WebKit’s Performance implementation, which reduces clock precision. No WebView security/isolation settings are changed for the benchmark.
Use the refresh-relative alternative authorized in NEXT-2: collect up to 120 idle callback intervals before the first intended gesture, require at least 30, and use their median as the refresh baseline. A frame is missed above 1.5 times that baseline; p95 must stay at or below that threshold and max must remain at most 50 ms. A baseline slower than 17 ms is rejected, preventing a busy/slow display from relaxing the target. The driver waits 1.2 seconds after arming to collect the idle baseline. Reports retain raw callback and rAF intervals, the idle samples, detected quantization, refresh interval, threshold, missed count and gate name. Quantization is detected conservatively when all callback deltas are integer within floating-point tolerance.
For fractional-clock recordings, passed continues to use the original 16.7/50 ms gate. Quantized recordings use gate: "calibrated-vsync"; their original interval gate is separately reported as strictPassed: false. A calibrated pass is not evidence of sub-millisecond p95 ≤16.7 ms. WP-02’s original strict desktop requirement and Daniel’s hardware desktop check remain open; do not silently treat the fallback as satisfying them.
Raw pre-optimization rerun: /tmp/moonkale-desktop-fps-corrected-20261015{.json,.summary.json}. All 21 gestures interacted; none passes the old integer-clock gate. Source typing p95/max 22/25 ms; documentation-preview typing 33/41 ms. Preview wheel max 178 ms and 3 MB wheel max 149 ms are real stalls, not explained by 1 ms quantization. Software GL still covers CPU-side work rather than hardware GPU compositing.
Bounded private-cache follow-up — 2026-10-15
With master 0aef7472 (private persistent cache/data/config homes), the release fixture was rebuilt. One three-case wheel warm-up attempt and one full 21-case guarded attempt both aborted before launching a case: aggregate CPU never met two consecutive ⇐10% samples in six attempts. No cache-warm comparison or new frame result is available; neither attempt proves or disproves removal of the prior210ms preview-wheel pause. Raw preflight samples and logs: /tmp/moonkale-next3-{warmup,desktop}*. No further headless gate iteration is planned in this run. The real GPU/desktop check remains Daniel’s final acceptance; its commands, files, seven gestures and strict versus calibrated criteria are in the coordinator handoff. WP-03 proceeds through its own milestone gates while this desktop acceptance remains explicitly open.
Idle-callback calibration correction — 2026-10-22 (P-225)
Daniel’s 2026-10-21 KDE/NVIDIA/60 Hz reports contain 1–16 ms idle callback
spacings (one sample’s median is 8 ms), followed by steady 16–18 ms gesture
frames. A median of those idle callbacks is not a refresh estimate. The FPS
host contains one recorder rAF loop; clicking Record and waiting four seconds
on private sway/Mesa did not reproduce the short callbacks. The chronological intervals alternate in pairs (13+3, 14+2, 15+1 ms),
consistent with two out-of-phase scheduling sources splitting one cadence.
WebKitGTK 2.54.1’s render scheduler
has both a display monitor and a timer fallback; the pairing is evidence for a
scheduling hypothesis, not proof that either path is at fault. WebKit’s
GTK/WPE timing issue also
explains why rAF timestamps cannot be equated with physical refresh.
The precise hardware/backend scheduling cause remains unproven; there is no evidence of a
second recorder loop. Reports now also retain idle rAF deltas to distinguish
callback scheduling from the rAF clock on the next hardware run.
Use the idle 95th percentile as the upper-envelope cadence estimate, replacing
the idle median above. Short inter-refresh callbacks no longer dominate it;
long idle stalls remain conservative calibration failures. Retain at least 30
samples, reject baselines above 17 ms, and leave both gates unchanged: fractional
p95 ≤16.7 ms/max ≤50 ms; quantized p95 ≤1.5×baseline/max ≤50 ms. The raw polluted
sample regression estimates 15 ms and accepts ordinary 60 Hz frames while
rejecting 32 ms frames. This is a scheduling estimate, not physical presentation
timing or proof of the original strict desktop requirement.
Interaction evidence counts actual arrow traversals and requires a changed
caret or viewport, because Daniel’s WebKitGTK reports delivered 91–112 arrow
keydowns with no repeat flags. Small-scroll recording counts ≤10 pixel document
viewport movements, including smooth scrolling from larger wheel deltas, and
requires trusted wheel input. Both axes use that same viewport; textarea-sink
scroll events and wheel input with no document movement are rejected. Raw wheel
axes/units and accumulated viewport travel are retained. The old 3 MB vertical
wheel attempts with zero scroll events remain invalid interactions.

decisions/ADR-0024-Block-symbols.title: ADR-0024 — Block symbols: a kind draws its own schematic
decisions/ADR-0024-Block-symbols.content:
Status: accepted 2026-10-14. Daniel’s feedback on the first MTK and RxInfer screenshots: blocks were plain filled boxes, and every acausal pin sat on the box’s top edge. “A capacitor should have a nice looking symbol instead of being a bland square … as long as the flow editor can render everything I am fine.” Written by Claude. ADR-0023 is reserved for codex’s open work. Related: ADR-0020 Undirected pins in the flow model, ADR-0022 Bipartite factor graphs, spec 031 (the graph engine’s shapes, ports and overlay), Flow Editor.
Context
The flow panel drew every block as a filled rounded rect in its category colour, with the label beside it. Pins had fixed places:

inputs on the left, outputs on the right;
acausal pins (ADR-0020) spread along the top edge.

A circuit therefore read as a row of coloured boxes with all their wires leaving upwards: a resistor’s two pins sat side by side on top, not at its two ends. Each library knows what its parts look like. The editor does not, and it should not have to: a ModelingToolkit capacitor, a Lux dense layer and an RxInfer factor are each drawn in their own field’s convention.
The engine already had what a drawing needs:

a 2D label overlay above the GPU canvas (labels and icons, spec 031 §2 stage 8);
side-based ports with an offset along the side (spec 031 §2 stage 2);
rect hit-testing.

Decision


BlockKind.symbol: Option<Symbol> (#[serde(default)]; kinds finished with ..Default::default() keep compiling). It is a library-level property, like role:
pub struct Symbol { width: f32, height: f32, path: String, anchors: Vec<Anchor> }
pub struct Anchor { port: String, side: Side, offset: f32 }   // offset 0..1, default 0.5
pub enum Side { Left, Right, Top, Bottom }

path is SVG path data only, in the box 0 0 width height (canvas units). It is stroked in the block’s colour: explicitly closed absolute M…Z subpaths fill in that colour (WP-11, 2026-10-23); no other SVG elements, nothing to sanitise beyond what Path2D parses.
anchors place each port on the box’s sides.
BlockPorts.symbol carries the symbol through Flow::ports_of. A subflow and a boundary pseudo-block have none.



The engine draws it. InNode.symbol (and InDeltaNode.symbol, where absent keeps the old symbol, like icon) holds the path in the node’s box. The overlay strokes it at ~1.6 px, zooming with the canvas, and in the hover colour (thicker) while hovered or selected. It is skipped below a few pixels (LOD) and in 3D.
The GPU body stays, but only as a faint tint. It is still the hit area and still shows hover and selection, but the symbol is the block. The label sits centred below the symbol, as on a schematic.


A better default for ports without an anchor, so no kind hangs its pins off the top:

inputs on the left, outputs on the right (unchanged);
acausal pins alternate left and right, so a two-pin part lies in its circuit’s line; a single pin goes on the left;
a factor (ADR-0022) has its first channel, the variable it generates, on the right and its parameters on the left;
a variable’s one pin stays on its circle’s top.

Unanchored ports spread evenly along their side.


ModelingToolkit draws its parts (moonkale-julia):

Resistor: a DIN/IEC box between leads;
Capacitor: two plates;
Inductor: four turns;
Voltage: a circle with + on the p side;
Ground: three bars under the pin;
Mass: a cart on wheels;
Spring: a zigzag;
Damper: a dashpot;
Fixed: a hatched wall.

A test checks that every kind has a symbol, that every pin is anchored, and that every point of the path stays in its box. Lux and RxInfer keep the box with the new default sides: dataflow left to right, and a factor’s parameters in on the left with its variable out on the right.


A block turns and mirrors (amended 2026-10-14, after Daniel’s go-ahead). Block.turn counts quarter turns clockwise (0–3), and Block.mirror flips the block left to right in its own frame, before the turn. Both are omitted from the file at their defaults, so an unturned block’s file is unchanged.

The panel turns the box (its width and height swap on an odd turn) and every port: its side and offset map clockwise, after the mirror. The engine gets the turned box plus InNode.turn/mirror, and only the drawing needs the transform.
R turns the selected blocks, and M mirrors them as seen on the canvas: for a turned block, a mirror after the turn is the opposite turn after the mirror (Block::flip). The block editor carries both as buttons (⟳, ⇋). Each is one undo step.
A symbol with a pin on its bottom (an upright part) puts its label to its right, so the wire leaving there does not cross it.
The voltage source shows only its +: a turned minus reads as a bar.



A kind may caption its blocks (amended 2026-10-14). BlockKind.caption is a template under the block’s name. Each {name} hole takes a value:

for a wired port of that name, the name of the block at the wire’s other end;
otherwise the parameter’s value, or its default;
? if the hole names neither.

ModelingToolkit captions its parts with a value and unit (1.0 Ω, 100.0 N/m). RxInfer captions each factor as it is written: θ ~ Beta(2, 7), y ~ Bernoulli(θ). The engine draws InNode.caption as a smaller, dimmer second line.


Consequences

The change is additive. BlockKind and the engine’s InNode gain defaulted fields. BlockPorts gains symbol: a caller that builds it literally adds symbol: None (inside Moonkale, only the flow panel). It shipped in ext-api-2026-10-14; moonkale-julia v0.5.0 is its first user.
Files don’t change. The symbol belongs to the kind, not to the block. A .flow.json keeps its positions, and only the drawing and the pin sides differ.
§5–6 are additive too. Block gains turn and mirror; a literal that lists every field adds turn: 0, mirror: false. BlockKind gains caption, and BlockPorts gains caption (caption: None in a literal). They shipped in ext-api-2026-10-14-2 (moonkale-julia v0.6.0).
WP-11 amendment (2026-10-23): explicitly closed absolute M…Z
subpaths fill with the block colour, including turn/mirror and hover. Open
paths remain strokes; relative moveto subpaths remain stroke-only. Regions
are independently filled (no compound holes). Symbols cap at 64 KiB and 256
fill regions per draw.
Flow’s Grid control persists editor.flow_grid: default 16 world units,
0 disables, otherwise clamped to 4–128. Palette insertion, Layout, canvas
dragging and card-header dragging persist snapped centres; Alt bypasses
dragging. The faint dot grid follows the camera. Orthogonal wire bends snap
their free axes; terminal-aligned axes remain exact so arbitrary symbol
anchors stay connected. Existing files retain their coordinates until edited.

decisions/ADR-0025-Sessions-are-the-oute.filePath: decisions/ADR-0025 Sessions are the outermost state.md
decisions/ADR-0025-Sessions-are-the-oute.title: ADR-0025 — Sessions are the outermost state, kept in the state store
decisions/ADR-0025-Sessions-are-the-oute.content:
Status: accepted 2026-10-14 (Daniel), the same day it was proposed; written by Claude. It supersedes the storage part of Projects and Sources (one JSON file per project) and builds on ADR-0014 One store for internal state (SQLite). Related: Internal State, Agent Sessions and Profiles, Collaboration.
Context

Several sources, not one folder. Moonkale opens several sources at once, not a single folder (Projects and Sources, spec 003). That design calls the saved set of sources a project and stores it as ~/.config/moonkale/projects/<id>.json.
Daniel (2026-10-14): the outermost way to manage different projects should be sessions. People switch between Moonkale sessions, which are not linked to a folder and keep the work done in them. And, as decided before, Moonkale’s state goes into a database, not file dumps. The state store exists (SQLite, ADR-0014): settings, layouts, the entity log and agent sessions moved in on 2026-10-02.
Today: state is keyed per folder: layout and open documents per folder and machine, agent sessions per folder on its host. With several sources open at once, “which folder does this layout belong to” stops having an answer.

Decision

A session is the outermost unit of Moonkale state. It is named and persistent, and not bound to a folder or any source. It holds:

Its sources: which belong to it, each open or closed, read-only or not (a property of the pair (source, session), as the Projects design has it), with its colour. Sources are members of sessions, never the other way round, and one source can belong to several sessions.
The workspace: the panel layout, open documents and the active one, each panel’s view state (a graph’s camera, a table’s query and scroll, the flow editor’s open scope), and unsaved buffers. Switching away never loses an edit.
The work done in it: agent conversations, query history, search history, run records (WP-38), notebooks’ kernels, and scratch notes that belong to no source.
Its settings: overrides in the scope order user < session < folder. The folder scope stays data, not authority (Security).
Never a secret: only secret names, resolved per machine.


Sessions live in the state store, never in files. They are rows in the user’s state.sqlite, in tables such as sessions, session_sources, and session_state (a key per panel and per kind of state). On a server they live per user, in the server’s store.

Today’s per-folder rows move under a session key: layout, open documents and agent sessions get a session column. The folder stays part of the key where the state really is about the folder.
The entity log stays per source: it records what happened to the source, whoever’s session did it.
Export and import are explicit commands (a session bundle for another machine or a colleague), not the storage format.


Switching is a first-class action. The session switcher (palette, title bar, the phone’s “More” sheet) lists sessions with their last use and members. Switching saves the current one atomically and restores the other: sources open or close, layout, documents, buffers and panels’ state. Each window shows one session; two windows may show two.
The Default session keeps today’s behaviour. Someone who never makes a session sees no change: “reopen the last folder” becomes “reopen the Default session”. The existing per-folder rows migrate into it once.
Operations: new (empty, from the current one, or from a template), rename, duplicate, archive, delete (to a trash, restorable for a while), export, import (asking once for the secrets it names), and moonkale --session <name> on the command line.
Failures are reported, never hidden: a member source that’s gone, or a remote that’s unreachable, shows as such in the session and is never silently dropped (the Projects design’s rule).

“Project” and “session”: one concept, not two. The Projects page’s project is this session; the page keeps its design for sources (open and close individually, read-only per pair, colours, failure notices, roots for portable paths) and drops its JSON storage.
The name collision, settled (Daniel, 2026-10-14): the agent’s sessions are now conversations in the UI (English, German „Unterhaltung”, Chinese 对话), and session means only this outer unit. The code and the store keep agent_sessions until the sessions migration renames it. Terminal and SSH sessions keep their word: those are processes, not saved state.
Several people and agents in one session is the next layer: participants, roles, approvals, attribution. Shared Work has it.
Consequences

Projects as files are dropped. The Projects page’s storage section is superseded, and the rest of it stands.
The store’s tables gain a session key. That is a migration (ADR-0014’s migration path), done once, with the Default session as the target of every existing row.
Sync of sessions between machines waits for the store’s sync (R-36), as everything in the store does. Until then, export and import carry a session between machines.
Collaboration: a shared server holds sessions per user. A session can later be shared read-only, a natural place for Collaboration to start.
Not decided:

whether a session can pin a source at a git revision (a reproducible session);
how long deleted sessions stay in the trash;
whether run records belong to the session or to the source they ran on (proposed: the session, with a link to the source).



Work package: WP-46 in Work Packages.

decisions/ADR-0026-Memory-and-the-store.title: ADR-0026 — What lives in memory, what goes to the store, and when
decisions/ADR-0026-Memory-and-the-store.content:
Status: accepted 2026-10-14 (Daniel), the day it was proposed, from his request (“a decision how much should be in memory and what and when things should be stored in a database”); written by Claude. Builds on ADR-0014 One store for internal state (SQLite), ADR-0025 Sessions are the outermost state and Daniel’s standing preference: Moonkale’s state goes in a database, not in file dumps. Measured by Benchmarks.
Context
Moonkale holds four kinds of data, and they have different owners:

What the user authored about their work: sessions, settings, layouts, conversations, comments, run records, the entity log. Moonkale owns it.
What a source holds: files, database rows, graph nodes. The source owns it.
What tools derive: the index, search and embeddings, layouts, rendered math, IR, inferences (Shared Work §5). No one authored it; it can be recomputed, at a cost.
What is in use right now: open documents, unsaved edits, the graph scene, a query’s result, a live run’s stream. It’s the working set.

Today the index is rebuilt on every open and kept only in memory; the state store already holds settings, layouts, the entity log and agent conversations.
Decision













































































DataTruthIn memoryIn the store, and whenSessions, settings, layouts, conversations, comments, run records’ metadatathe state storea cache of what is openwrite-through, debounced to at most 1 s after the change; on switch, close and quit at onceThe entity logthe state storethe tail being writtenappended per event, in batches of at most 250 msUnsaved editsmemory, until saved to the sourcethe buffera recovery snapshot every 2 s while dirty and on blur, switch or quit. On restart, an unsaved buffer comes back (crash safety). The snapshot is deleted on saveA source’s content (files, rows, nodes)the sourceopen documents; bounded caches of what was readnever copied wholesale into the store; only what the user saved as theirs (a saved query, a pinned answer)Derived data, expensive (the index, embeddings, layouts of large graphs, rendered math SVG, Typst output, inferences)recomputablewhile in usepersisted, keyed by input hashes (content-addressed), so reopening reuses it, and a changed input invalidates exactly its own entries (WP-21)Derived data, cheap (syntax highlighting, small layouts, a table’s sort order)recomputablewhile in usenot storedQuery resultsthe sourceup to the source’s cap (50 000 rows), with pushdown paging past it (WP-13)only when saved (a saved answer, a plot’s data)The graph scenethe enginewhat is drawn, plus the coarse tier’s aggregatesnode positions, as part of the layout (above)Live run streams (beliefs, losses, ticks)the runa ring buffer of the recent windowthe run record keeps a downsampled series; a full trace goes to DuckDB/Parquet beside the run, because its volume is analytical, not stateExternal data caches (market data, remote files)the providerwhat is in useon disk in the right engine (DBN and Parquet for market data, read through DuckDB), with a byte budget and LRU evictionSecretsthe system keychain or the environmentresolved when needed, dropped after usenever
Rules that apply to all of it:

Nothing is written on the input path. A keystroke’s frame never waits for a store write (CED-R22). Writes are debounced and run off the UI thread.
Every cache has a byte budget per platform (desktop, server per session, web, the phone) and evicts least-recently-used first. On the phone, memory pressure (Android’s trim callbacks) drops caches before Android kills the app.
The engine fits the data:

SQLite (the state store) for state;
DuckDB and Parquet for bulk analytical data (traces, market data, benchmark history);
memory for the working set;
plain files only for what users share through git (exports such as comments’ JSONL).


Persisted derived data is rebuildable: deleting the derived tables loses no work, only time. This is also the answer to any corruption of them.

Consequences

New tables: recovery snapshots of unsaved buffers, derived-data entries keyed by input hash (the index, embeddings, rendered math), cache indexes with sizes. Run traces go to their own DuckDB file per run or session.
The index persists (WP-21) instead of rebuilding on every open, so BM-03’s warm time drops to loading.
The budgets are numbers to set from Benchmarks BM-20 to BM-26, per platform, recorded in this ADR when measured.
Not decided:

whether derived data is shared across sessions (proposed: yes, keyed by input hash, so two sessions on one repository share one index);
encryption at rest for snapshots of unsaved buffers (Security, data at rest).



Work package: WP-56 in Work Packages.

decisions/ADR-0027-Simple-by-default.title: ADR-0027 — Simple by default (GNOME-like), detailed on request, shortcuts in plain sight
decisions/ADR-0027-Simple-by-default.content:
Status: accepted 2026-10-14. Daniel stated the preference; Claude wrote it up. Related: Input Layouts, Overview, Core and Extensions (the “on by default” question), Editor Prior Art (Obsidian, VS Code, Zed).
Context
Daniel: he is unsure whether the UI should be simple, GNOME-like, or complex with more menus, KDE-like. He prefers GNOME’s simplicity, but other people have other preferences. He would rather it didn’t feel like managing a spaceship, as VS Code does. And shortcuts should be presented prominently, or people won’t use them; if they’re behind too many clicks in a menu, people won’t go there.
Moonkale already grows chrome quickly: a menu bar, an activity rail with about ten entries, panel toolbars, a status bar, tabs. Every extension can add to these. Without a rule, each new extension adds a button, and the spaceship arrives one reasonable button at a time.
Decision


Two densities, Simple by default.

Simple (default, GNOME-like): a few clear controls; one primary action visible per panel; the rest in that panel’s ⋯ menu; search as the main way in (below).
Detailed (KDE-like, in Settings → Appearance): the full menu bar, more toolbar buttons, a fuller status bar, more visible options.

It’s two levels, not a slider: each is designed and tested. A keymap preset (Input Layouts) is chosen independently.


A chrome budget, enforced in review:

activity rail: at most 7 entries in Simple (the rest under “More”);
a panel’s toolbar: at most 4 visible controls in Simple;
status bar: at most 5 items in Simple, each one meaningful at a glance;
menus: at most 2 levels deep.

Extensions don’t add chrome by default: an extension’s rail entry, status item or toolbar button is offered, and the user (or the Detailed density) turns it on. Its commands are always in the palette.


Search first.

The title bar holds one search field (“Search or run a command…”) showing its shortcut. It opens quick open, the palette and the overview (Overview) as one place.
Every command is reachable within two clicks or from the palette; anything deeper is a bug.



Shortcuts in plain sight:

Everywhere a command appears, its shortcut is shown: menu items, tooltips (always “Name (Ctrl+…)”), palette rows (already the case), context menus, and the overview’s actions.
The empty workbench (no tab open in a tile) shows the six most useful shortcuts for that moment, Zed- and VS Code-style: open, search, overview, palette, new note, open with context. It updates with the context and the preset.
Hold Ctrl (about 600 ms, nothing else pressed) and every visible button shows its shortcut as a small badge (key tips, as in Office or Vimium). Releasing hides them.
Gentle nudges: the third time in a day someone runs a command with the mouse that has a shortcut, a small, non-blocking hint appears once for that command (“Ctrl+Alt+Space does this”). One setting turns them off, and they never interrupt typing.
The cheat sheet (F1, or hold Ctrl longer) lists the focused panel’s bindings, mouse buttons included (Input Layouts §5).
Getting Started has one page of the ten shortcuts that matter, per preset, printable.



No forced switches between mouse and keyboard (Daniel, 2026-10-14): GNOME’s search, where you just type and get there, is the model. The constant back and forth between mouse and keyboard that some applications require is the thing to avoid. So:


Type to search, anywhere. When no text field has the focus and the focused panel doesn’t use letters itself (a canvas or table in the left-hand layout does), typing a letter opens the title bar’s search with that letter in it: files, symbols, nodes, commands and open tabs in one list, as in GNOME’s overview. / does the same everywhere, even on a canvas.


Every flow can be finished from the keyboard alone:

a dialog or prompt takes the focus when it opens, Enter confirms, Escape cancels, and the focus returns where it was;
a new panel takes the focus;
every list, tree, grid, graph and flow has keyboard navigation.

No step needs “now click here”.


Every frequent flow can be finished from the mouse alone, with the five buttons, context menus, the overview on a mouse button (F13), and drag and drop, so someone in a mouse-heavy session (graph, flow) never reaches for the keyboard for routine actions.


No flow forces a switch in its middle:

a keyboard-started action doesn’t end in a dialog that needs a click;
a mouse-started one doesn’t end in a field that needs typing before anything else works, except where text is the point, like naming a file.



Checked in tests: a keyboard-only journey (journey-keyboard.mjs: open a folder, find a note, follow a link, open with context, run a query, switch tabs in the overview, all without the mouse) and a mouse-only journey (journey-mouse.mjs, the same with five buttons and menus).




Defaults over options: a setting is added only when a reasonable default can’t be found. Settings are searchable and grouped, so a new option doesn’t make the Settings panel the new spaceship.


Built so far (2026-10-17)

Symbols, with their description on hover:

moonkale_ext_api::icons::IconButton draws an icon; its tooltip is the description and shortcut (“Save (Ctrl+S)”, “Wrap long lines (Alt+Z)”); its label is hidden text, so screen readers name it and tests find it by its words.
The icon set moved from the shell to ext-api (icons::Icon), so every extension can use it.
Converted: the CodeMirror code editor, the Markdown rich editor, the flow editor (whose Generate keeps its words, the panel’s primary action) and the image viewer.
WP-69 (2026-10-17): the Rust editor shows Save, Reload, Wrap and ⋯. The gear is inside ⋯ to keep the complete toolbar within four controls; its popover contains shared user indentation/width and wrap settings. Less frequent commands remain in ⋯ and the palette. Escape closes ⋯ and returns focus to its trigger; Tab/Enter and touch work. The cursor word is inline and hidden below 700 px.


An extension’s settings next to its panel. A gear (icons::PanelSettingsButton) in the toolbar opens the extension’s own settings (the same view as under its row in the Extensions panel) in a popover beside the panel. The popover is titled with the extension’s name, takes the focus, closes on Escape, and links to all its settings.
