Child edges always address classes. The Rewrite provenance checkbox hides
or shows rewrite edges; selecting an operator highlights the incoming rewrite
chain, and hovering a rewrite edge shows the rule name. Selection remains
separate from that highlight. Single-class and all-class operations keep the
camera and restore hidden members’ positions. Snapshots are capped at 4 MiB,
4096 nodes, 32768 edges and 4096 groups. Live producer integration remains open.
Coarse source navigation (WP-06, 2026-10-23)
The panel chooses exact (<1,500), approximate (through 100,000) or coarse
(above 100,000) at open/Reload. Hierarchical sources answer
Query::Coarse { level, region } with stable representatives, hidden member
counts and weighted projected relations; a complete source count accompanies
the response. Auto/Detailed/Coarse overrides are remembered per source for the
mounted panel. Detailed still respects the 100k query cap. Non-hierarchical
sources keep the capped detailed path and show a lower-bound count when cut.
Double-click one coarse representative to open a region. Its members start
around the representative’s world position; context nodes are pinned and the
engine’s existing delta/group path lays out the region without fitting the
camera again. Boundary relations use the first stable member as a proxy.
Collapse removes members/group, reinstates the representative at its original
position and restores boundary relations. Only one region can be open; nested
region navigation and precise boundary membership remain future work.
The hermetic graph-coarse.mjs host exercises the production panel with a lazy
million-node source; native core tests separately project a fully generated
million-node snapshot. Source-native cached cuts/layouts remain open; the
default fallback enumerates a bounded complete snapshot (or folder metadata
walk) for each uncached region query. See Case Selector.

editors/Linked-Panels.title: Linked panels — a node's content and its context, together and marked as belonging together

editors/Markdown-Diagrams-and-Math.title: Markdown — Typst math, TikZ, Mermaid, tabs
editors/Markdown-Diagrams-and-Math.content:
From Prompt19 (2026-09-20). Two Obsidian plugins and two conventions Daniel relies on, plus the rule he set: JavaScript for these is permitted as an extension for the desktop editor when there is no Rust engine — the one sanctioned exception beyond the three editor bundles (JavaScript Inventory). Formulas via KaTeX already work (013).








































featurein Obsidianmarkdown syntaxhow in MoonkaleengineTypst mathWypst renders $…$ / $$…$$ with Typst instead of MathJax/KaTeXthe same $…$ — the content is Typst math (integral_0^1 x^2 dif x = 1/3) rather than LaTeXa setting per folder, .moonkale/markdown.json → "math": "katex" | "typst" (default katex): with typst, the rich editor’s math nodes are rendered by the typst crate that is already compiled in for the Typst preview — each formula becomes an SVG (typst compiles $…$ inside a minimal page, typst-svg renders), cached by content hash; Quartz already renders Typst math for the site via @myriaddreamin/rehype-typst, so the vault reads the same both placesRust, exists; the wiring is a Milkdown node view that asks Rust for an SVG instead of calling KaTeX (onMath(id, source) → mathResult(id, svg))TikZ diagramsInline TikZ / TikZJax renders ```tikz fences with TeX compiled to wasm in the page```tikz code fence (a full \begin{tikzpicture}… body; optional \usepackage lines)a desktop-only extension tikz (opt-in) with two backends behind one trait, chosen by what is installed: (1) native TeX — tectonic or pdflatex + dvisvgm/pdftocairo on PATH, tikz fence → SVG, cached; (2) TikZJax — the wasm TeX engine + its JS glue as a packages/js/tikzjax bundle (≈ 10 MB with the TeX memory dump; loaded on first use, never in the web build). Rust rewrite: none exists — a TeX engine in Rust is not on anyone’s roadmap; CeTZ (Typst’s TikZ analogue) is the Typst-native way to draw, and a ```cetz fence rendered by the compiled-in typst crate is the Rust path for new diagrams, offered next to tikzJS or an external binary, desktop only; never on web or mobileMermaidbuilt in (also in Quartz: this vault uses it)```mermaid fencea packages/js/mermaid bundle behind the same code-fence renderer trait (FenceRenderer { languages, render(source) → svg/html }), loaded lazily; no Rust Mermaid exists (the diagram layout engines are the hard part). Platform: desktop and web (it is plain JS, 2.5 MB, so lazy and opt-in on the phone)JSTabsan Obsidian plugin renders ```tabs blocks (tab: Title sections) as a tab strip```tabs fence with tab: headerspure Rust/Dioxus: the fence renderer trait’s first native implementation — a tab strip whose panes are markdown rendered by the rich editor itself; source stays a fence so Quartz/GitHub degrade to a code block (a Quartz plugin later)Rust
The one mechanism: code-fence renderers
The rich editor gets a fence renderer contribution (FenceRenderer in ext-api, contributed by extensions): a fence whose language matches is shown as the renderer’s output (SVG/HTML/Dioxus) with click to edit back to the source, exactly like the KaTeX block today. Tabs (Rust), CeTZ and Typst math (Rust via typst), Mermaid and TikZJax (JS bundles, desktop/web as stated) all plug into it; the source editor shows the fence with highlighting. Rendering is asynchronous and cached by content hash under .moonkale/cache/.
Platform and rules

Rust first where an engine exists: Typst math, CeTZ and tabs never touch JavaScript.
JS only as an opt-in desktop extension (Daniel’s exception): TikZJax; Mermaid is allowed on web too because it is just JS and Quartz users expect it.
Never in the core bundle: each is its own lazily loaded asset; the phone gets tabs and Typst math, not TikZ.
Static/Quartz parity: the markdown stays valid for Quartz (rehype-typst, Mermaid, code fences); tabs need a small Quartz transformer to look the same on the site.

Order (when scheduled)

Fence renderer contribution + tabs (proves the mechanism in pure Rust).
Typst math setting, SVG through the typst crate; CeTZ fence with the same path.
Mermaid bundle (JS, lazy).
TikZ extension: native TeX backend first, TikZJax second.

editors/Markdown-and-Typst-Editor.title: Markdown and Typst Editor
editors/Markdown-and-Typst-Editor.content:
Crate: editors/markdown. The knowledge half of the project.
Markdown (Obsidian conventions)

[[wiki-links]], [[page#heading|heading]], [[page|alias]], ![[embeds]], frontmatter, tags, callouts.
WYSIWYG via Milkdown (ProseMirror) behind RichTextBackend (JS Interop Boundary); source mode = the Code Editor with lang: markdown.
Milkdown round-trips to Markdown; we store Markdown, so ProseMirror-only state is intentionally lost. That’s what makes the backend replaceable.
Rust-side model (pulldown-cmark → block tree) exists regardless of backend: outline, link extraction, embeds and rename-propagation work without JS.

Parser fallback (P-212, 2026-10-17): the native Markdown presentation,
math/list/table/callout/image providers, wiki preview and documentation rendering
retain plain source when parsing fails. NUL, vertical tab and form feed bypass
pulldown-cmark before parsing on every profile; unwind builds also catch complete
parse failures. The known 0.13.4 offset-iterator crash is covered by stable tests
and four fuzz corpus inputs. Canonical bytes are unchanged; see
P-212 Markdown offset iterator can panic and Security.
Links are edges
Every link is a Links edge extracted by Indexing. Backlinks = Query::Neighbours{direction: In, kind: Links}. The “local graph” pane is the Graph View at depth 1 — no separate implementation. Links can target any node, including a database row or a symbol: [[users]] may resolve to a Postgres table. Resolution uses Obsidian’s shortest-unique-path rules, extended with source scoping.
Typst

typst is pure Rust and compiles to wasm → in-process compile on every platform (ADR-0007 Typst via the native crate).
World impl backed by the folder source (files, fonts, packages cache).
Editing: code editor + live SVG preview. A structured/WYSIWYG Typst editor is research (Typst’s AST is available via typst-syntax, which makes a block-level editor plausible later).
Diagnostics map to editor ranges like LSP diagnostics.

Diagrams
Mermaid blocks render in preview via a small JS package if/when needed (same interop rules); Typst diagrams (CeTZ) come for free with Typst. Excalidraw: open question — embed the web app behind the interop boundary, or treat .excalidraw JSON as a Block graph in the Flow Editor canvas. Leaning to the latter, later.
Phases

Source-mode markdown with link completion + backlinks + local graph.
Milkdown WYSIWYG.
Typst preview.
Embeds of any node (![[users]] renders a table).

Relative images in Rich mode (P-218, 2026-10-22)
Rich image node views resolve Markdown destinations relative to the document’s
folder in its source, through the same source lookup, image limits, freshness
checks and bounded data-URL cache as native Markdown previews. The view keeps
the original destination in Markdown, including after editing and saving.
Missing, escaping and external destinations receive no display URL. Each mount
requests at most 128 images with destinations no longer than 4096 bytes.
rich-images covers a percent-encoded subfolder image, refusal of outside and
remote paths, and saving without embedding display URLs.

editors/Math-Delimiters-and-Renderers.title: Math — any delimiter, LaTeX or Typst, error only when both fail
editors/Math-Delimiters-and-Renderers.content:
From Daniel (2026-10-14): Markdown formulas sometimes come in $, sometimes $$, sometimes \\( or \( or \[ or \\[, and all this is a pain. The Markdown editor should be robust against these choices, or be able to rewrite a file to one standard. Like the Wypst plugin, it should render in LaTeX formula style or Typst formula style, and only when both fail should it not render and show an error.
Status: planned, not built. It builds on 013 (KaTeX in the rich editor, done) and the Typst-math row of Markdown Diagrams and Math, which had one setting per folder ("math": "katex" | "typst"). This request replaces that setting with a per-formula decision.
1. Delimiters: read them all


















































FormDisplayWhere it comes from$…$inlinePandoc, Obsidian, Quartz (remark-math)$$…$$block (also inline when on one line inside text)the same\(…\)inlineLaTeX, MathJax\[…\]blockLaTeX, MathJax\\(…\\), \\[…\\]inline / blockMarkdown that escaped its backslashes (LLM output, Jupyter exports, some converters)```math fenceblockGitHub$`…`$inlineGitLaba bare \begin{equation}…\end{equation} (also align, gather, …)blockLaTeX pasted into notes
Rules, so prose and code stay prose and code:

Never inside code spans, code fences, HTML blocks, link destinations or front matter.
Dollar heuristics (Pandoc’s): an opening $ must be followed by a non-space, a closing $ must be preceded by a non-space and not followed by a digit. So “costs 5 and 10” is not math. \$ is a literal dollar.
A delimiter that opens and never closes within its block is text, not an error. Matching never spans paragraphs, except for $$ and \[, which may span lines inside one block.
The parser records which delimiter it saw, so the file is written back exactly as it was (no silent rewriting on save) and the normaliser (§3) knows what to change.

2. Renderer: LaTeX or Typst, per formula
Each formula is tried with both renderers: KaTeX for LaTeX, and the typst crate already compiled in for the Typst preview, which turns a formula into an SVG cached by content hash. The first that parses and looks like its own language renders it. The order is a setting (default: LaTeX first).
Why “parses” is not enough. Typst math is often valid LaTeX: KaTeX renders integral_0^1 x^2 dif x as italic letters without complaint. So each candidate gets a confidence, not only success or failure:

LaTeX signals: \commands, {…} groups, ^{…} and _{…}, environments.
Typst signals: multi-letter Typst symbols without a backslash (integral, sum, alpha, dif, arrow.r, RR), quoted text "…", _(…) and ^(…) groupings, frac(a, b)-style calls, .-modifiers.
A candidate that parses with no signal of its own language and with signals of the other loses to the other.
A tie (x^2 + y^2: both parse, neither has signals) renders with the first renderer in the order. Both would look the same anyway.

Only when both fail does the formula not render. It then shows its source, outlined as an error, with both messages on hover (KaTeX’s and Typst’s), and it appears in the diagnostics of that document. It never breaks the rest of the document.
Settings, layered like every Moonkale setting (user → folder .moonkale/markdown.json → document front matter):
{ "math": {
    "order": ["latex", "typst"],
    "force": null,
    "katex_macros": ".moonkale/katex.toml",
    "typst_preamble": ".moonkale/math.typ"
} }

order sets the tie-break and the try order.
force: "latex" or force: "typst" switches detection off for a folder or document, which is the old per-folder setting.
Macros (spec 013) apply to LaTeX; a Typst preamble (#let definitions) applies to Typst.
A formula can also say what it is: $$typst …$$, or a fence ```math typst, overrides detection.

3. Normalise: rewrite a file to one convention
A command, Normalise math, for one file, a selection, or a folder:

Target delimiters: $/$$ (the default, which Quartz and Obsidian read) or \(/\[.
It also turns doubled backslashes (\\() into single ones and bare \begin{equation} blocks into $$ blocks.
Optionally, it marks each formula’s language: $$typst …$$ for formulas detected as Typst, so another tool or another person’s setting reads them the same.
It always shows a diff first, touches only math (never code or prose), and is one undo step. A folder run lists the changed files and can be reverted as one entry in History.
On save: a folder setting "normalise_on_save": true applies it automatically. It is off by default, since rewriting a file someone else also edits should be a choice.

Converting a formula between LaTeX and Typst (tex2typst-style) is a later, separate command. Normalising changes delimiters only.
4. Where it applies

Rich editor: both renderers inline and in blocks; clicking a formula edits its source as today (013).
Source editor and the native live preview: the same parser (one Rust crate, shared), so highlighting, folding and preview agree on what is math.
Index and search: formulas are indexed as math (their source), not as prose.
The website (Quartz): remark-math reads $ and $$ only, so the normaliser’s default target is what the site needs. A note written with \( renders in Moonkale today and on the site after normalising.

5. Acceptance

A fixture note containing every form in the table renders every formula.
“costs 5 and 10” stays text, and code spans and fences are untouched.
Side by side: \int_0^1 x^2\,dx renders with KaTeX, integral_0^1 x^2 dif x with Typst, x^2+y^2 with the first in order, and \frac{a}{ shows the error with both messages.
Normalising the fixture yields only $/$$, and re-reading it gives the same formulas, rendered the same.
Saving a file without normalising leaves its bytes unchanged.

Work package: WP-36 in Work Packages.

editors/Notebook-Editor.title: Notebook editor (.ipynb) — plan
editors/Notebook-Editor.content:
From Prompt19 and the follow-up (2026-09-20): Daniel does not want dependencies of this kind in the core, but would not object to a notebook window safely behind an extension. The file and the kernel separate cleanly, so the extension can have the first without committing to the second.
The file — easy, no new dependencies
.ipynb is JSON (nbformat 4): cells[] of type markdown / code / raw, each code cell with execution_count and outputs[] — stream (stdout/stderr text), display_data / execute_result (a MIME bundle: text/plain, text/html, image/png and image/jpeg as base64, image/svg+xml, text/markdown, text/latex, application/json), error (traceback) — plus metadata.kernelspec and metadata.language_info naming the kernel and language.
Everything needed to show it exists:

markdown cells → the rich editor (with KaTeX, 013, and wiki-links, 012);
code cells → the code editor with the grammar from language_info.name (Python and Julia both highlight, 010); the LSP can be attached later by writing the concatenated cells to a shadow file;
outputs → text, inline images, SVG, KaTeX for text/latex, markdown through the rich renderer, and text/html in a sandboxed iframe srcdoc (the webview renders it; no JavaScript dependency of ours). application/javascript outputs are shown as source, never run.
editing: cell text, add / move / delete / change type, clear outputs, save back with unknown fields preserved (#[serde(flatten)] extra: Map on cells, outputs and metadata — the same round-trip discipline as the flow files), nbformat_minor kept.

Size: about the table editor plus glue. Platforms: desktop, web, phone (viewing).
Execution — medium; where the dependencies would be
Running a cell means the Jupyter kernel protocol: discover kernelspecs (kernel.json under ~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels, /usr/share/jupyter/kernels, or jupyter kernelspec list --json), launch the kernel process with a connection file (ports, key, transport), and speak ZeroMQ on five sockets (shell, iopub, stdin, control, heartbeat) with HMAC-SHA256-signed JSON messages (execute_request → execute_reply + stream / display_data / error on iopub; kernel_info_request; interrupt / shutdown).
The one real dependency is ZeroMQ: the zeromq crate is pure Rust (no libzmq), so it lives behind a Cargo feature (moonkale-ext-notebook/kernel) that desktop and the server enable and the web client never does; HMAC/SHA-2/uuid are already in the tree. Around 1 500 lines. It gives Python via ipykernel and Julia via IJulia — also the honest path to the Julia REPL wished for in Julia and Lenticulum, since a kernel is a REPL with rich output. The web client executes through the server like the terminal; the phone views only.
Out of scope, stated up front
ipywidgets (need a JavaScript comm layer and kernel-side state — exactly the dependency to avoid); running application/javascript outputs; the .py percent-format notebooks (a later importer); collaborative editing of a notebook (the entity log covers the file like any other).
Shape
packages/extensions/notebook/ — opt-in (Extension Catalogue): an editor contribution for .ipynb (is_notebook), the cell list as a Dioxus panel reusing CodeEditorPanel/rich views per cell, a NotebookBackend trait with View (all platforms) and Kernel (feature kernel, desktop + server, wired like spawn_terminal through WorkspaceConfig). Cell outputs are cached by cell id; big base64 images fall under the size tiers of Case Selector. The agent gets notebook.run_cell as a tool under the policy gate (Mutating: it executes code).
Steps (when scheduled)

nbformat types + round-trip test on a real notebook; the viewer (cells, outputs, sandboxed HTML).
Editing and saving; keyboard model (Esc/Enter, A/B, Shift+Enter = run when a kernel exists).
kernel feature: kernelspec discovery, launch, ZeroMQ session, execute/interrupt/restart, status in the toolbar; E2E with ipykernel on the server.
IJulia, LSP shadow file, the agent tool.

editors/Overview.title: Overview — every open tab at a glance, then switch
editors/Overview.content:
From Daniel (2026-10-14): GNOME has a feature where one key shows all open windows of the desktop at once, and you switch between them from there. Moonkale can’t use the Windows key, but similar behaviour, where you immediately see what each open tab holds (or schemas or symbols standing for it), would be good.
What it is
The overview is a full-window layer above the workbench. It shows a card for every open tab, in every tile and every window of the session, and a search field that already has the focus. Choosing a card switches to that tab and closes the overview. It complements quick open (Ctrl+P), which finds files you have not opened, and the tab bar, which shows names, not content.
Opening it (decided)

Ctrl+Alt+Space on desktop and web. It is free in Moonkale’s keymap and rarely taken by desktop environments or browsers; Ctrl+Tab is not possible in the web build, where the browser owns it. Configurable like every keybinding.
A button in the activity bar (top) and in the phone’s More sheet. On the phone the overview is the natural tab switcher.
Optional hot corner (off by default): moving the pointer into the window’s top-left corner.
Escape, the same shortcut, or a click on the background closes it without switching.

The cards
Each card is a preview drawn by the extension that owns the tab: a small, cheap schematic of its content, not a screenshot (screenshots of webview panels are expensive and stale). Examples:













































TabPreviewMarkdown noteits title, the first lines rendered (headings, a formula, a list), its tagsCode filefile name, language, the outline of its symbols as a minimap-like column, the cursor’s line markedGraph viewa miniature drawing of its current layout (dots and lines from the engine’s positions, in the nodes’ colours), node and edge countsFlowthe blocks as their symbols at thumbnail size, the issue countTableits columns and the first rows, the row countImagethe image itself, scaledTerminalits last linesConversationthe last exchange, and a dot when the agent is working or waiting for approvalPlot, runthe plot at thumbnail size; a run’s state and progress
On each card:

the tab’s title;
its unsaved dot;
its git status letter;
its link group’s colour and marker (Linked Panels);
who else is looking at it (presence);
the source’s colour.

A tab whose extension has no preview yet shows its icon, title and path.
Layout and finding

Grouped: by link group first (a note and its local graph side by side as one cluster), then the ungrouped tabs; each window of the session is a labelled section. The order inside each is most recently used first.
Typing filters at once: by title, path, kind and the preview’s text. A lone match is preselected, so Enter switches.
Below the open tabs, the same query runs through quick open (files, symbols, nodes) and the command palette, so one shortcut and a few letters reach anything. This is what GNOME’s overview does with apps and files.
Keyboard: arrows move between cards, Enter switches, Shift+Enter opens the card in the tile beside, Delete closes the tab (with the usual unsaved-changes prompt), and Tab moves to the next group.
Mouse: click switches, middle-click closes, and dragging a card onto a tile’s edge in the overview docks it there.

Performance and behaviour (decided)

It opens in under 100 ms, with 50 tabs open. Previews are rendered lazily at card size, cached per document revision, and only for cards on screen (virtualised like the table grid). Measured as a benchmark (BM-01’s family, Benchmarks).
It is a snapshot. Previews don’t update live while the overview is open, except the conversation’s working dot and a run’s progress, which are cheap.
Animation: a 150 ms zoom-out from the current layout to the cards, off when the system or the user asks for reduced motion.
Other windows: on the desktop, choosing a card from another window focuses that window. On the web, a card from another browser tab says “open in another tab” (a page can’t focus another tab) and offers to move the tab here.
Accessibility: the overview is a grid of named items, each card’s accessible name is its title plus kind plus state, and it’s fully usable from the keyboard.

Extension API
Extension::preview(panel_id, ws, size) -> Option<Element> is a new, optional method that draws a small, static preview. Its rules:

no subscriptions, no I/O beyond what the panel already holds;
a time budget, beyond which the card falls back to icon and title.

The graph engine gains a snapshot(width, height) that draws its current positions into a small canvas, so graph and flow previews don’t need a second view.
Steps

The overview layer with icon-and-title cards, grouping by window and link group, typing to filter, the keyboard, and the shortcut. It is useful at once.
Extension::preview and previews for Markdown, code, table, image, terminal and conversation.
The engine’s snapshot, giving graph and flow previews.
Quick open and the command palette below the open tabs.
Other windows, drag-to-dock, the hot corner, the animation.

Acceptance (overview.mjs):

with twelve tabs open in two tiles, Ctrl+Alt+Space shows twelve cards in under 100 ms;
typing “alp” leaves Alpha.md alone and Enter switches to it;
a linked note and its graph appear side by side with their group’s marker;
Delete on a card closes that tab.

Work package: WP-60 in Work Packages.

editors/Rust-Code-Editor-Accessibility-a.filePath: editors/Rust Code Editor Accessibility and Cutover.md
editors/Rust-Code-Editor-Accessibility-a.title: Rust Code Editor Accessibility and Cutover
editors/Rust-Code-Editor-Accessibility-a.content:
Status: acceptance work on 2026-10-15. The release default is still CodeMirror.
This page records the gates that do not need Daniel’s desktop or phone. See
Rust Code Editor Roadmap, Rust Code Editor Native Acceptance,
Code Editor Requirements and P-198 Rust editor accessibility and backend activation.
Accessibility contract
The Rust engine owns the text, caret, selection and history. The input textarea
is a transport, not a second text document. Its accessible name includes the file
path. It is the single editable textbox; the virtualized source is a named reading
region. One stable polite, atomic status exposes the canonical caret and selection
endpoints plus a bounded current-line excerpt (at most 160 source scalars and a
leading ellipsis). Long lines never create a full accessible textarea mirror.
The hidden input remains empty; this does not implement the full native
editable-text document API. Reading arbitrary source uses engine arrow navigation
and its canonical context, or the mounted source reading region.
Primary-M toggles Tab between indentation and focus movement, announced in the
status and explained by the input’s help. The default remains indentation.
Shift-Tab can return to the input after leaving it. The transport has a fixed
viewport position so programmatic focus does not scroll the page mid-gesture. Search, rename, completion,
references/actions and hover have keyboard paths; Escape returns to source.
Primary-Enter follows a wiki-link, or a Markdown link/standalone image with preview enabled, at the caret through the same guarded resolver
as pointer navigation. Preview controls retain their own native button/input
behavior. Focus uses theme tokens, and prefers-reduced-motion disables editor
animations/transitions and smooth scrolling.
native-editor-accessibility.mjs checks the actual Chromium accessibility tree,
not only DOM labels, and a mouse-free editing/tool/focus journey. It checks source
contrast under the production built-in palette with reduced motion: observed
minima 5.54:1 light, 4.58:1 dark. These are sampled source/gutter colors in the
fixture, not a guarantee for arbitrary user themes or every rendered widget.
native-editor-accessibility.py creates a private session/accessibility bus and
owned headless display, then inspects GTK WebKit’s actual AT-SPI tree. It verifies
the named input/help and a status-bar text interface containing caret/selection
context with live=polite. WebKit exposes dynamic context in the status text;
its input description may contain only the static help. The runner uses the
installed GI/Atspi typelib and dbus-daemon and uses short temporary socket paths
(never a temporary build target). It stops its display and session bus and retains
logs under this worktree’s target. It never inspects the user’s bus or screen.
These checks establish accessibility semantics and keyboard behavior. They are
not a speech-engine transcript, a real OS-input/IME test, or acceptance on Android,
macOS or Windows. Earlier Linux physical-input/IME evidence remains in
Rust Code Editor Native Acceptance.
One setting, no destructive migration
The existing editor.implementation is the only user backend setting:

























Stored valueResolved behaviorabsent or unknownsettings::DEFAULT_CODE_EDITOR, currently codemirrorcodemirrorexplicit CodeMirror preferencenativeRust; implicitly activates its shipped extension unless explicitly disabledexplicit Rust extension disablefallback to CodeMirror, including when the global backend preference is Rust
Resolution does not rewrite the stored file or extension lists. Explicit
per-document toolbar choices win for the current session; they are not new
persisted state. User/workspace/environment precedence is unchanged. The core
Code extension also honors Rust selection when the optional adapter is absent in
a minimal distribution. This keeps the future release-default flip in one public
constant, without requiring a second extension-default edit or another UI switch.
A test deliberately asserts that the release constant is still codemirror.
Canonical open documents keep their NodeId, source, text and dirty state while
panels change. The Rust view restores the active canonical UTF-16 caret/range on
mount, including reversed selections and CRLF/non-BMP text. Its Workspace history
continues for subsequent Rust edits; CodeMirror’s private pre-switch undo stack is
not converted into Rust transactions. Existing Rust history can be invalidated by
external CodeMirror edits according to the existing revision contract. No save,
reload or source write is a side effect of a backend change.
editor-migration.mjs checks two live unsaved buffers, exact Unicode/CRLF saves,
active reversed selection, one-setting activation without an extension enable
list, per-document fallback across global changes, and saved-document/layout
restoration after reopening the folder. A browser reload restores saved tabs;
it does not promise crash recovery for unsaved buffers (WP-56 owns that).
Build and size evidence
editor-build-cost.py builds the production-panel desktop fixture into a new
worktree-local target, then measures no-change and application-only rebuilds in
the same target/profile/features. Dependencies are already downloaded; the
compiler/toolchain and filesystem caches are not asserted cold. It records wall
time and compiler/linker maximum RSS, not application resident memory. It also
records raw/gzip sizes of the native fixture, current release web server/wasm and
the CodeMirror bundle. The optional --desktop phase also builds the actual
moonkale desktop binary in the existing, partially cached target, recording its own time,
compiler/linker RSS and raw/gzip size. Reserve bench.lock and both heavy slots; use heavy.sh.
The web bundle directory retains old fingerprinted assets between builds, so its
accumulated disk usage is not the shipped client size. Use the current wasm
artifact and its reachable asset set, not du over old fingerprints. Both
backends still ship. The matched CodeMirror-versus-Rust setting comparison uses
the same artifacts and build: backend selection is runtime configuration,
not a Cargo feature or rebuild, so switching alone changes build/size cost by
zero. These measurements cannot predict savings from a future native-only build;
that comparison belongs after the zero-consumer removal audit.
The first fresh-target attempt failed after 257.54 s because upstream
dioxus-code writes its generated CSS into the read-only Cargo registry. That
failed attempt is retained in target/next4-build-cost-20261015.json; it is not a
clean-build pass. The retry uses --prebuilt-theme-assets (upstream’s DOCS_RS=1
skip-generation branch) with already-generated registry CSS. The variable applies
to the fixture and a separate cargo build -p dioxus-code theme seed in the
product target. The actual desktop phase removes it because native database
build scripts also interpret it. Cargo reuses this upstream script’s output
(it does not watch DOCS_RS); both normal product compilation and linking still
run. The first normal desktop attempt also failed at the registry write after
511.99 s, retained in target/next4-build-cost-assets-final.json; that time is
not a successful desktop clean-build result. No registry files/permissions are changed.
The surviving NEXT-4 report ends at that failed desktop phase: its fixture
fresh-target/no-change/application-only phases completed in 213.365/0.217/4.683 s,
with compiler/linker maxima 1,533,996/128,116/673,292 KiB. Its artifacts table is
empty. Those fixture timings were not the final isolated repeat and remain
diagnostic evidence. The proposed isolated repeat, final native report and actual desktop
release binary were never produced; they are not acceptance results. The initial
AT-SPI pass remains target/next4-native-accessibility-5.json. The post-link gate
log also ends during compilation; the earlier complete gate log and Claude’s
subsequent green merged-base gates/CI are separate evidence.
NEXT-5 fixes the build-cost tool’s obsolete public/wasm/web_bg.wasm assumption.
It follows index.html to its shipped bootstrap and the bootstrap’s explicit wasm
reference, rejecting missing/ambiguous paths before building. Reports include
exact artifact paths and SHA-256 hashes, so stale fingerprinted assets cannot
silently become the measurement.
The NEXT-4 release-web frame run is 20/21 strict, not an accepted matrix:
preview-on Rust scrollbar dragging p95/max 33.335 ms missed 16.7 ms. Other cases
passed. Raw target/next4-fps-web/editor-fps.json retains every frame; the bench
lock and both heavy slots were reserved. It preceded only the final keyboard
link/image follow addition. Earlier 21/21 WP-02 evidence is a separate run; do not
replace this failed case with that result. Physical desktop frames remain open.
Final isolated build and size results
Report: target/next5-build-cost.json; logs/RSS files: target/next5-build-cost-logs/, orchestration /tmp/moonkale-next5-build-cost-final.log. Bench lock and both heavy slots held through every phase and size capture. Worktree-local fresh target target/next5-isolated-native; jobs=2, release, locked/offline; downloaded dependencies and warm filesystem/compiler caches are allowed. Report HEAD is base 6cd65e30 plus the uncommitted NEXT-5 changes. The initial product attempt fails at the upstream Ladybug registry metadata write/source fallback (P-199); the identical normal retry is separately measured in target/next5-desktop-retry.json, with compiler output target/next5-desktop-retry.log. The freshly measured release fixture also passes GTK WebKit/AT-SPI and the visible focus-border probe: target/next5-isolated-native-accessibility.json, log /tmp/moonkale-next5-isolated-a11y.log. This independently executes the fresh/prebuilt-theme-assets artifact; the earlier final native report tested the ordinary release fixture. Both owned displays/buses are stopped.
Reproduce with fresh target/report names:

  env MOONKALE_SLOTS=1 ~/.claude/projects/-home-daniel-Code-Moonkale/scratchpad/heavy.sh \

Release-web focus decoration regression
NEXT-5 reproduced NEXT-4’s failure on the unchanged release build:
target/next5-fps-baseline/editor-fps.json is 20/21 strict; preview scrollbar
p95/max 33.335/33.340 ms. A quiet-machine diagnostic CPU/timeline capture is in
target/next5-fps-profile/{scrollbar.cpuprofile,scrollbar-trace.json}. Native DOM
replaceWith accounts for about 955 ms of sampled self time over the gesture;
the timeline records only 83 ms layout and 51 ms style updates.
Same-build CSS removal/restoration isolates the new surface focus outline.
Changing only the selector, focus-visible matching and overlay/composited rings
all failed first-drag acceptance; those experiments are discarded. In particular,
a repeated drag must refocus the input and reset caret/viewport just as the full
matrix does. Repeating a drag without that reset can hide the initial failure.
The focus-state trace is target/next5-fps-focus-states/scroll-focus.json.
The final design reserves a transparent 2 px border on all four surface edges and
changes only its color on :focus-within. Focus cannot change layout. The surface
is excluded from the generic control outline selector; individual controls retain
their outlines. This preserves the visible source ring for both keyboard and
pointer focus, including descendant tools, without ever outlining the ancestor
of the virtual rows. The viewport has 4 px less content space in each dimension;
its existing mounted-rectangle geometry remains authoritative. Live accessibility
context, canonical selection restoration, input location and reduced motion are
unchanged. No Rust input/rendering logic is modified.
The routed-CSS diagnostic target/next5-fps-border/editor-fps.json passes all
seven preview gestures. Its log /tmp/moonkale-next5-border.log additionally
retains three independently refocused/reset scrollbar drags, all p95/max
16.670/16.670 ms. This subset is not full release acceptance. The keyboard suite
checks ring entry, exit, return and descendant hover focus; the native accessibility
probe verifies the same border in GTK WebKit.
The rebuilt full 21-case strict release-web matrix passes 21/21:
target/next5-fps-final/editor-fps.json, Chromium153.0.8010.12, no page errors.
Every p95 is ⇐16.670 ms; maximum frame is 33.335 ms. Preview scrollbar:
132 frames, interacted=true, p95/max 16.670/33.335 ms. The unchanged full runner
retains the input/caret/viewport reset before every gesture and all interaction
assertions. Bench lock and both heavy slots were held; bounded CPU settling
samples are in the adjacent preflight.json. No failed case or warm-up sample
was removed. This is web acceptance only; physical-desktop and Android remain
separate gates.
The after-change diagnostic profile is
target/next5-fps-final-profile/{scrollbar.cpuprofile,scrollbar-trace.json}.
It runs the same 12-case source/preview prefix through scrollbar dragging, not
the full matrix. Sampled replaceWith self time is about 726 ms versus 955 ms
before; timeline layout/style totals are 43/26 ms versus 83/51 ms. Scroll event
coalescing differs, so these gesture totals are not a per-event speedup claim.
The profile itself also passes that scrollbar case; only the separate unprofiled
21-case report is used for full web acceptance.
NEXT-5 repository gates pass (/tmp/moonkale-next5-gates-final.log): fmt,
dependency/color/string/frontmatter checks, 673 tests passed, 5 ignored,
workspace all-target Clippy with warnings denied, minimal/Julia distribution,
public rustdoc and web wasm. The desktop fixture release build and all-target
Clippy pass too. The fresh native WebKit/AT-SPI report
target/next5-native-accessibility-final.json passes named input/help, polite
caret/selection text and a visible 2 px solid source border. Its private display
and buses are stopped. All 41 native-editor Chromium suites pass on the rebuilt
fixture (/tmp/moonkale-next5-native-accepted.log, per-suite output under
target/next5-native-e2e). The earlier browser attempt overlapped a fixture
rebuild and hit a missing wasm bootstrap; it is not final acceptance evidence. No physical desktop, speech transcript or Android
acceptance is implied.
Retirement sequence

Now: keep CodeMirror as the release default and explicit fallback. Both
implementations, the switch UI and generated bundle remain. Test accessibility,
migration, builds and release web frames. No setting or saved layout is erased.
After Daniel’s desktop and Android gates: change DEFAULT_CODE_EDITOR to
native and update its deliberate guard test. Unspecified preferences use Rust;
explicit CodeMirror settings and per-document fallbacks continue to work.
Keep the fallback for an accepted release while checking remaining consumers.
After that fallback release and a zero-consumer audit: make the core Code
extension’s stable editor: identity the Rust owner; retain an alias for old
editor-native: layout IDs during restoration. Map legacy implementation values
deliberately rather than discarding open documents. Markdown Source and SVG
source views must be on the Rust path first.
Remove code-view/src/backend/codemirror.rs, CodeMirror-specific panel/bridge
paths, code-view/assets/codemirror.js, packages/js/codemirror and its build
scripts/dependencies only after window.moonkale.codemirror has no production
consumers. Move shared toolbar/LSP/URI/edit contracts rather than deleting them.
Convert control-only browser tests/selectors to the Rust semantic hooks; keep
shared UTF-16 conversion, revision, source and workspace tests. Remove obsolete
extension/switch/settings UI only after persisted IDs have an explicit mapping.
Re-run full platform, fidelity, accessibility, large-file, frame, size/build and
dependency gates; update Code Editor, Code Editor Implementations,
Extension Catalogue, Status and crate notes. Milkdown, xterm and other JS
views remain outside this retirement.

This is a conditional retirement plan, not a deletion or a default flip in this
change. ADR-0029 is unused; the plan implements the accepted Rust-editor direction.
What remains for Daniel before the flip

Physical Linux desktop frames: the existing 21-case CED-R22 checklist in the
handoff, using release builds, the real GPU/session, highlighted 5000-line Rust
with Doc preview off/on and the 3 MB line. Seven gestures per mode. Retain raw
strict/calibrated results, inspect the earlier ~210 ms preview-wheel pause and
confirm smooth real input. Do not substitute the headless software-GL result.
Android: test the integrated shipped app after selecting Rust with the one
setting. Open/reopen source tabs; type and select Unicode; exercise a real soft
keyboard and Chinese IME, copy/cut/paste, undo/redo and exact save/reload. Check
touch selection/wrap/scroll, Markdown Source/wiki behavior and accessibility
names/focus. Missing local LSP must leave editing usable; remote-server LSP is a
separate supported connection path. Record device/OS/app build, failures and
saved bytes. No Android install or acceptance is claimed here.

macOS/Windows remain explicitly unverified. Optional spoken-reader review can
improve the bounded-context experience; the automated reports do not claim to
capture spoken output.
WP-69 toolbar follow-up — 2026-10-17
Activating a command in the ⋯ menu restores its trigger when the command does not move focus to editing or a dialog. Show hover leaves that trigger focused; Tab traversal across gutter buttons preserves the popup until it can receive focus, and Escape restores the input sink. The browser keyboard journey asserts trigger restoration explicitly. Native comments use the shell’s readable hint token, and selected source uses its code foreground token, covering the actual light/dark code and selection backgrounds at the existing 4.5:1 threshold. This adds no speech-engine or physical-device acceptance claim.

editors/Rust-Code-Editor-Implementation.title: Rust Code Editor Implementation
editors/Rust-Code-Editor-Implementation.content:
WP-69 — compact toolbar (2026-10-17)
The Rust toolbar shows four controls: Save, Reload, Wrap and ⋯, using SVG symbols,
hidden accessible labels and descriptive tooltips with available shortcuts. The
extension’s gear sits in ⋯ so the overflow trigger also fits the four-control
budget. Indentation style and width are shared user preferences, now edited in
that gear’s settings popover. Both adapters share these controls in code-view;
the core Code extension contributes the Rust palette routes too, so the minimal
distribution’s Rust fallback keeps them. Preview, LSP tools, comments, folding and the
CodeMirror switch are in ⋯; commands remain available in the palette. Tab reaches
the disclosure and its commands, Enter or touch opens it, and Escape closes it
and returns focus to the trigger. Choosing a command closes the disclosure.
The cursor word is inline in the toolbar, hidden below 700 px, so it consumes no
source row. The path truncates on narrow screens and language/version metadata
is hidden there. toolbar-icons.mjs covers native icons, the four-control budget,
overflow keyboard/touch behavior, indentation settings and phone height;
code-native.mjs opens ⋯ before switching backends.
Focus outline and virtualized subtree replacement (2026-10-15)
NEXT-4’s unconditional ancestor focus outline (:focus-within) regressed release-web documentation-preview
scrollbar dragging to 33.335 ms p95. The Chromium CPU profile attributes about
955 ms to replaceWith over the gesture, versus 83 ms layout and 51 ms style
updates. Removing/restoring the rule on the same running build removes/restores
the steady failure; removing only the separate control focus rule does not.
Changing only the selector or using focus-visible/overlay rings did not pass the
first-drag gate. The final CSS reserves a transparent 2 px surface border and
changes its color on focus-within; the generic control outline excludes the
surface itself. This retains a visible ring for source and descendant focus
without an outline on the virtual rows’ ancestor. Focus does not move layout;
the viewport’s mounted rectangle accounts for the 4 px reserved in each dimension.
Canonical accessibility context, selection restoration, keyboard exits and visible
focus remain. The keyboard suite checks the surface ring on entry, exit, return
and descendant hover focus. See Rust Code Editor Accessibility and Cutover
for retained diagnostic reports and the final release matrix.
Profile-led geometry transport (2026-10-15)
A WebKit Inspector wheel trace recorded 1070 synchronous resize events for 69 scroll events. Proportional runs now share a geometry-only resize observer, skip redundant initial entries and report actual dimension changes asynchronously. Removal/replacement closes subscriptions; the last removal disconnects both observers. Rust still owns source, selection, presentation and stale-geometry validation. The browser font/remount suite verifies exactly one watcher per live run and cleanup after unmount.
Atomic preview source now sends one representative complete grapheme to the browser instead of redundant records that the existing adapter immediately deduplicates. Scalar/UTF-16 positions still count all source; partial-grapheme overlaps remain unchanged. Two unit tests cover a 16,384-character range and Unicode boundaries. These reduce synchronous IPC/allocation work; they do not by themselves establish the frame gate.
Profile-led Rust highlighting (2026-10-15)
The desktop CPU profile identified full-file highlight query collection, rather than the incremental parse itself, as the dominant Rust typing stage. native_highlight.rs keeps the Rust tree and cached global spans, edits the tree in normalized byte coordinates, and re-queries affected root children with neighbouring boundaries. It includes text-only predicate changes, shifts unaffected spans, expands through coalesced captures and retains zero-width missing-token captures at EOF. Other grammars still use dioxus-code’s buffer. The direct arborium-theme edge reuses the already-locked 2.18.2 package to preserve capture-to-class mapping; no new package/version or public extension API is introduced.
Differential tests compare against fresh whole-file highlighting, including Unicode, lexical changes and edits across separated items. The matched release CPU profile reduces highlight p95 from approximately 7.5 to 2.0 ms and edit callback p95 from 7.7 to 2.1 ms. Validation: 671 workspace tests, all repository gates, native fixture desktop Clippy/release build, all 40 native browser suites and recorder transport pass. The latest strict release web matrix passes all 21 cases (p95 about 16.67 ms, max 33.33 ms). Overall software-GL desktop frame results remain variable and failing; this does not establish a frame pass. Both WebView clocks are quantized, so reports distinguish the calibrated-vsync fallback from the original strict interval gate. See the roadmap and ADR-0023 for raw reports and remaining acceptance.
Documentation preview (2026-10-14)
The opt-in native editor has a separate, default-off Doc preview setting for Rust, Python and Julia. Syntax-recognized documentation renders a text/code Markdown subset; source entry or selection reveals the exact owned comment/string, with code wrapping unchanged. Unsupported literals and media/execution syntax remain source or literal text. See ADR-0017 for recognition, ownership and cache rules.
Functional checks pass: 664 workspace tests and all 40 native browser suites. Twelve earlier full-app suites passed, including all three languages’ CRLF save/undo/redo and lsp2; all 16 CodeMirror Source corpus files round-trip byte-exact. The final same-file two-core typing check measured Source 80/114 ms and previews 90/91 ms median/p95 with unchanged bounds. The release web 60 FPS matrix passes all 21 cases at approximately 16.67 ms p95, with a longest frame of 33.33 ms. Desktop release acceptance remains open: headless software-GL runs confirm both public clocks are quantized and still expose real frame stalls; the recorder retains both clocks and labels a calibrated-vsync fallback separately from the original strict interval gate. The native fixture supports manual trusted-input recording and the private-display compositor harness. editor-fps.mjs records frame intervals and long-task diagnostics separately; see ADR-0023 Native editor frame measurements.
Default renderer investigation (2026-10-07)
The native fixture now has a mounted DOM probe for focus, editing, selection replacement, undo and resize. With Dioxus’s default Linux configuration and no externally supplied renderer flags, it passes; an updated native pixel capture also shows the edited source. A production renderer defect was not reproduced, so no compositing override was added to Moonkale.
native-editor-renderer.py isolates one fixture process, removes external renderer overrides, applies a bounded initialization wait and cleans up its owned process. Optional OS/pixel tests find the owned window by PID; the desktop input script also validates that the Workspace report belongs to that PID. Concurrent fixtures had stalled startup and generic window-title selection could target a different instance.
The current optional OS run still stops at mapped-window detection. The DOM probe is explicitly synthetic and does not accept OS input or IME. Default native OS acceptance remains pending, alongside the existing platform/accessibility/theme gates; Rust remains opt-in. Native fixture build and Clippy pass. See Rust Code Editor Native Acceptance for commands and precise scope.
M5 real-server and native acceptance (2026-10-07)
The real rust-analyzer integration now checks diagnostics, didChange, hover, completion, definition, references, rename and code actions using the shared protocol client. The edited source contains emoji and CRLF; assertions check UTF-16 definition/reference and rename ranges. The installed rust-analyzer 1.98.1 passes. This establishes transport/protocol coverage, not combined native UI navigation against a live server.
The production-panel fixture now supports desktop as well as web. Native XWayland/WebKit checks pass for actual OS pointer focus and forward/backward drag selection, typing, keyboard selection, Unicode copy/cut/paste, undo/redo and input after resize. The test preserves the previous text clipboard. Direct cargo runs embed the exact production styles; optional Workspace text and measured-cell reports are fixture instrumentation only.
The native drag failure came from a cursor-word row being inserted above the viewport during mouse-down. The panel now reserves its height and clips long words to keep source geometry stable. The regular desktop test includes forward/backward drag replacement and undo; the browser geometry suite checks visibility changes during both drag directions. Native focus tests wait for the asynchronous input-sink focus request.
Remaining gates: default-configuration native OS input is still pending; the default native DOM/painting probe now passes without external renderer flags. Integrated real IME, accessibility, themes, Wayland gestures and other native platforms remain open. Rust stays opt-in. See Rust Code Editor Native Acceptance for commands, scope and platform limits.
Verified: nine LSP/local tests, LSP-local and desktop-fixture Clippy with -D warnings, desktop fixture build, formatting/diff checks and the production browser workspace/resize/remount suites. The browser 3 MB check measured 1039 ms with 21 rows / 2184 cells. The native baseline now includes and passes pointer dragging. The drag fix also passes 74 code-view tests, native-desktop Clippy, the forward/backward browser geometry regression, hover and the full editing suite; its 3 MB check measured 886 ms with 20 rows / 2080 cells.
M4 reveal and workspace integration (2026-10-06)
Native views republish their retained caret, selection and word context on activation. Switching documents clears the previous cursor/presence context until the new view reports its caret. External replacement/reload synchronizes the model and republishes its actual position; reveal synchronizes canonical text before converting UTF-16 coordinates. Closing a document clears its pending reveal while a workspace-owned counter keeps subsequent requests monotonic.
Pending viewport measurements now check that their model and local signals still exist after browser geometry promises return, preventing a close-time crash. The blank-line hit area includes the presence gutter slot, so it no longer covers the last characters of a line. Root-owned view state retains caret, history and scroll across dock moves and remounts.
The existing cross-window protocol transfers saved source nodes. Dirty documents are therefore not offered for a move; the user must save first. A move acknowledgement also preserves the origin if it acquired unsaved edits after the offer. This keeps changes available without adding a text-transfer protocol or writing implicitly. Concurrent editing/CRDT transport remains outside this editor milestone.
native-editor-integration.mjs covers Unicode/CRLF reveal, scroll visibility, retained tab context, dock movement, mounted and unmounted replacement/reveal, workspace replacement, reload and close/reopen ordering. native-editor-windows.mjs uses the existing BroadcastChannel session pattern across two browser pages to check clean moves, refusal of dirty offers and retention of edits made after an offer. Workspace integration tests also cover cursor clearing, reveal ordering and dirty move acknowledgements. Native OS drag gestures, real-server acceptance and remaining platform gates are still outstanding.
Verified: full workspace tests 397 passed, 5 ignored; workspace Clippy with -D warnings; web wasm build; formatting, dependency, string and colour checks. All twelve native browser suites pass, including the new integration/window suites and the final line-end hover regression. The final 3 MB check measured 1087 ms, with 21 rows / 2184 cells.
M4 Markdown wiki links (2026-10-06)
Markdown Source now renders Rust-computed resolved/unresolved link marks, including headings and aliases. Marks rebuild from canonical text immediately after local or external edits, retaining known target resolution within the current index epoch; index resolution debounces for 300 ms and refreshes on the graph epoch. Byte offsets become normalized engine scalar offsets in one forward pass, preserving emoji and CRLF coordinates. Other languages do not receive wiki behavior.
Typing [[ or invoking completion within a page target queries the existing workspace candidate API without requiring LSP. The shared accessible completion menu supports keyboard/mouse selection, suffix replacement, existing closing brackets and a single Workspace undo transaction. Heading/alias suffixes remain intact. Candidate queries time out after five seconds; revision, selection, document identity and active-tab checks reject stale results.
Ctrl/Cmd-click follows the page or creates a missing page beside the source document through follow_wiki_guarded. Resolved nodes retain their source identity across folders. Guard checks run after lookup and file loading and before opening; changes to the originating text, caret or active tab cancel navigation. Once a valid creation begins, the source transaction may finish even if navigation is later cancelled.
Verified: 74 code-view tests, ext-api unit/integration/doc tests and the new guarded wiki-loading test; code-view/ext-api Clippy with -D warnings; web wasm, formatting, dependency, string and colour checks. Wiki, LSP completion, workspace editing and presence browser suites pass. Coverage includes marks, index refresh, local Unicode edits, candidate completion, undo, stale replies, cross-folder navigation and missing-page creation. The workspace suite’s 3 MB check measured 890 ms with 21 rows / 2184 cells. Real-server and native WebView acceptance remain outstanding.
M4 presence gutter (2026-10-06)
The native editor now displays other windows’ initials beside their active logical line, with full names in the tooltip. Presence changes update the gutter without remounting; the current window and members viewing other files are excluded. A fixed three-cell slot keeps line numbers, diagnostics and folding controls visible and is included in wrapping measurements. Wrapped continuations do not repeat badges; folded or off-screen lines render when visible. This uses the existing workspace presence channel independently of LSP.
Verified: 72 code-view tests; code-view Clippy with -D warnings; full web wasm check; formatting and colour checks. The native presence, workspace interaction and resize/review browser suites pass. The deterministic native-editor-presence.mjs scenario checks filtering, Unicode-containing text, cursor movement, remount retention, document isolation and leaving the room. The 3 MB interaction check measured 869 ms with bounded rendering.
Claude review fixes (2026-10-06)

Canonical undo now stores localized forward/inverse transactions, capped at 100 transactions and 16 MiB of edit payload. It preserves selections changed after an edit. The view discards redundant engine undo after publishing each command; Workspace remains the undo owner across remounts.
Closing or renaming a document disposes its root-owned session, view and nested native signals. Typed view cleanup and lazy shared runtime state are public Workspace APIs.
CodeMirror, Rust and Markdown source views share a workspace LSP manager. One URI registry owns open/change/save/close leases and monotonic versions. Unversioned diagnostics persist until publication; versioned ranges are invalidated on edits. Server startup/initialization and waiting callers have 30-second timeouts, with cancellation cleanup.
Workspace edits reconcile stale unmounted native sessions from current canonical text in a staged copy. Final identity, text, session and server-version checks still run before the atomic commit.
Same-position insertion followed by replacement is accepted; duplicate insertions and overlapping ranges remain rejected. Null completion edit fields are treated as absent. Actions with an edit and a command expose/apply the declared edit, matching the earlier client behavior; command-only actions remain unsupported and commands are never executed. Actions that require a command beyond their edit may remain incomplete.
Viewports remeasure on resize and every 600 ms, ignoring hidden 0×0 rectangles. A line-height probe drives row geometry and scrolling. Caret-only callbacks avoid full snapshot clones and scans; canonical UTF-16 length and line offsets are cached. Width calculations touch changed lines, and structural scans debounce for 200 ms; explicit folding flushes pending structure.
Document identity keys the component hooks and async subscriptions. Attachment and input preparation reconcile external text before editing, including replacements that precede reactive effects. Borrowed text validation remains necessary because Workspace writers can mutate Document.text directly. Indentation dropdown options explicitly select persisted values on mount.
Inactive panels avoid subscribing to the active selection. Clippy findings, the node_modules symlink ignore rule, redundant native build assets and the unused legacy vendor workspace member are fixed. Upstream editor-core licenses/README and ext-api compatibility notes are included.

Verified: full workspace tests 392 passed, 5 ignored; workspace Clippy with -D warnings; web wasm and distribution no-default-features checks; formatting, dependency, string and colour checks. Native interaction, diagnostics, hover, completion, definition, rename, tools and review browser suites pass. The final 3 MB input-to-Workspace check measured 826 ms, with 21 rows / 2247 cells. Real-server and native WebView acceptance are still outstanding.
M3 code actions and references (2026-10-06)
Mod-. and the localized toolbar action request quick fixes/refactorings for the current selection or caret. Backward selections become sorted zero-based UTF-16 ranges. Published diagnostics intersecting that range are included in the request. The keyboard-accessible list orders preferred actions first, displays disabled reasons, skips disabled rows during navigation, and supports arrows/Home/End, Enter, mouse selection and Escape/Cancel. The selected row scrolls into view. Server text is escaped.
Actions with edits apply through the rename slice’s staged Workspace EditBatch path: every target and range is validated before the synchronous commit, dirty text and CRLF are preserved, closed targets become unsaved documents, and undo/save remain per file. Actions carrying data resolve lazily with the original server metadata and a five-second timeout. Strict parsing rejects malformed edits instead of partially applying them. Command-only actions are excluded. Edit-plus-command actions apply their declared edit, including after resolution; accompanying server commands are not executed. Dismissal when switching tools avoids stealing focus from the newly opened rename prompt.
Shift-F12 and the toolbar request references at the Rust-owned caret, including declarations. The list deduplicates identical locations and displays decoded folder-relative paths with one-based line/UTF-16 columns. Entries outside the originating folder or with malformed URIs remain visible but disabled. Keyboard or mouse selection reveals same-file targets, expands folded ancestors, or opens/focuses cross-file targets through guarded Workspace reveal. Already-open dirty targets are preserved.
Lists and pending requests capture revision, selection, active document, generation and open-document text/revisions.
