Two processes: only SQLite (and Helix) let a second process open the store. Moonkale’s windows share one process, but a CLI (moonkale --project …), an MCP helper or a crash-reporter would be a second one; with redb, Turso or RocksDB they would have to go through the running app.
Inspectable: a SQLite file opens in any sqlite3, DB Browser, or Moonkale’s own SQLite source — useful for debugging, export and support. redb and RocksDB need their own tools; Helix’s object-store layout needs Helix.
Maturity: SQLite and RocksDB are decades-old; redb is stable and pure Rust (1.x+); Turso is beta (WITHOUT ROWID still behind an experimental flag, found here); embedded HelixDB is an unpublished git dependency that writes a manifest even when opened read-only (P-145).
Conflicts: HelixDB’s transactions are optimistic; with its index, a write overlapping a concurrent read failed with “transaction conflict” until the backend retried.
Async: Turso and HelixDB have async APIs; behind a synchronous interface they need their own runtime (or spawn_blocking), the others are synchronous.
Pure Rust: redb and Turso have no C/C++; SQLite (C, bundled) and RocksDB (C++, bindgen → libclang on every platform) do.

Recommendation
SQLite (rusqlite, bundled) as the store for Moonkale’s state, in WAL with synchronous=NORMAL:

crash-safe for a killed process, 20 000 small commits per second — two orders of magnitude more than Moonkale writes — and sub-millisecond settings writes;
the only fast candidate a second process can open;
already in the dependency tree, small (2.7 MB), builds in about a minute on every platform including Android;
a file everyone can open, and the most proven embedded store there is.

redb is the runner-up, and the reason the interface is shaped after it: pure Rust, the fastest to build and the smallest, but every commit is an fsync (~4 ms; fine off the UI thread), and one process only. If a pure-Rust core ever matters more than multi-process access, it drops in behind the same trait.
RocksDB wins raw throughput and size (compression) but costs 6–14 minutes of C++ per clean build, locks the store, and its strength (a write-heavy LSM) is not what Moonkale’s state needs. Turso is promising but beta and the largest after Helix. HelixDB is not a key/value store and should not be used as one; it stays a candidate for the second store — a persisted graph + vector index — which is a separate comparison.

research/Trading-with-Databento.title: Trading with Databento — requirements for an editor
research/Trading-with-Databento.content:
Context (2026-10-14): a friend of Daniel’s trades and uses Databento, a market-data vendor. It serves historical and live data from exchanges in its binary DBN format, with official clients in Python, C++ and Rust (databento on crates.io, Apache-2.0; historical, live and intraday replay). Some of his requirements for an editor should be met. This also feeds the markets use case of Lenticulum Frontend Requirements (UC-04).
To confirm with him: which datasets (for example CME futures or Nasdaq equities), which schemas, historical or live, which language he writes strategies in, and what he uses today (TradingView, Sierra Chart, Jupyter, …). The list below is what such a setup usually needs; his answers reorder it.
Requirements
TR-nn.
Data


TR-01 Databento as a source: historical requests (dataset, symbols, schema, time range) and live subscriptions, through the official Rust client in-process. The API key is in Moonkale’s secret store, and the source is read-only.


TR-02 Costs before cost: historical data is billed per request. Before a download, the source asks Databento’s cost estimate (metadata.get_cost) and shows it, the way the KG studio shows billed rows (KG-02). An optional per-session budget refuses requests over it.


TR-03 Download once: a downloaded range is cached in the folder as DBN, and as Parquet for DuckDB, so a repeated query costs nothing and works offline. The cache knows which ranges it holds.


TR-04 The schemas, typed:

order book by order (MBO), top of book (MBP-1), ten levels of depth (MBP-10), top of book on each trade (TBBO);
trades;
bars (OHLCV at 1 s, 1 m, 1 h, 1 d);
instrument definitions, statistics, trading status, imbalances.

They show in the table grid with nanosecond timestamps (ts_event, ts_recv) and fixed-point prices, never rounded through floats. This needs typed cells (WP-15): Value today has no exact decimal and no nanosecond time.


TR-05 Symbology: raw symbols, parent symbols (ES.FUT), continuous contracts (ES.c.0) and instrument ids resolve both ways, and rolls are shown on the time axis. Exchange calendars and time zones are explicit.


Seeing the market

TR-06 Price charts: candlesticks or OHLC with volume, several timeframes in sync, a crosshair with values, and indicators as derived series (moving averages, VWAP) computed from the cached data. These are chart types of the plot extension (Plotting Requirements).
TR-07 Order book views: a depth ladder from MBP-10, time and sales from trades, and an order-book heatmap over time from MBO or MBP data (resting liquidity as colour, trades on top). This is millions of cells, a job for the GPU path, as the graph engine draws 100 k nodes.
TR-08 Replay: a historical day replays at a chosen speed (Databento’s intraday replay through the live client, or the local cache), driving every chart and the ladder together. Its cursor is the same time cursor runs use (LT-12).

Strategies

TR-09 Backtests are runs: a strategy (Python, Rust or Julia code, or a flow) runs over a data range and a parameter set. The run record keeps the data range, parameters, code version, fills, P&L and metrics (returns, drawdown, Sharpe), and runs compare side by side. It is the same run-record service as Lenticulum and workflows (WP-38/41).
TR-10 Notebooks for research, with Databento queries as cells (Notebook Editor).
TR-11 Alerts and watchlists: conditions on live data (price crosses, spread, volume spike) raise a desktop notification; watchlists of instruments sit in the Sources panel.

The trader’s own notes

TR-12 A journal linked to the data: a trade note links to an instrument and a moment (a wiki-link to an instrument node and a timestamp), and clicking it opens the chart and replay at that moment. Notes plus data in one place is what Moonkale has and trading tools lack.
TR-13 The market as a graph: instruments, their relations (correlations, spreads, the same underlying) and order flow between venues drawn as a graph, which leads into the markets factor graphs of UC-04.

Out of scope, or limited
The Scrutiny entries:

Order entry and execution. Sending orders to a broker is a different product, with compliance and risk responsibilities. If ever, it would be a separate extension behind an explicit gate, never in Moonkale’s core. Moonkale is for research, review and monitoring.
Execution-grade latency in the UI. Charts update smoothly (60 FPS), but Moonkale is not a low-latency trading terminal.
Republishing market data. Exchange data is licensed, and its redistribution is restricted. Reader mode and any publishing must not serve downloaded market data to others. A source can mark its data as non-redistributable, and publishing refuses it.

Where it would go
An extension in its own repository (like moonkale-julia): a market-data source for Databento, the cache, symbology, and the order-book views. It depends on the plot extension for the charts, on typed cells (WP-15) and on run records (WP-38). It is vendor-specific, so it stays out of the core (Core and Extensions).
Work package: WP-42 in Work Packages.

research/Use-Cases.title: Use cases — a collection
research/Use-Cases.content:
Why: Core and Extensions decides where things belong, and Work Packages what comes first. Both should rest on what people actually do. Add a case whenever someone describes a task, a request or a frustration. One case per entry; short is fine.
Template
### UC-nn — <the task in a sentence>
- **Who:** the kind of user (a modeller, a biologist, an app developer, a student …)
- **Today they use:** the tools and the pain
- **In Moonkale:** what they would do, step by step
- **Needs:** the features (link the requirement ids: LT-, KG-, PLT-, DBG-, WF-, …)
- **Placement it argues for:** core, extension here, own repository
- **Source:** who said it, when (or "imagined")

Cases so far
UC-01: Build and watch a large factor graph (Lenticulum)

Who: a researcher in probabilistic modelling (Daniel).
Today: Julia code (RxInfer, ModelingToolkit, Lux) and plots; the structure lives in the code and in the head.
In Moonkale:

compose the model in the flow editor from library blocks and subsystems;
bind data;
run in Julia;
watch beliefs flow on the graph, scrub the schedule, plot marginals, debug a diverging message.


Needs: LT-01 to LT-23 (Lenticulum Frontend Requirements), PLT-09, the model debugger.
Placement: the flow editor’s generic parts here; Lenticulum’s library in moonkale-julia.
Source: Daniel, 2026-10-14 (the reason Moonkale exists).

UC-02: A language model as a statistical logic program

Who: a researcher building a new kind of language model, Daniel’s group. Not transformers: a statistical Prolog in which functions and relations compose the model.
In Moonkale:

author relations, weighted rules and functions as a lifted program;
expand groundings for one query;
ask a query and read the answers with their derivations and probabilities;
train the rule weights and watch them move;
compare two weight sets on the same query.


Needs: LT-24 to LT-29, LT-25 (lifted/ground), LT-26 (proof graphs), LT-12/13 (runs), the Datalog dialect (WP-20), the coarse tier.
Source: Daniel, 2026-10-14 (corrected the same day: not transformers).

UC-03: Omics with factors as protein behaviour

Who: a computational biologist.
In Moonkale: factors cite UniProt and Reactome entries; observed variables bind to measurement tables (Parquet in DuckDB); units are checked; posteriors are plotted per protein.
Needs: LT-08, LT-09, LT-05, PLT-01, the table grid, the knowledge graph.
Source: Daniel, 2026-10-14 (imagined).

UC-04: Market interactions with learnable factors

Who: a quantitative modeller.
In Moonkale: a time-unrolled graph of agents; train the factors’ parameters; clamp a variable as an intervention on a scenario copy; compare runs.
Needs: LT-03 (time slices), LT-07, LT-13, LT-14, PLT-09, PLT-12.
Source: Daniel, 2026-10-14 (imagined).

UC-05: Notes and code in one vault

Who: anyone who uses Obsidian and VS Code side by side (Daniel daily).
In Moonkale: write notes with wiki-links into code symbols; see both in one graph; edit Markdown with formulas in any delimiter style.
Needs: the Markdown editor, the index, the graph view, Math Delimiters and Renderers.
Source: Daniel (the vault itself).

UC-06: Explore a database

Who: an app developer or analyst.
In Moonkale: open a DuckDB or SQLite file, query, scroll 50 000 rows, plot a column, see foreign keys as a schema graph.
Needs: the table grid, PLT-01, WP-13 (pushdown), WP-16 (schema view).
Source: Daniel, 2026-10-14 (the Supabase-like request).

UC-07: An RDF store and an agent’s layered memory

Who: a knowledge engineer and an agent developer.
In Moonkale: query an oxilite store in SPARQL; see why a triple was inferred; review a tiramemsu memory’s conflicts and what it believed last week.
Needs: KG-01 to KG-36 (Knowledge Graph Studio).
Placement: its own repository.
Source: Daniel, 2026-10-14.

UC-08: Debug a program

Who: a user who asked for a debugger.
In Moonkale: set a breakpoint, run, inspect variables and the call stack, step.
Needs: DBG-01 to DBG-09 (Debugger Requirements).
Placement: the DAP service core, the panel opt-in.
Source: a user request, relayed by Daniel, 2026-10-14. Ask them what they debug (language, local or remote), which decides the first adapter.

UC-09: Automate a pipeline

Who: someone running a recurring data job.
In Moonkale: a flow of steps (a SQL query, a Julia script, a plot) runs on a schedule or on file change; each run’s step outputs can be inspected.
Needs: WF-01 to WF-08 (Workflow Automation (n8n, Windmill)).
Source: Daniel, 2026-10-14 (n8n/Windmill as references).

UC-10: Trading research with Databento

Who: a trader (a friend of Daniel’s) using Databento’s market-data API.
Today: Databento’s clients and other trading tools (to ask him which).
In Moonkale:

pull a day of futures data with its cost shown first, cached;
look at candlesticks and the order-book heatmap;
replay the open;
backtest a strategy as a run and compare parameter sets;
write a journal note that links to the moment on the chart.


Needs: TR-01 to TR-13 (Trading with Databento), typed cells, plots, run records.
Placement: its own repository.
Source: Daniel, 2026-10-14.

UC-11: Moving from Obsidian, VS Code or Zed

Who: anyone switching (Daniel; most first-day users).
In Moonkale: open the Obsidian vault as it is (wiki-links, embeds, callouts, canvases); keep VS Code’s palette, keybindings and LSP habits; edit references across files in one buffer.
Needs: Editor Prior Art (Obsidian, VS Code, Zed)‘s “taken” rows.
Placement: core and on-by-default extensions.
Source: Daniel, 2026-10-14.

UC-12: Switch between pieces of work

Who: anyone with more than one thing going on (Daniel: Moonkale, Lenticulum, a paper).
In Moonkale: each piece of work is a session with its own sources, layout, open documents, unsaved buffers, conversations and query history. Switching sessions swaps all of it, and nothing is lost, even unsaved edits. Sessions aren’t tied to a folder, and they live in the state store, not in files.
Needs: ADR-0025 Sessions are the outermost state (WP-46).
Placement: core platform.
Source: Daniel, 2026-10-14.

research/Versioning-Prior-Art.title: Versioning Prior Art
research/Versioning-Prior-Art.content:
Companion to Version Management and ADR-0012 Two histories. Descriptions are from public documentation; verify details before borrowing code.























































systemmodelborrowgitDAG of snapshot commits; diffs computed on demand; identity = paththe checkpoint idea; history-as-graph rendering; gix (pure Rust) / git2 bindingsDatomicimmutable facts (entity, attribute, value, tx, added?); database as of any transactionthe fold model exactly: our events are Datomic facts at entity granularity; “as-of” queriesXTDBbitemporal: valid-time and transaction-time per factkeep both timestamps — “when was it true” vs “when did we learn it” matters for imported database rowsTerminusDBgit-like branches/merges over an RDF graph, stored as deltasbranching a graph; delta storage; merge as set operations on triplesDoltgit semantics (branch/diff/merge) for SQL tables, cell-level diffsproves table history is tractable; a Dolt source could map its history to the log directlyUnisoncode is content-addressed by hash; names are metadata; no diffs — definitions are added, never changedthe “append, never mutate” stance; renames as metadata; strong reason to treat a Unison codebase as a first-class sourceAutomerge / Loro (CRDTs)per-replica operation logs with causal ordering; text, lists, maps merge automaticallythe content layer under Content events; logical clocks (loro 1.x is Rust-native)Event sourcing (general)append-only events, state by projection, snapshots for speedvocabulary and the snapshot/compaction disciplineFossilSCM with an append-only artifact store; “unversioned” vs versioned contenttombstones (“shunning”) as a first-class, auditable operation
Take-aways for the design

Append-only + fold is well trodden (Datomic, event sourcing); the risks are storage growth and slow folds, both solved by snapshots.
Two timestamps (XTDB) cost little now and are painful to retrofit; include valid_at alongside recorded_at for imported facts.
Structural merge is easy, content merge is hard — every system above separates the two; so do we (entity log vs text patch/CRDT).
Content addressing (Unison, git objects) is the right key for content, UUIDs the right key for identity; Moonkale uses both: NodeId for the thing, a content hash for its text at a point in time.

research/WASM-Extension-Runtimes.title: WASM Extension Runtimes
research/WASM-Extension-Runtimes.content:
Decision: ADR-0004 WASM components for extensions.








































OptionSandboxPortabilityLanguagesNotesNative dylib (libloading)noneper-OS buildsRustfastest; unsafe; no web. Rejected.Scripting (Lua mlua, JS boa/quickjs)partialgoodone scripting langsecond language for authors; JS engine in the app is what we’re avoiding. Rejected.WASM core modules (extism 1.30)✅✅manysimple ABI (bytes in/out); no typed interfaces; plugin host on web via extism-js. Runner-up.WASM components (WIT) — wasmtime 49 native, wasm_component_layer 0.1 on web✅✅manytyped interfaces generated from ext-api; WASI p2 for scoped fs; browser side least mature. Chosen.
Browser hosting notes
The app is wasm; it can’t embed wasmtime. wasm_component_layer implements the component model over a pluggable backend (JS WebAssembly in the browser). Run in a Worker for isolation; messages instead of calls. Alternative: transpile components to core modules + JS glue at publish time (jco) — pushes work to the publisher, simplifies the client. Evaluate both; ranked very high difficulty in Problem Ranking.
Mobile
No runtime code loading in v1 (store policy risk on iOS; unverified for wasm). Static only.

research/Workflow-Automation-(n8n,-Windm.title: Workflow automation — requirements from n8n and Windmill, under scrutiny
research/Workflow-Automation-(n8n,-Windm.content:
Context (2026-10-14, Daniel): n8n and Windmill are a good source of requirements, but they should be put under scrutiny. Moonkale’s Flow Editor today is a modelling editor: typed ports, generated Julia code (Lux, ModelingToolkit, RxInfer). Workflow tools are execution editors: a graph of steps that runs on triggers. Some of their requirements fit Moonkale; some would pull it toward being a SaaS automation platform, which it is not.
Licences: requirements only, no code (Scrutiny rules):

n8n is source-available under its Sustainable Use License (fair-code, not OSI open source).
Windmill’s repository is AGPLv3, with its OpenFlow spec Apache-2.0. Its prebuilt Community Edition mixes in proprietary code.

Neither is compatible with copying code into MIT Moonkale, and this study took nothing from their code.
What they offer


















































Arean8nWindmillGraphvisual nodes and connections, branching, merging, loopsflows as DAGs of steps (the OpenFlow format)Steps400+ integration nodes, a Code node (JS, Python)scripts in many languages (Python, TypeScript, Go, Bash, SQL, Rust …) with typed parameters from signaturesTriggerswebhooks, schedules, app events, manualschedules, webhooks, HTTP routes, email, Kafka-style queuesDataJSON items passed between nodes, expressions to map fieldstyped inputs and outputs (JSON Schema from script signatures)Credentialsencrypted per workspace, shared by roleresources and variables, secrets per workspaceRunsexecution history with every node’s input and output, retries, error workflowsjob queue, logs, retries, timeouts, concurrency limits, cachingPeople—approval steps (suspend until a human approves), auto-generated forms and appsVersionsworkflow versionsscripts and flows versioned, deployable from git
What fits Moonkale
WF-nn.

WF-01 Typed step data: Windmill’s typed inputs and outputs from function signatures match Moonkale’s typed ports. A step’s ports come from its signature (a Julia or Rust function, a SQL query’s columns). n8n’s untyped JSON items don’t.
WF-02 Runs as records: every run keeps each step’s inputs, outputs, logs, timing and errors, inspectable on the graph (select a step, see what went through it). It is the same need as Lenticulum’s run records (LT-13), so one mechanism serves both.
WF-03 Re-run from a step, with the earlier steps’ outputs cached; retries and timeouts per step.
WF-04 Scripts as steps in the core languages, run by the toolchains Moonkale already starts (Julia, Python, Rust, SQL on a source), locally or on the server.
WF-05 Triggers that make sense for an editor: manual, on file change (the folder watcher exists), on a schedule (desktop or server), and on a source event (SourceEvent). Webhooks only in server mode, behind the gate.
WF-06 Approval and human steps: a step that pauses for a person, the way the policy gate already pauses an agent’s write.
WF-07 Versions from git: a flow is a document in the folder; its version is the commit, or a content hash.
WF-08 Credentials through Moonkale’s secret store, scoped to a source or a project, never inside the flow document.

Rejected or limited
The Scrutiny entries:

The integration catalogue as a goal (400+ SaaS connectors). It is the product of an automation company, and maintaining it is a business of its own. Moonkale gets its integrations from sources and extensions, and an HTTP or OpenAPI step covers the rest.
Untyped JSON items with field-mapping expressions (n8n’s model). They lose types at every wire, and Moonkale’s flows are typed (ADR-0020). An expression language for mapping can come later, typed.
A hosted multi-tenant runner (workers, queues, quotas, billing). Moonkale’s runner is the desktop or the user’s own server. Scale-out execution is a backend’s job (an extension may hand runs to Windmill or a cluster through their APIs).
Auto-generated end-user apps and forms (Windmill). That is out of scope for an editor. Reader mode (Publishing Sources) and dashboards (Plotting Requirements) are Moonkale’s ways to show results to others.

Where it would go

An optional extension, not core: execution on the flow editor’s model, with a runner service on desktop and server. The flow model gains a step role beside variable and factor (ADR-0022’s roles), so modelling and workflow graphs share one editor, one engine and one run-record mechanism.
First: WF-02 run records and WF-03 re-run, because Lenticulum needs the same. Then scripts as steps (WF-04) and triggers (WF-05).

Work package: WP-41 in Work Packages.

research/dioxus-flow.title: dioxus-flow — evaluation
research/dioxus-flow.content:
Crate: dioxus-flow 0.1.2 · repo · same author as dioxus-workbench, which we already depend on. ~8.3k lines, deps: dioxus, serde (optional), web-time; no JS.
What it offers (from README + source, 2026-09-17)
Pannable/zoomable canvas, draggable nodes, connectable handles (drag to create an edge, snapping), bezier/straight/smooth-step edges with labels, arrowheads, animated edges, layered auto-layout in four directions with animation, “seat anchoring” for crossing-free endpoints, minimap/controls/background, custom node and edge rendering with any Dioxus component, keyboard/ARIA, dark mode via CSS variables, 60 fps at ~1000 nodes. Roadmap: box selection, edge reconnection, sub-flows/grouping, viewport culling.
Fit for Moonkale













































need (Flow Editor)dioxus-flowverdictdrag-and-drop blocks wired by typed portshandles + connections + custom node views✅ direct hitvalidation (port types, cycles)not built in; we validate on the connect event and reject/colour the edge✅ our layerstorage as ordinary nodes/edges (Block, flow.wire)nodes/edges are plain signals we own✅ maps 1:1 onto corelayered layout for DAGs (ML models, MTK)built-in, animated✅ replaces our own hierarchical for flowsvery large flowsDOM-based, ~1000 nodes⚠️ fine for flows; the wgpu graph view stays for the knowledge graphRust-only, no JSyes✅ no interop boundary neededmaturity0.1.x, one author, CI⚠️ same risk profile as dioxus-workbench, which worked out
Recommendation
Adopt dioxus-flow as the canvas of the Flow Editor (Phase 5, R-24): it removes the SVG canvas, wiring, snapping and layout work from packages/editors/flow and leaves us the parts that are actually ours — block libraries as extension contributions, port-type validation, and codegen (Lux.jl / ModelingToolkit.jl). Keep the graph view (wgpu) separate; the two crates address different scales and interaction models. One design implication for now: editors/flow should model blocks/ports so they convert to dioxus_flow::{Node, Edge} without a second representation.
Not adopted yet — nothing in Milestone 2 needs it. Recorded in Flow Editor.

research/egui-and-Dioxus.title: egui and Dioxus — what egui would bring, what it would cost, and how to compare them cheaply
research/egui-and-Dioxus.content:
Context: Moonkale’s UI is Dioxus (ADR-0001 Dioxus instead of Lumino and Tauri), rendered in a webview on the desktop and Android and in the browser on the web. ADR-0016 Freya is a reference, not a target settled the same question for Freya. egui came up because the ArtCraft suite (clean-room Rust rewrites of desktop apps) is built on it.
What egui would bring

Pure Rust, no webview. No WebKitGTK quirks (Moonkale’s desktop already works around several, P-001 onward), a smaller desktop footprint, and the same pixels on every platform.
Fast to build tool UIs. Immediate mode: the UI is a function of state, redrawn on input. Panels, inspectors, property grids and debug views come together quickly.
A mature ecosystem for the kind of tools Moonkale has: egui_dock (docking), egui_extras (virtual tables), egui_plot (plots), several node-graph editors (egui_snarl and others), egui_graphs.
Custom GPU drawing is first class: a wgpu paint callback draws inside any egui region. Moonkale’s graph engine (UI-free since ADR-0018) could draw inside an egui app, which is the interop point with ArtCraft.
Testable UIs: egui_kittest drives an egui UI in tests through its AccessKit tree, headless, without OS input injection. That’s exactly what Moonkale lacks on native Wayland.
Web from the same code, as one canvas.

What it would cost Moonkale


Text is where Moonkale lives, and the browser’s text engine is the strongest one available:

IME composition (Chinese and Japanese input), complex scripts, bidirectional text, font fallback for CJK;
selection and find across a page;
rich WYSIWYG Markdown;
spell checking.

egui has IME support and is improving, but it doesn’t match a browser here. The Markdown rich editor (Milkdown), CodeMirror and xterm are DOM components with no egui equivalent.


The web as a canvas loses what makes a web app a web app: native text selection, browser find, links you can open in a new tab, screen readers reading the DOM, crawlability (relevant to reader mode, Publishing Sources).


Theming and layout: spec 030’s themes are CSS variables. egui’s styling is code, and responsive layouts are harder in immediate mode.


Every extension’s UI is Dioxus. Extension::render returns a Dioxus Element, and Workspace state is Dioxus signals. A switch means rewriting the shell and every panel, more than 40 crates’ UI. The model crates (moonkale-core, moonkale-graph-render, the sources, the server, the state store) have no UI dependency and would survive.


Is comparing them later troublesome?
Comparing: no. Switching: yes, and more so every month. The comparison is cheap because the parts that matter are UI-free and benchmarks exist:

A spike (one agent, a small package): an egui app showing one real panel twice (the virtualised table grid on a 50 000-row result, and the graph engine through a wgpu paint callback), reading the same model crates, beside the Dioxus panels.
Measured with Benchmarks:

frame times while scrolling and panning (BM-11, BM-14);
memory (BM-20);
the web download (BM-30);
Chinese IME input;
screen-reader output;
how long each took to build.



The switch, not the comparison, is what grows expensive. The rules that keep the option open are already in place:

models are headless (ADR-0016 decision 2);
logic lives outside components (the table’s grid.rs, the flow model in ext-api, the Markdown parser in markdown.rs are pure and tested);
Dioxus stays out of model crates.

Every package that follows them keeps a later UI change a rewrite of views, not of Moonkale.
Verdict

No switch. Moonkale is text-heavy and web-first, and that is where Dioxus with a real browser engine is strongest. The planned exit from the webview stays Blitz (dioxus-native), which renders the same elements and CSS without a webview.
egui is an interop target: the graph engine embedded in egui apps (ArtCraft’s node editors), and egui_plot and egui_kittest as references for the plot extension and for UI testing.
Revisit if Blitz stalls, or egui’s text input reaches browser quality (IME, bidi, CJK), or Moonkale drops the web client. Then run the spike above first.

Work package (only if revisited): WP-58 in Work Packages.

specifications/001.title: Spec 001 — Flow editor: editing a parameter field
specifications/001.content:
Inserting an element into the flow editor currently is somewhat problematic for editing the vaulues. If I click on the filed and press ⇐ or entf the element gets deleted.

Done 2026-09-19. The parameter fields inside a block now keep their keys and pointer events to themselves: Backspace/Delete edit the text instead of deleting the block, arrows move the caret instead of nudging the block, Enter/Space no longer toggle the selection, and clicking into a field no longer starts a drag. Ctrl/Meta combos (Ctrl+S) still reach the editor. Change: packages/editors/flow/src/panel.rs (mk-flow-params stops keydown unless Ctrl/Meta, and pointerdown). Covered by a step in packages/web/tests/e2e/flow.mjs.

specifications/002.title: Spec 002 — HelixDB as an embedded graph source
specifications/002.content:
HelixDB has an embedded mode (docs) — open it like LadybugDB or DuckDB, without the helix daemon or an HTTP server. Moonkale should offer it as an opt-in source (moonkale-sources-graph, feature helix) on desktop and the server, same Source shape as LadybugDB; the browser build keeps the plain-HTTP server mode (POST /v2/query) only.
Findings (2026-09-19)

Embedded mode exists in the repo: sdks/rust (crate helix-db 3.0.0) has embedded = ["dep:db"]; with it Client::open(HelixDbSource::Disk { root, database }).await (also Memory, and S3-compatible object storage) opens storage in-process; queries use the same QueryRequest contract as server mode (HelixQL through helix-dsl-macros). No daemon, no CLI at runtime.
Not on crates.io yet: the published helix-db 3.0.0 (2026-08-04) has features = { default = [] } and no db dependency — the engine (crates/db 0.1.0) is an unpublished workspace crate. Embedded Helix therefore means a git dependency on HelixDB/helix-db, and crates/db pulls a git fork of slatedb (pinned rev) plus tantivy, foyer, object_store (aws), rkyv, rayon, … — a heavy tree that follows main. Storage is SlateDB (LSM over disk/object storage), not LMDB as in Helix 1.x/2.x.
Where it would pay off beyond “another graph engine”: graph + vector in one store for the RAG index (moonkale-index::embed).

What “done” looks like

sources-graph/src/helix.rs implements Source for the embedded client behind helix (git dep, pinned rev; desktop + server only; never the web client), with the server mode (HTTP) as the second backend of the same file.
Explorer: a .helix/ folder (or a configured path) opens as a graph source; the graph editor draws query results as it does for LadybugDB (Cypher → HelixQL dialect in dialect.rs).
One unit test against HelixDbSource::Memory; an E2E step only if the server build enables the feature by default (it should not until the crate is published).
Crate note + Problem Log entry with the measured clean-build cost.

Decision
Wait until crates/db is published on crates.io (or the git tree stabilises), unless the RAG index needs Helix’s vectors first. Until then the stub stays as it is.
Done 2026-09-28 (Milestone 17)
Embedded HelixDB is a source: sources-graph feature helix (git dependency on HelixDB/helix-db, pinned to f0d1b554f4), HelixSource in src/helix.rs. A *.helix directory (the object-store root; its one database, or main) opens from the Sources tree, read-only (open_reader): node and edge labels as tables, vertices and edges as a graph (v:<Label>:<id>, EdgeKind::Custom), the helix dialect (nodes [<label>] [limit n], edges …) in the table editor, Show in Graph included. Tests: sources-graph/tests/helix.rs (a Disk store written through the SDK, then read through the source), E2E stores.mjs. The HTTP server mode is not done. Known: an open writes a manifest into the store (P-145). See Milestone 17 - Implementation Log.

specifications/003.title: Spec 003 — Projects: several sources, a selector, sync
specifications/003.content:
Opening several folders at once is intended. A project is a saved Moonkale state (not a folder): a set of sources — folders, folders over SSH, GitHub/GitLab/Codeberg repositories, databases, REST APIs — each opened and closed individually, some read-only, each with a colour; a project selector; import/export; synchronisation; and failure notices when a source is missing.
Documented 2026-09-19 as Projects and Sources (desired behaviour, project file format, selector, failure report, three sync tiers, what already exists, open questions). Implementation: a milestone of its own — the plan will reference that page; this spec turns done when the selector, close/suspend, colours, read-only and the open report work with folders and the existing database files, with the remote/repo/API kinds allowed to follow.

specifications/004.title: Spec 004 — Unicode input: \int → ∫ in every text field
specifications/004.content:
Like the Julia REPL and the Julia/Lean VS Code extensions: an escape (\) followed by a name opens a dropdown while typing and Tab/Enter inserts the symbol — \int → ∫, \alpha → α, \:ladybug: → 🐞 — as the default in every text input of Moonkale, with several names per symbol and an editable, extensible table (start from Julia’s unicode-input list).
Documented 2026-09-19 in Unicode Input: behaviour (trigger, ranking, Tab/eager acceptance, emoji, cursor templates, undo, reverse lookup), the layered table (built-in Julia + Lean tables, user, workspace, extension; TOML with names = [...], -name removals, language scope), where it lives (Rust owns the table; one completion source in CodeMirror, a UnicodeInput wrapper for plain inputs, palette command for the terminal), settings — including a per-language escape: LaTeX, Markdown and .ipynb use \ as source, so they default to ; (or off); Typst does not, renders Unicode directly, and keeps \ — and the five-step plan. Not implemented.

specifications/005.title: Spec 005 — A Claude Code extension (no API key)
specifications/005.content:
An extension for Claude Code itself, usable on a Claude subscription without an API key.
Planned 2026-09-19 in Claude Code Extension: possible because the claude CLI carries the subscription login — Level 1 runs it in the terminal panel (works today), Level 2 makes Moonkale its IDE (lock file + WebSocket MCP server: selection, open file, diffs you accept in Moonkale), Level 3 makes it an agent provider (claude -p --output-format stream-json …) with Moonkale’s policy gate as its permission prompt and Moonkale’s MCP tools (graph, search, databases) available to it. Not implemented.

specifications/006.title: Spec 006 — Android graph: pinch to zoom, two fingers to rotate
specifications/006.content:
The Graph window in Android does currently not allow for zoom in/out or rotation with two finger gesture.
Done 2026-09-20. The renderer’s pointer handlers (graph-render/src/web.rs) now track touch pointers (with pointer capture, pointercancel handled): a second finger starts Drag::Pinch — the distance between the fingers zooms at their midpoint (Camera::zoom_at, so in 3D it dollies), the midpoint’s motion pans, and in 3D the fingers’ rotation turns the camera’s yaw. Lifting one finger continues as a one-finger pan without a click; a node picked up by the first finger stays pinned. GraphView::camera_state() exports [scale, cx, cy, yaw, pitch, dist] for tests. Verified in Chromium with CDP touch events (graph3d.mjs: 2D pinch ×4, 3D rotation 1.2 rad with the distance stable) and on the Galaxy S10e through the WebView’s DevTools socket (packages/web/tests/e2e/android-pinch.mjs: scale 1.6 → 8.0, yaw 0.6 → −0.4). Note: 2D has no rotation — the canvas has no orientation to rotate; two fingers pan and zoom there.

specifications/007.title: Spec 007 — Android app name and icon
specifications/007.content:
The Android app on my smartphone is currently called “Mobile” and has no Logo. If that is just for the development version then no problem, however I would like the build version to display correct name and Logo.
Done 2026-09-20. Cause: dx 0.7.10 labels the Android app after the crate name in PascalCase (mobile → “Mobile”) and always writes its own template launcher icons into the generated Gradle project; [application] name and [bundle] icon in Dioxus.toml do not reach Android. Fix: packages/mobile/build-android.sh runs the dx build, then writes strings.xml (Moonkale), generates launcher bitmaps for every density plus an adaptive icon (foreground = the picture inset, background = the icon’s own backdrop colour) from assets/icon.png, removes the template’s vector icon, reassembles with Gradle (incremental, seconds) and, with install, installs and launches. Renaming the binary would also fix the label but moves the output under target/dx/moonkale/, which the desktop crate uses. Verified on the phone: the drawer shows Moonkale with the Moonkale icon. The script also clears stale hashed assets first (P-092).

specifications/008.title: Spec 008 — View png / jpg / svg inside Moonkale
specifications/008.content:
It would be good if I can look at the content of png, jpg, svg without leaving Moonkale.
Done 2026-09-20. A new optional extension moonkale-editor-image (image.md): clicking a png / jpg / gif / webp / svg / bmp / ico / avif in the Explorer opens a viewer tab — Fit / 100 % / − + zoom (Ctrl+wheel too), drag to pan, dimensions and size in the toolbar, Source on SVGs to edit the markup as text. Bytes travel through a new Source::fetch_bytes (folder natively; base64 over /api/sources/fetch_bytes on the web) into a data: URL, so it works on desktop, web and the phone alike; images over 24 MB are refused with a message. Suite image.mjs (png opens with 4 × 3, zoom states, SVG renders and its Source opens in the code editor).

specifications/009.title: Spec 009 — Activity bar, fuller menus, source icons and colours
specifications/009.content:
The left rail and the menu bar are mostly unused; sources have no visual type. Wanted: a real activity bar on the left, menus that expose what already exists, and an icon + colour per source.
Today

Left rail: ActivityRail with one dead “Explorer” button (ui/src/shell.rs); the side tile holds Explorer, Search, Links, Git, History as tabs; Agent lives in the right tile, Terminal in the bottom one.
Menus: File (Open Folder, New Flow, Settings, Save, Close Editor, Exit) · Edit (Undo, Redo, Find in Workspace) · View (Palette, Go to File, New Window, New Terminal, Reset Layout, Toggle Developer Tools) · Help (About). The palette knows more: view.panel.{explorer,search,graph,terminal,agent}, git.{commit,history,refresh}, history.show, agent.focus.
Phone: a bottom bar (Files, Search, Editor, Graph, Terminal, Agent, Settings) that is, in effect, the activity bar already.
Explorer: source roots are text only; SourceFamily (Folder, Sql, Graph, KeyValue, Index, Remote, Custom) is not shown.

Activity bar (left rail, desktop ≥ 700 px)
One registry drives the rail and the phone’s bottom bar, so both lists stay in sync; extensions add entries through PanelContribution.activity: Option<Activity { icon, order, badge }> (a small SVG per panel, inline — no icon font).



















































































orderentryopensbadge1Sources (Explorer)side tilenumber of sources not ok (missing / unreachable — Projects and Sources)2Searchside tile—3Links (backlinks)side tileunresolved links in the active document4Version management (Git: Changes)side tilechanged files5History (entity log)side tile—6Agentright tilepending approval prompts7Terminalbottom tilerunning processes8Graphmain tile——(extensions append here, ordered by order)their hometheir badgebottomPresence (who is here)popover: members with initials, file:linemember countbottomExtensions (Settings → Extensions)settings panel, Extensions tabdisabled-because-incompatible countbottomYou / Settings (gear)settings panel—
Behaviour: click = show that panel in its home tile and focus it (the view.panel.<id> command, generalised to every panel); click the active side entry again = collapse the side tile (view.toggleSide, Ctrl+B); right-click = Move to … (side / right / bottom); drag to reorder, order saved in user settings; keyboard Ctrl+1…9 for the first nine. Tooltips carry the keybinding. Badges are counts (max 99+), never text.
Other candidates worth a rail entry once they exist, documented so the order is decided now: Projects (the selector, above Sources — Projects and Sources), Problems (LSP diagnostics across open files), Outline (symbols of the active document from the index), Tables (open database sources), Flows (open *.flow.json). None of these is a new panel type; each is an existing view given a rail slot.
Mobile (< 700 px)
The bottom bar is the activity bar: the same registry, first six entries as tiles, the rest behind a More… sheet (a grid of the remaining icons with labels); Settings stays last as now. Badges appear on the tile icons. Presence and Extensions live in the More sheet. No rail on the left — the width is not there — and no drag-reorder on the phone (the desktop order is used).
Menus (desktop title bar), built from the command registry so keybindings show

File: New File… (file.new, in the active source’s folder — the Explorer has the inline edit already), New Flow…, Open Folder…, Open Recent ▸ (settings.recent_folders), Close Source ▸ (per open source), Save, Save All (file.saveAll), Revert (Reload), Close Editor, Close All Editors, ─, Settings…, ─, Exit.
Edit: Undo, Redo, ─, Find (Mod+F, editor search panel), Replace (Mod+H), Find in Workspace…, Replace in Workspace…, ─, Rename Symbol (F2), Code Actions (Mod+.), Go to Definition (F12), Find References (Shift+F12), ─, Insert Symbol… (Unicode Input, when built), Toggle Comment (needs language comment rules — Core Languages).
View: Command Palette…, Go to File…, ─, Show ▸ (one entry per panel: Explorer, Search, Links, Git, History, Agent, Terminal, Graph — from the same registry as the rail), Toggle Side Bar (Ctrl+B), Toggle Bottom Panel (Ctrl+J), ─, Graph: 2D / 3D, Fit, Relayout (when a graph is open), ─, Rich / Source (markdown), ─, New Window, New Terminal, Reset Layout, Toggle Developer Tools.
Git (new, only when the git extension is enabled): Refresh, Commit…, Show Changes, Show History as Graph, Diff Active File.
Agent (new, when enabled): Focus Chat, New Transcript, Approve All Pending / Deny All Pending, Open Policy Settings.
Help: About Moonkale, Documentation (the vault site), Keyboard Shortcuts (Settings → Keybindings), Report a Problem (opens markdown/specifications/ with a new numbered file when the vault is the open folder), Toggle Developer Tools (moved here from View).

Everything listed exists as a command or is a one-line wrapper of an existing panel action except Save All, Close All Editors, Toggle Side/Bottom, Open Recent and Close Source — small additions.
Source icons and colours

Icon by kind, drawn from SourceFamily plus the descriptor’s detail: folder · remote folder (folder with a link mark; SSH) · git-host repository (branch mark) · database (cylinder: SQL) · graph database (three joined dots) · key-value (key) · data folder (grid: the DuckDB view over CSV/Parquet) · API (plug) · index (hidden, as now). Shown before the root’s name in the Explorer, in the source picker of the Table editor, and in the status bar’s source item. A lock overlay for read-only sources (driver, credentials or user choice — Projects and Sources).
Colour: the per-source accent from Projects and Sources — user-chosen or a stable hash of the source id over an eight-colour palette that works on both themes — as a 3 px stripe on the Explorer root row, on every tab of a document from that source, and as a dot next to the file name in the status bar. Colour never encodes state; icons and badges do.
SourceDescriptor gains nothing: kind comes from family + Custom("…") names already used ("git", "data"); the accent lives in the project/session, not in the descriptor.

Done when
Rail with the eight entries + bottom three, badges for git/agent/terminal, Ctrl+B/Ctrl+J, phone More… sheet, the menus above, icons on source roots with the read-only lock, stripes on tabs; E2E shell.mjs (rail click opens/collapses, badge count after a git change, menu → command), phone.mjs extended (More… sheet).
Done 2026-09-20 (rail, menus, source icons/colours; the per-project colour choice and the read-only override wait for Projects and Sources).

Activity bar: PanelContribution.activity: Option<Activity { icon, order, badge, label, phone_secondary }> — one registry for the desktop rail and the phone bar. Entries: Files 10, Search 20, Links 30, Git 40 (badge = changed files), History 50, Agent 60, Terminal 70 (badge = open sessions), Graph 80, Settings 900 (pinned bottom); plus People (presence count, click shows who is here). Click = show the panel (reopening a closed one); click on the current entry = hide it. Icons are inline SVGs (ui/src/icons.rs); badges are counts.
Ctrl+B / Ctrl+J (view.toggleSide, view.toggleBottom): hide every panel of the side / bottom area and remember them; the next press brings them back.
Phone: the same registry — Files, Search, Editor, Agent, Terminal, Graph in the bar, a More sheet for Links, Git, History, Settings and anything past five primary entries.
Menus (built from the command registry, keybindings shown): File — New File, Open Folder, Close Folder, Open Recent, Settings, Save, Save All, Close All Editors, Close Editor, Exit; Edit — Undo, Redo, Find, Replace, Find in Workspace, Rename Symbol, Code Actions, Go to Definition, Find References, Toggle Comment (Command::Editor(EditorAction) → the active CodeMirror view’s run(action)); View — Palette, Go to File, Show  for every static panel, Toggle Side Bar / Bottom Panel / Word Wrap, Fold All / Unfold All, New Window, New Terminal, Reset Layout, DevTools; Git and Agent menus appear from the extensions’ commands (grouped by the “Category: …” title prefix); Help — About, Keyboard Shortcuts, Documentation.
Source icons and colours: icons::source_icon(descriptor) (folder, remote folder, repository, database, graph database, key-value, data folder, API, index) and icons::source_color(id) (a stable 8-colour palette by hash) — the Explorer’s source row gets the icon, a 3 px stripe in the colour and a lock when the source cannot write; the status bar’s source item shows a dot in the same colour.
Suites: shell.mjs (rail order/active/bottom, badge, source row, hide/show, Ctrl+B, menus incl. Edit → Find opening the search panel), phone.mjs (More sheet). Deferred: drag-to-reorder the rail, Ctrl+1…9, Move-to context menu, Report a Problem, tab stripes per source.

specifications/010.title: Spec 010 — Syntax highlighting
specifications/010.content:
Codemirror does not do syntax highlighting right now for the requested languages.
Done 2026-09-20 for the languages that have a grammar. Decision P-093: highlighting is a view concern, so the CodeMirror bundle now carries grammars — the one exception to “no language knowledge in JS” (tree-sitter is native-only; per-keystroke server round trips for highlights would be worse than the rule). Rust still decides the language (Node::language_hint, passed as language in the init message; extended for .c .h .cc .cpp .hpp .cu .jsx .tsx .nix .cypher .cql .hx .tql .graphql .gql .sh .lua .ipynb). packages/js/codemirror/src/languages.ts: Lezer — Rust, JavaScript/TypeScript (+JSX), C/C++, Go, JSON, Markdown, SQL (SQLite dialect), YAML, Python, CSS, HTML, Typst (codemirror-lang-typst/lezer); legacy stream modes — Julia, TOML (Pixi), Cypher, shell, Lua. With a grammar the editor also gets folding (gutter), bracket matching, indent-on-input and Mod-/ comment toggling. Bundle 368 KB → 1 021 KB. Still plain: Lean 4, Nix, HelixQL, TypeQL, GraphQL (cm6-graphql needs the 500 KB graphql package — not worth it yet). LSP discovery grew at the same time: clangd, nil/nixd, taplo, tinymist, LanguageServer.jl, JSON/YAML/GraphQL servers. Suite highlight.mjs.

specifications/011.title: Spec 011 — Every panel closeable
specifications/011.content:
Graph, Agent, Terminal, Links, Git, History, Search, Explorer and Settings are closable: false today (PanelContribution.closable in each extension), so their tabs have no ×. Wanted: an × on all of them — closing a panel just removes it from its tile; nothing is lost because none of them holds unsaved state (the terminal asks first if a process is running).
Behaviour: every panel is closeable; reopening is via the activity bar / View → Show ▸ / the palette (view.panel.<id>) — 009. When a tile becomes empty it collapses (the side bar folds, the bottom panel hides) and the neighbouring split takes the space; Reset Layout restores the defaults. The last main-tile panel closing leaves the empty “open something” tile as now. The phone shell keeps its bottom bar regardless.
Change: closable: true in all contributions (the on_panel_closed hook already exists in the shell), the empty-tile collapse in shell.rs, and view.panel.* commands for every panel (not just five). E2E: close Graph, reopen from the View menu; close Terminal with a running process → prompt.
Done 2026-09-20. Every panel is closeable (closable: true in all contributions). A closed static panel (Graph, Agent, Terminal, Explorer, Search, Links, Git, History, Settings, Typst preview) goes into Workspace::closed_panels and contributes nothing until brought back; documents still close through their extension. Bringing one back: the palette’s View: Show  — now generated for every static panel, not just five — the phone bar, the Explorer rail button, Ctrl+Shift+F / agent focus, or any Command::ShowPanel. When the last panel of a tile is closed the workbench prunes the tile, so the side bar / bottom panel collapse and the neighbours take the space; on reopening, the panel docks back at its edge (home_zone: side → left, bottom → bottom, right → right) and the new split gets the default proportion (22 % / 72 % / 70 %) instead of 50 %. The terminal’s sessions live in the extension, so closing the Terminal panel hides it and reopening shows the same sessions — no prompt needed. Reset Layout still restores the defaults. Suite panels.mjs (close Graph → back via palette; close all side panels → main widens by >100 px; Show Explorer → left, 22 %; Terminal close/show).

specifications/012.title: Spec 012 — [[wiki-links]] should work like in Obsidian
specifications/012.content:
[[links]] are in the markdown files and the index understands them (index/extract/wikilinks.rs parses [[target#heading|alias]], resolves by path or by stem, and the Links panel shows backlinks), but in the editors they do not behave like in Obsidian.
Today

Rich editor (Milkdown): [[Target]] is plain text — remark escapes the brackets (un-escaped on the way back, unescapeWiki), nothing is rendered as a link, and the only interaction is Ctrl/Cmd+click on the text, which finds the brackets around the caret (wikiLinkAt) and opens the target through the index (open_wiki_link in editors/markdown/src/rich.rs).
Source editor (CodeMirror): plain text, no link, no click, no completion.
No [[ autocompletion, no alias/heading rendering, no distinction between resolved and unresolved targets, no “create on click”, and renaming a note does not update the links pointing at it.

Wanted (Obsidian behaviour)

Rendered as links in the rich editor: [[Target]] shows as Target (or the alias after |, with #heading kept), styled as a link; plain click follows (Ctrl+click opens in a new tab / split); unresolved targets are styled differently (dashed/muted) and a click offers to create Target.md next to the current note (or in the folder set in Settings → Links → new note location).
Round trip is exact: the markdown on disk keeps [[Target#heading|alias]] byte-for-byte — the link is a ProseMirror inline node (a Milkdown plugin: [[…]] ↔ node) so the escaping hack goes away.
[[ autocompletion in both editors: typing [[ opens a dropdown of pages from the index (fuzzy on title/stem/path, most recently opened first), # after a target lists that note’s headings, | starts an alias; Enter inserts and closes the brackets. The source editor uses the existing completion channel (Milestone 7); the rich editor its own popup. Same ranking as Quick Open.
Source editor: links get a decoration (underline, resolved/unresolved colour) and Ctrl+click follows; hover shows the target path.
Hover preview (both editors): a small popover with the first lines of the target — the index has the text.
Rename updates links: renaming or moving a note (Explorer inline edit / Op::Rename) rewrites [[old]] → [[new]] in every file that links to it (the index knows the backlinks; the same replace path as Replace in Workspace, shown as a preview with a count first). Aliases are kept; path-style links are rewritten to the new relative path.
Embeds ![[Note]] / ![[image.png]]: render the target inline in the rich editor (read-only block); pictures need 008 first.
Links panel: unresolved links listed with a Create button; clicking a backlink opens the source at the line.

Notes

Resolution rules stay the index’s (resolve: path-like → relative then root; otherwise by stem; Obsidian’s “shortest path when unique” is what stem matching gives). Ambiguous stems (two Notes.md) should offer both in the completion and mark the link as ambiguous.
All of this is Rust-owned data: the JS plugin only renders a node and asks Rust (completion, resolution, preview) — rule of packages/js.
E2E: links.mjs extended — click follows, unresolved click creates, [[ completion inserts, rename rewrites a backlink.

Done 2026-09-20 (items 1–4, 6, 8; 5 and 7 deferred). Rust owns it: moonkale_ext_api::wiki — spans() parser, Workspace::{resolve_wiki, wiki_spans, wiki_candidates, follow_wiki, wiki_backlinks, rewrite_wiki_links} over the index’s page list (path-like → relative then root; else by stem, same directory first, then shortest path; ambiguous stems complete as paths). Rich editor: a ProseMirror plugin (packages/js/milkdown/src/wiki.ts) decorates the literal [[…]] text — brackets (and the target when an alias is shown) hidden unless the caret is inside, unresolved dashed — so the markdown round trip is byte-exact; plain click follows; [[ opens a popup fed by Rust (wikiQuery → wikiCandidates), closed on blur, never inside an already closed link. Source editor: setWikiLinks marks (UTF-16 offsets, mapped through edits), Ctrl/Cmd+click follows, [[ is a second completion source. Follow creates Target.md next to the note (# Target heading) when unresolved; the Links panel’s phantom rows get Create. Rename (Workspace::rename_node) asks the index for backlinks first, then rewrites [[old]], [[old|, [[old# (stem and path forms) in every linking file — open documents get the edit as an unsaved change, closed files are written. Status re-checked 300 ms after the last edit and on every index change. Suite wiki.mjs (8 steps). Deferred: hover preview (5), embeds ![[…]] (7, needs 008).

specifications/013.title: Spec 013 — Formulas (KaTeX) in the rich markdown editor
specifications/013.content:
$…$ / $$…$$ do not render in the rich editor. Cause: Milkdown Crepe’s LaTeX feature is explicitly switched off in our wrapper (packages/js/milkdown/src/index.ts: [Crepe.Feature.Latex]: false — “keep the surface small”), and the bundle build strips fonts (--loader:.woff2=empty), so KaTeX’s fonts would be missing even if it were on.
Wanted

Inline $E = mc^2$ and block $$ … $$ render with KaTeX in the rich editor; clicking a formula edits its source (Crepe’s Latex feature does this: inline → a popup editor, block → a code-like block with live preview); the markdown on disk stays $…$/$$…$$ (remark-math syntax, what Quartz and Obsidian read).
The source editor highlights math spans once 010 (highlighting) exists; no rendering there.
Errors (bad LaTeX) show KaTeX’s red message inline, never break the document.
Typst preview is unaffected (it has its own math).

Change

Enable Crepe.Feature.Latex (KaTeX is a dependency of @milkdown/crepe’s feature; add katex explicitly to pin the version). Bundle cost to measure: KaTeX ≈ 280 KB JS + CSS; fonts ≈ 60 files / 1.2 MB — ship them as assets under editors/markdown/assets/katex/ (copied by the build script like xterm.css) and point KaTeX’s CSS at them, instead of --loader:.woff2=empty; on Android that is more APK bytes (Android Extensions and Bundling), so the fonts could be a separate dx asset group loaded on first formula.
Macros: a \newcommand block per vault (.moonkale/katex.toml → KaTeX macros), because papers define their own notation; the same file Unicode Input scopes could extend.
E2E rich.mjs: a note with $\alpha$ shows a .katex element; editing the formula updates the markdown.

Acceptance: this vault’s theory-style notes (see Julia and Lenticulum — the Lenticulum vault is full of formulas) render in the rich editor as they do in Quartz.
Done 2026-09-20. Crepe.Feature.Latex is on with throwOnError: false; KaTeX 0.18.7’s stylesheet and its 20 woff2 fonts are copied by packages/js/milkdown/katex-assets.mjs into editors/markdown/assets/katex/ (a dx folder asset, asset!("/assets/katex", AssetOptions::folder()), so the relative fonts/… urls keep working; woff/ttf sources stripped) and linked by the rich view through the new moonkale_ext_api::StylesheetUrl. Per-folder macros: .moonkale/katex.json → { "macros": { "\\R": "\\mathbb{R}" } }, read by Workspace::read_text_at and passed in the init message. Bundle +65 KB. Covered by rich.mjs (inline + block render, .katex elements, CSS linked, fonts loaded, \R macro, markdown unchanged on disk). Source-mode highlighting of math spans comes with 010’s markdown grammar.
Shared assets, 2026-10-13: native source-owned math also uses KaTeX 0.18.7. CSS/fonts now live in packages/ext-api/assets/katex/; Rich mode imports the shared folder asset. Native preview reads the same saved .moonkale/katex.json configuration and retains canonical dollar syntax.

specifications/014.title: Spec 014 — Word wrap in the code editor
specifications/014.content:
The code in CodeMirror should have a setting to wrap at the end of the line.
Done 2026-09-20. A user setting editor.wrap (default off) in settings.json; three ways to flip it: the Wrap button in every code editor’s toolbar (lit when on), Alt+Z / palette View: Toggle Word Wrap (editor.toggleWrap, contributed by the code editor extension), and Settings → Editor → Wrap long lines. Every open editor follows the setting live (an effect calls CodeEditorBackend::set_wrap; the bundle reconfigures an EditorView.lineWrapping compartment), including the markdown source view. Change: ext-api::settings (EditorFile/EditorSettings), editors/code (extension.rs command, panel.rs effect + button, backend set_wrap), js/codemirror (setWrap, features.wrap), ui/settings_panel.rs. Covered by a step in highlight.mjs (button, Alt+Z, persisted in the settings store).

specifications/015.title: Spec 015 — Close an open folder
specifications/015.content:
Once a folder is opened in the explorer I cannot close it.
Done 2026-09-20. Three ways: right-click the folder’s name in the Explorer → Close Folder; File → Close Folder; the palette command workspace.closeFolder (closes the first folder). Workspace::close_source(id) closes the source’s documents and the index derived from it; it refuses while a document of that folder is unsaved (status: “…: save or reload N unsaved document(s) before closing it”) so nothing is lost silently; if it was the folder the workspace settings belong to, the history log is flushed to .moonkale/history.jsonl and the presence room left. A new user setting reopen_last = false is written on close (and true on open), so the next desktop start begins empty instead of reopening the folder that was just closed. Covered by a step in files.mjs (refusal while dirty, then close: tree empty, no document tabs, “No folder open”). Per-source close/suspend for the multi-source projects of Projects and Sources builds on this.

specifications/016.title: Spec 016 — A .jl file stays at "Loading editor…"
specifications/016.content:
Opening lib/Mycelium.jl/src/free_energy.jl on the desktop shows “Loading editor…” and never finishes (screenshot markdown/prompts/load_editor.png, 2026-09-20; polarity_resolution.jl in another tab, a 195-node graph rendering in the tile above, “julia: language server exited” in the status bar).
Done 2026-09-20. Two things, one cause found by inspection (the web build could not reproduce it — the same file opened fine in Firefox):

Cause: the code editor mounted its view from a use_effect. On desktop the DOM mutation reaches the webview asynchronously, so an eval started from an effect can run before the host element exists; the script then returned silently, no ready ever came, and the panel showed “Loading editor…” forever (the P-047 family — the graph and rich editors were moved to onmounted for the same reason in Milestone 6/9; the code editor was not). It is timing-dependent, which is why it hit a heavy moment (a big graph laying out in the neighbouring tile). Fix: the view is mounted from the host div’s onmounted.
Never hang silently again: the mount script wraps cm.mount in try/catch and reports an error message; the panel shows “The editor could not start … please report it with the message below” with the JavaScript error and stack instead of “Loading editor…“. A grammar that throws while being set up (languages.ts) now degrades to plain text instead of taking the editor down.
Not related: “julia: language server exited” is LanguageServer.jl not being installed (julia --project=@lsp -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.add("LanguageServer")' — the hint in the status bar); the editor does not wait for it.

How to file this kind of thing: exactly like this — a screenshot into markdown/prompts/ and one line saying what you did and what you saw; the number and the “Done” paragraph are mine to add.

specifications/017.title: Spec 017 — The graph view resets on resize / when another window is drawn over it
specifications/017.content:
The graph view resets when the window gets resized or another window gets drawn over it.
Done 2026-09-20. The panel reloads its graph whenever an input changes — the active document, the index epoch, the filters — and on desktop a focus change or a relayout of the window can trigger such a reload; until now every set_graph discarded the positions, restarted the force layout from the spiral and refitted the camera, which looked like a reset. Now GraphView::set_graph is incremental: when the new graph shares at least half its nodes with the current one, known nodes keep their positions and pins, only new nodes are placed (at the mean of their known neighbours, nudged apart), the layout is warmed (temperature 3) instead of restarted — and not even that when nothing changed — and the camera is left exactly where the user put it. A graph with nothing in common (another folder, a database schema) still starts fresh with a fit. The earlier resize rule stays: a view the user never panned or zoomed re-fits when its canvas is resized (P-091); a touched view does not. Verified in graph3d.mjs: zoom, change the active document (a reload), camera identical afterwards.
Follow-up the same day, while taking the screenshots (the vault’s own graph looked like a white smear): four graph-quality fixes. (1) [core.md](github.com/…) links to other sites were indexed as phantom pages with the URL as label — 28 of them in this vault; the index skips targets with :// now. (2) Labels are placed with a screen-space collision test, most important first (hovered, then degree), so a dense cluster shows the hubs’ names instead of a pile. (3) Hubs pull less per edge (ForceAtlas2’s “dissuade hubs”: attraction ÷ (1 + ½ ln(1 + degree))) so a vault whose Home/index link to everything no longer folds onto one line; isolated nodes feel stronger gravity. (4) Camera::fit measures the connected part when it is the majority, so a few isolated notes no longer shrink the picture. GraphView::layout_state() joins camera_state() for tests.

specifications/018.title: Spec 018 — Splices, not the whole document, per keystroke (P-037)
specifications/018.content:
Since Milestone 1 the code editor’s JavaScript reported the whole text after every keystroke (P-037): a JSON hop of the entire file per key, O(n) per keystroke — the thing that made big files sluggish and blocked the plain-text tier of the Case Selector.
Done 2026-09-21. The CodeMirror bundle now reports splices: for each transaction, iterChanges yields (from, to, insert) in UTF-16 offsets of the text before the change, in document order, plus the new length as a consistency check. Rust keeps a mirror of the view’s text (view_text) and applies the splices to it in place (backend::apply_splices, applied back to front so old offsets stay valid, UTF-16 → byte offsets via utf16_to_byte), then the document takes the mirror (a memcpy, not a serialisation). A mismatch (out-of-range offset, length disagreement) is logged and the view is resynced from the document. Text pushed into the view (agent edits, reload, rename rewrites) is no longer mirrored eagerly: the view echoes the splice it applied, which keeps the mirror honest. The LSP still gets didChange with the full text (incremental sync is a separate step). Unit test for apply_splices (order, unicode, out of range); the editor suites pass unchanged; highlight.mjs gained a 3 MB file step — a keystroke is dirty in Rust after 87 ms (was seconds).

specifications/019.title: Spec 019 — Front matter in the rich editor
specifications/019.content:
The rich markdown editor showed a note’s YAML front matter as raw text at the top of the document (title: …, tags: … between two --- lines) — Obsidian folds it into a Properties block.
Done 2026-09-21. The rich view receives the body only; the front matter stays in Rust (rich.rs: split_frontmatter, frontmatter_yaml, join_frontmatter) and is shown above the editor as a Properties bar — collapsed: title: … · tags: … · description: … (first three keys); open: the YAML in a small editor. Edits to the YAML and to the body both go into the same document text, so Save writes ---
<yaml>
---
<body> exactly; an emptied YAML removes the block; a note without front matter shows “Properties: none” and the bar adds one when filled. The source (CodeMirror) view still shows everything, as it should. Unit test for the split/join round trip; rich.mjs step: front matter hidden from the ProseMirror text, summary shown, YAML edited + body edited, file saved intact.
Native live preview, 2026-10-14 (P-194). The Rust editor now provides the same collapsed summary and expandable YAML interface above the document. Apply commits one prefix transaction into the shared editor history; Cancel discards the local draft, and Save applies a current draft first. Comments, ordering, delimiters and body bytes remain literal, with LF/CRLF-aware edits. A revision check rejects stale drafts. The source-owned prefix collapses in preview and reveals for source caret/selection/search; disabling Preview shows the entire document. Rich remains available.

specifications/020.title: Spec 020 — Several folders in one graph
specifications/020.content:
With two folders open, the Graph view drew only the first folder’s index. Sometimes one wants the folders in separate graphs, sometimes in the same one — a repository next to the repository it depends on, or two Obsidian vaults about to be merged.
Done 2026-09-21. The Graph panel queries every open folder’s index and draws them in one graph — nodes coloured per folder, with a legend — and the source picker gains one entry per folder (folder: <name>) next to “all folders” to narrow the view to a single one; databases and traces stay in the picker as before. Local mode (two hops around the active document) queries every index too and merges the answers. What is not there yet: edges across folders — a [[wiki-link]] in vault A to a page that exists only in vault B stays unresolved (each index resolves within its own folder). Resolving across folders is the “project” idea of Projects and Sources: one index over several sources, saved as a project. graph/src/panel.rs (indices, picked_index, per-folder colours through label_color).

specifications/021.title: Spec 021 — Rich mode by default, and opening must not dirty the file
specifications/021.content:
Two observations about the markdown editor: (1) Rich mode should be the default for markdown files; (2) opening a file in Rich mode sometimes altered the markdown slightly — the yellow dot said there were unsaved changes before anything was typed.
Done 2026-09-21. (1) editor.markdown_rich (Settings → Editor → Open markdown files in Rich mode, default on; .moonkale/settings.json or the user file can turn it off) decides the mode a markdown document opens in; the Source | Rich buttons still switch, and a choice made by hand sticks for that document in that window. (2) The false dirty flag came from Milkdown’s parse → serialize round trip at load — remark normalises bullets, escapes and blank lines and reported the normalised text as a change. The bundle now keeps that normalised text as the baseline (entry.last after crepe.create(), with change reporting suppressed during the load) and reports only real edits; the file is rewritten in the normalised form only once the user changed something, which is the existing “the markdown is what gets saved” rule. Verified by rich.mjs: a file with * bullets and a setext heading opens in Rich mode with no dirty dot; typing then sets it. packages/js/milkdown/src/index.ts, editors/markdown/src/extension.rs, ext-api/src/settings.rs.

specifications/022.title: Spec 022 — Julia (and Python) symbols in the graph
specifications/022.content:
Rust files show up in the graph as their fn, struct, impl and the edges between them; Julia files were dots with no connections — is an add-on needed?
Done 2026-09-21. No add-on: symbols come from the index’s tree-sitter extractors, and only Rust had one. Two more now, bundled in moonkale-index (native, so desktop and server): Julia (tree-sitter-julia, symbols_julia.rs) — function and short-form f(x) = …, struct / mutable struct, abstract type, primitive type, module, macro, const; definitions inside a module link to it with Contains; dotted names such as Base.show are kept — and Python (tree-sitter-python, symbols_python.rs) — def and class, decorated or not, methods inside a class linked to it. Each symbol is a node with a Defines edge from its file, exactly like Rust’s. What “interconnections” means today, for every language: file → symbol (Defines) and container → member (Contains); calls and references are not extracted for any language (that is LSP territory or a later tree-sitter pass — see Core Languages). The other core languages (C/C++, Go, TypeScript, Lean, Nix, …) still show as dots. Unit tests parse a module with every form.

specifications/023.title: Spec 023 — Why a build takes 30 minutes after a pull
specifications/023.content:
Observation: on the machine where I write, a rebuild takes seconds; after git pull on the other machine, dx serve (desktop) takes 1 767 s. Is there a reason, and a way to cut it?
Answer (2026-09-21) — what a desktop dx serve does here, measured on this machine (8 cores, 30 GB):

It is two full builds. A fullstack desktop app builds the client (the moonkale binary, 1.8 GB in debug) and the server (target/dx/moonkale/debug/web/server, 1.7 GB) — every workspace crate twice, with different features, and two links of a gigabyte-plus binary each. The release equivalents are 193 MB and 188 MB; the difference is debug info.
Feature changes rebuild almost everything. The Milestone 11 commit made tokio a non-optional dependency of api with more features, and added axum-server, rustls, tokio-rustls, reqwest (remote). Any change to the feature set of a crate as central as tokio recompiles it and everything above it — hyper, reqwest, axum, dioxus-server, the LLM client, … — i.e. most of the 991 crates. A pull that changes Cargo.toml features costs a near-clean build; a pull that changes only Rust source costs seconds. (A clean release desktop build here: 361 s; the debug clean build with its two gigabyte links is what you saw.)
The shared target/ thrashes. (dx compiles the desktop client into target/debug, the same directory cargo test/clippy use.) dx serve, cargo test -p <crate>, cargo clippy, the web build and the server build all write target/debug with different feature unifications: it held 178 GB, 15 727 files in deps/, and 2 370 incremental directories (46 GB) when measured — each combination keeps its own artefacts and switching between them re-links. My own checks and tests now use CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target/agent, so they never invalidate what your dx serve built.

What cuts it (in order of effect):

Less debug info. In the root Cargo.toml:
[profile.dev]
debug = "line-tables-only"   # backtraces with file:line, ~4× smaller binaries, far faster links
[profile.dev.package."*"]
debug = false                # no debug info for dependencies at all
Applied 2026-09-21 and measured: a clean debug desktop build (client + server, 1 084 crates, while a browser test batch ran on the same 8 cores) took 399 s and the binaries came out at 449 MB + 470 MB instead of 1.8 GB + 1.7 GB. That full build is already in target/debug on this machine, so the next dx serve here starts from a warm cache; on the other machine the first pull after this costs one full build. Set debug = 2 back for a session in which you need to step through a dependency in a debugger.
Keep Cargo.lock and features stable between pulls where possible; a feature change on a leaf crate is cheap, on tokio/serde/dioxus it is the whole tree.
Don’t mix invocations in one target/: give scripts and tests their own CARGO_TARGET_DIR (done for the agent’s runs); cargo clean when target/ passes a few hundred GB.
Linker: rustc 1.98 already uses rust-lld on x86_64 Linux, so mold gains little; sccache would carry compiled dependencies between the two machines (cargo install sccache, RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache) — not set up.
Long term: the server half is only needed on desktop for remote mode’s client code, not as a second binary; a desktop build without the fullstack server build is a dioxus configuration question (P-101).

specifications/024.title: Spec 024 — Go to definition and graph focus from the symbol under the cursor
specifications/024.content:
Follow-up to Code Editor Implementations (the “word under the cursor” question) — cursor tracking matters because of what should hang off it:

A menu entry or a (double) left/right click on the name of a function, variable, type or macro jumps to its definition, and/or centres a graph view on it — one graph view of several, since a workspace may show more than one (020: several folders in one graph; a second Graph panel is a later spec).
The two actions should be separate and both reachable from the same symbol: Go to definition (opens/scrolls the editor) and Show in graph (the graph pans to the node, highlights it, optionally switches to Local mode around it).

What exists (2026-09-21): Workspace::cursor / cursor_word() for both editors (Milestone 14); LSP Go to definition in the CodeMirror editor (Milestone 7, keyboard/menu); the index’s symbol nodes (Defines/Contains edges) for Rust, Julia, Python (spec 022); the Graph panel’s Local mode around the active document; GraphRequest for “draw this”.
What is missing: a symbol → index-node resolution (cursor_word + the document → the Symbol node whose key is <path>#<kind>:<name>@<line>, or by name across the folder when it is a use, not a definition); a Workspace::focus_graph_on(node) request the graph panel answers by centring (and a way to say which graph panel); mouse-button bindings (025); the same for the Rust editor, which has no LSP — there the index is the only source of definitions, which is fine for a first version.
Not implemented — documented for later. Suggested order: (1) focus_graph_on + graph centring, (2) symbol resolution through the index, (3) the context-menu entries and double-click in CodeMirror, (4) the Rust editor.

specifications/025.title: Spec 025 — A five-button mouse is the expected input device
specifications/025.content:
Expect users to have a 5-button “gamer” mouse: left, middle (wheel click), right, and the two thumb buttons (browser back/forward, buttons 4 and 5 in X/Wayland terms, MouseEvent.button 3 and 4 in the DOM).
What that should mean in Moonkale (to design with 024):

Thumb buttons = navigation history: back/forward through the documents and graph positions visited (the editor stack and the graph camera), like a browser — the most common use of these buttons and what people already expect.
Middle click on a file, a symbol or a graph node: open in a new tab / new split without switching focus (the browser convention).
Double left click / right click on a symbol: the actions of 024 (definition, graph focus); the context menu should list them so a two-button user is not locked out.
Wheel + modifiers: Ctrl for zoom (graph, editor font later), Shift for horizontal scroll — already true in the graph.
Bindings should be configurable next to the keybindings (Settings → Keybindings; a mouse section in the settings file), and the defaults must not conflict with the webview’s own handling of buttons 3/4 (WebKitGTK maps them to history navigation of the page — Moonkale has to preventDefault them or the app “navigates back” out of itself; check on desktop, web and Android).

Not implemented — documented for later, together with 024.
2026-10-14 (Daniel): a five-button mouse is now a requirement for full functionality, not only the expected device. The plan, with the default and extended mouse maps, keymap presets and other keyboard layouts, is Input Layouts (WP-61). Everything stays reachable with two buttons and the keyboard.

specifications/026.title: Spec 026 — Fonts in the rich (Milkdown) editor
specifications/026.content:
The Milkdown extension should have the option to change the font sizes (or fonts in general) — Prompt23.
Done 2026-09-22. Three settings under the Markdown extension’s row in the Extensions panel (user or workspace scope): font size (px, 8–48, default 16), font (a CSS font-family for the note body; empty = the theme’s), code font (for code blocks and inline code). They become CSS variables on the rich host (--mk-rich-size, --mk-rich-font, --mk-rich-code-font) that rich.css applies to the ProseMirror content; headings scale with the size (Crepe sizes them in em). Settings file keys: editor.rich_font_size, editor.rich_font, editor.rich_code_font. Verified in rich.mjs (22 px Georgia). Not done: a font picker (type the family), and fonts for the code editors (CodeMirror has its own theme; a follow-up).

specifications/027.title: Spec 027 — macOS keybindings: Ctrl is not Cmd
specifications/027.content:
From a friend testing a macOS build from source (Prompt25): “the keybindings are a mix of those intended for Linux and Windows — Ctrl+O acts like Cmd+O, Ctrl+N like Cmd+N. macOS users use Ctrl+N for Emacs-style cursor navigation.”
