Cause. Keybinding::matches took a single ctrl_or_meta flag and every caller passed m.ctrl() || m.meta(): one table for all platforms, at the price of both modifiers firing everywhere. On a Mac that makes Ctrl+O, Ctrl+N, Ctrl+S, Ctrl+P… application shortcuts, which on macOS they are not — Ctrl+letter belongs to the text system (Emacs keys in every text field) and Ctrl+click is the context menu.
Done 2026-09-22. moonkale_ext_api::keys: is_mac() (desktop: cfg!(target_os = "macos"); web: navigator.platform/userAgent), primary(&Modifiers) = Cmd on a Mac, Ctrl elsewhere — never both — and primary_name() so menus and the palette print Cmd+O on a Mac. Every site that said “Ctrl or Meta” now asks keys::primary: the frame’s command dispatch, Ctrl+S in the CodeMirror, Rust and flow editors and the rich editor, Ctrl+click in the image viewer, both terminals (file links), git’s Ctrl+Enter, and in the JavaScript bundles the wiki-link clicks (CodeMirror, Milkdown). The Rust terminal sends control bytes for Ctrl only, on every platform — Cmd+C on a Mac is copy, not ^C. The keybinding text in Settings says so. Unit test on the rule; the keybinding-sensitive browser suites unchanged.
Not verified on a Mac — nobody in the project has one; the friend who reported it is the test. If Cmd+Q, Cmd+W or Cmd+, behave oddly in the webview, that is the next report. The CodeMirror and xterm bundles already used Mod- keymaps (Cmd on a Mac) and are untouched.
macOS in Docker? It exists (docker-osx: macOS in QEMU/KVM inside a container; needs KVM, tens of GB, slow), but Apple’s licence allows macOS virtual machines on Apple hardware only, so it is not a route this project uses. The legitimate way is the GitHub macOS runner the release workflow already uses for .dmg builds — which builds but cannot click. Testing stays with people who own a Mac.

specifications/028.title: Spec 028 — Export and import the phone's vault
specifications/028.content:
Found while testing the release APK (2026-09-22, Problem Log P-131): the Android app keeps its vault in the app’s private storage, and there is no way to get it out or back in from inside the app. Today the only route is adb exec-out run-as … tar -cf - files, which works on a debug build only — a release-signed build is not debuggable, so the same command cannot restore into it. Consequences:

Switching a phone from a debug-signed build to a release-signed one (which every user does once, when the signing key lands) destroys the vault: the install refuses, the user uninstalls, the private storage goes with it.
A user without adb cannot back up anything they typed on the phone, cannot move it to a desktop, and cannot recover it if the app is removed.
Notes typed on the phone are the least backed-up files in the project, and they are the ones a new user produces first.

What is wanted

Export: File → Export vault… writes the whole vault as a single .zip (or .tar) through Android’s file picker (ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT), so it lands in Downloads, Drive, or wherever the user points it. No permissions needed — the picker grants the one URI.
Import: File → Import vault… takes such an archive back (ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT), asking whether to merge or replace. A file that already exists is kept under name (imported).md rather than overwritten.
Open a folder outside private storage (the bigger version): ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT_TREE gives the app a persistent URI for a real directory — the phone’s Documents, an SD card, a Syncthing folder — and Moonkale opens that as a source. Then the vault survives uninstalls by construction, and Syncthing or a git client can sync it. This is the proper fix; 1 and 2 are the cheap ones that unblock the signing switch.
Single-file export for one note (share sheet) — small, and what someone actually wants when they typed a thought on the bus.

Notes on the implementation

The moonkale-project-fs source works on paths; a SAF (Storage Access Framework) tree is not a path. Either mirror the tree into private storage and write back on save, or add a source that speaks DocumentFile. The first is simpler and wrong in the long run; the second belongs next to Data Sources.
The JNI call surface is small (ACTION_* intents plus a result callback); dioxus-mobile exposes the Activity, so this does not need a fork (Android).
Until this exists, Install and packages/mobile/README.md tell users to copy anything important to a server (File → Connect to Server…) before the one-time reinstall.

Related: Android · Milestone 12 - Implementation Log (Connect to Server) · Problem Log P-131.

specifications/029.title: Spec 029 — The app's name and icon must come from configuration, not a post-build patch
specifications/029.content:
Daniel, 2026-09-22: “the app from the apk has no logo and is called ‘mobile’“.
What happens. dx build --platform android generates a Gradle project and names the app after the crate (mobile → Mobile), with its own template icon; [application] name = "Moonkale" and [bundle] icon in packages/mobile/Dioxus.toml are not applied to Android (spec 007 saw the label half of this). packages/mobile/build-android.sh therefore patches the generated project after dx build and before gradlew: it writes res/values/strings.xml and renders ic_launcher for every density plus an adaptive icon.
Why it broke. The patch is a post-processing step over a tree Gradle also caches. Gradle keeps per-variant intermediates, and a variant that was not rebuilt keeps the pre-patch values: on 2026-09-22 the release APK was correct (Moonkale, adaptive icon) while the debug APK built minutes later from the same tree said Mobile with the template icon — and that was the one installed on the phone (P-132). The label on disk and the label in the artefact had silently diverged.
Done already (2026-09-22): the script drops merged_manifest(s), merged_res, packaged_res and incremental before building, and afterwards reads the finished APK back with aapt2 dump badging, refusing to hand out an APK whose label is not Moonkale or which has no launcher icon. Cheap, and it turns a silent wrong artefact into a failed build.
Still wanted.

Configuration, not patching. [application] name (and an Android icon) should reach the generated project — upstream in dioxus-cli, or, until then, by writing the values into the generated strings.xml/manifest from a single place that also owns the icon rendering, so nothing depends on which Gradle variant ran last.
One source for the icon. packages/mobile/assets/icon.png is rendered to five densities plus an adaptive foreground by a Python/Pillow block inside the shell script. That belongs in a small Rust or dx step, not in a heredoc that a missing Pillow silently turns into a broken build (the CI job installs Pillow separately for exactly this reason).
The same check for the other platforms: the .deb, the AppImage and the macOS bundle take their name and icon from Dioxus.toml/packaging/linux/moonkale.desktop, and nothing verifies the built artefact. A dx bundle that renames the app would be noticed by a user, not by CI.
Version code. The generated project hardcodes versionCode = 1; two releases therefore carry the same code. Sideloading tolerates it, an app store would not, and “is this the newer build?” has no answer on the device. It should be derived from the version.

Related: Android · Packaging Overview · Problem Log P-132 · spec 007.

specifications/030.title: Spec 030 — Languages (English, German, Chinese) and themes
specifications/030.content:
Daniel, 2026-10-02: “Please do localization in English, German and Chinese. Please make light/dark mode or better yet themes. Do it whenever you see fit.”
What is wanted

The UI in three languages — English, German, Chinese (Simplified) — chosen in Settings → You, defaulting to the system language (desktop: LANG/the OS locale; web: navigator.languages; Android: the device locale), falling back to English for anything not translated. Switching applies without a restart.
Themes, not only light/dark: a theme is a named set of colours (and maybe fonts) for the whole app — workbench, editors (CodeMirror, Milkdown, the Rust editor, xterm, the Rust terminal), the graph view, the flow canvas, tables, KaTeX. At least Dark, Light, and Follow system (prefers-color-scheme); more themes as files, so users and extensions can add their own.

Where things stand (checked 2026-10-02)

Text: every UI string is a Rust literal in the panels, menus, the palette and the status bar (about 130 in shell/src alone, more in each editor and in the JS bundles’ own strings). No translation layer exists.
Themes: Settings.theme exists ("dark" by default) but only the Rust code editor reads it; the shell’s CSS uses dioxus-workbench’s --wb-* variables and our --mk-* ones, with about 580 hard-coded hex colours across the stylesheets; CodeMirror ships the one-dark theme; the graph renderer has its own colours.

Design notes (for whoever does it)

Strings: a t!("key")-style lookup with Fluent (fluent-bundle, Mozilla’s format; plural and gender rules for German, no inflection trouble for Chinese) or a smaller key → string table per language; files under packages/shell/locales/{en,de,zh-CN}/*.ftl. Each extension brings its own strings (a contribution, like settings), so the catalogue split of Milestone 18 - Library Refactor phase 4 is the natural moment. Keys, not English text, are the ids, so a changed English wording does not orphan a translation.
JS bundles keep no strings of their own where possible (rule of packages/js: Rust owns the text); the few they have (CodeMirror’s search panel, Milkdown’s menus) get their phrases from Rust at init.
Chinese: a CJK font in the font stacks (Noto Sans CJK / system), and the IME paths that issue #19 already flags (Enter during composition must not send).
Themes: one token set (--mk-bg, --mk-fg, --mk-accent, --mk-border, syntax colours, graph palette, the eight source colours of spec 009) defined per theme, mapped onto --wb-* for the workbench; every stylesheet uses tokens only (a CI check can grep for hex colours outside theme files). CodeMirror, xterm and Milkdown get their themes generated from the same tokens; the graph renderer takes its palette as data. Theme files as TOML/JSON in the user’s config directory and as an extension contribution.
Both are settings that belong in the state store (Internal State), synced across devices.

Done when
The three languages switch live in Settings, with every built-in panel, menu, command title and dialog translated (German and Chinese reviewed by a native speaker — Daniel for German); Dark, Light and Follow-system work everywhere listed above with no hard-coded colour left outside the theme files; a fourth theme can be dropped into the config directory and selected. E2E: a suite switches language and theme and checks a few labels and computed colours.
Outcome (2026-10-03)
Done on the spec-030 branch in three parts — Fluent strings for the shell and the workspace, every extension in three languages, themes. How it works and the rules: Languages and Themes. Problems met: P-151 (subscribing inside a command effect), P-152 (dynamic text in a style element breaks hydration).
Open from Done when: the German and Chinese texts are drafts that still need a native speaker’s review; the JS bundles’ own phrases (CodeMirror’s search panel) are English; the IME composition case of issue #19 is unchanged.

specifications/031.title: Spec 031 — Frontend graph engine
specifications/031.content:
Scope: Rust frontend graph engine, using the existing WebGL renderer where practical. This specifies visualization and interaction, not database storage, graph semantics, or execution/simulation logic. Inspect the current renderer before refactoring; extend existing abstractions where possible.
1. Architecture
Separate (1) input graph/view data, (2) visual scene and layers, (3) layout/routing, and (4) rendering/picking. Stable semantic IDs must be distinct from visual-instance IDs: one entity may appear in multiple views or positions. Keep styles and viewport state separate from topology. Support incremental updates without rebuilding the entire scene.
2. Visual primitives

Nodes: variable size, shape (circle, rectangle, diamond, polygon/custom), color, stroke, icon, label and optional expanded content. Support nested/compound nodes.
Ports/channels: colored, typed-looking boundary markers with configurable placement, direction and multiple connections; expose independent hit targets.
Edges: directed/undirected, self-loops, parallel edges, configurable color, width, opacity, dashes, arrowheads, labels and clickability. Routes: straight, curved/Bézier and orthogonal/grid-aligned; optional manually routed points.
Animated edges: optional moving particle/pulse along a path with adjustable speed. Animation is presentation only; external simulation state may drive it.
Higher-order connections: low-degree hyperedges (junction or enclosing region), simplicial faces (filled triangles, etc.), and highlighted cliques/subgraphs (hulls or tinted regions). Do not conflate a graph clique, hyperedge and simplex.

3. Layers and overlapping representations
One underlying edge/node can belong to multiple independently toggleable visual layers. Example: blue static function-call edges and a yellow stack-trace path; shared edges may show both using offset parallel strokes, dashed overlay or priority styling. Layers independently control style, visibility, labels and interaction. Support persistent layers and temporary overlays (debugging, selection, search, profiling).
A stack trace is an ordered sequence of frame/call occurrences, not just a set of edge IDs: recursion can revisit the same function or call edge. Preserve occurrence identity and order independently of semantic entity IDs. Layers must not mutate graph topology.
4. Hierarchy, grouping and zoom

Support nested structural groups/modules, overlapping visual memberships (cliques/communities), and marked subgraphs.
Distinguish structural expansion (revealing actual internals) from visual aggregation (LOD clustering).
On zoom-out, replace dense groups with aggregate nodes and bundled/proxy edges; on zoom-in, reveal members, internal connections and ports. Preserve selection and cross-boundary connectivity through transitions.
Allow layouts centered on one or multiple focal nodes.

5. Layout and interaction
Provide manual/fixed positioning plus pluggable automatic layouts (initially force-directed and hierarchical; orthogonal routing for flow diagrams). Support pan/zoom, selection and multiselection, dragging, hover, edge/port picking, collapse/expand, and optional edge clicks. Keep graph exploration and flow/canvas editing as distinct interaction modes over the same renderer; do not implement a separate graph renderer for each domain.
6. Level of detail and performance
Decide visibility from projected pixel size, local density and frame budget, not zoom alone. Progressively suppress tiny labels/ports, disable tiny hit targets, stop barely visible animations, simplify edges, bundle connections, and cull off-screen geometry. Prefer batched/instanced WebGL drawing, reused geometry, cached text and partial buffer updates. Picking may use spatial indexing and/or GPU ID picking. Avoid mounting rich UI components for every node; reserve them for selected/expanded nodes.
7. Domain compatibility
The frontend engine should be configurable for RDF/ontology graphs, code/dependency/call graphs, no-code/low-code flows, Simulink/ModelingToolkit-style port diagrams, factor graphs, low-degree hypergraphs/simplicial complexes, and spatial hardware layouts. Domain-specific validation and simulation remain outside the renderer. Preserve meaningful coordinates when a spatial layout requires them.
8. Acceptance checks

Render nodes of different shapes/sizes/colors/icons, with colored ports and independently selectable edges.
Render multiple parallel edges and straight/curved/orthogonal routes, arrowheads and variable-speed moving particles.
Toggle blue call-graph and yellow stack-trace layers; shared edges display both, and recursive trace occurrences retain order.
Show nested groups, overlapping highlighted cliques, a hyperedge and a filled 2-simplex without treating them as equivalent.
Collapse/expand a group across zoom levels while keeping external connections and stable selection.
At low zoom/dense scenes, suppress subpixel detail and animation while preserving responsive navigation.
Switch graph-exploration and flow-editing modes without duplicating rendering infrastructure.

Implementation guidance: First map these requirements onto Moonkale’s current Rust/WebGL architecture. Propose minimal interfaces and a staged plan before broad rewrites. Prefer incremental, testable changes; do not introduce a new rendering backend solely for this specification.

Mapped onto the current renderer, with minimal interfaces and a staged plan: Frontend Graph Engine Mapping. The flow editor’s move onto the same engine is ADR-0018.

specifications/README.content:
Small, numbered notes (001.md, 002.md, …) on how a UI element should behave, or a little bug — not big specifications (those are the milestone plans — see the Roadmap). Daniel writes them; whoever fixes one edits the same file: add status: done and a short “Done ” paragraph naming the change and the test that covers it. Bigger findings still go to the Problem Log.
































































































































































#topicstatus001Flow editor: Backspace/Delete in a parameter field deleted the blockdone002HelixDB as an embedded graph source — done in Milestone 17 (git dependency, read-only; HTTP mode open)done003Projects: several sources at once, a selector, import/export and sync — desired behaviour in Projects and Sourcesdocumented004Unicode input: \int → ∫ with a dropdown, in every text field — design in Unicode Inputdocumented005A Claude Code extension without an API key — plan in Claude Code Extensionpartly done — the provider (Level 3) since Milestone 12, login since 15; empty tiles collapse and come back at their edgedone012[[wiki-links]] like in Obsidian: rendered, clickable, [[ completion, create-on-click, rename rewrites (embeds + hover preview deferred) | done || 013Formulas (KaTeX) in the rich editor, with per-folder macrosdone014Word wrap in the code editor: editor.wrap, toolbar button, Alt+Z, Settings → Editordone015Close an open folder: Explorer context menu, File menu, palette; debug = "line-tables-only" applied: clean debug build 399 s, binaries 449 + 470 MB instead of 1.8 + 1.7 GBdone024Go to definition / centre a graph view from the symbol under the cursor (menu, double or right click); builds on cursor_word and the index’s symbolsdocumented025A five-button mouse is required for full functionality (2026-10-14): thumb buttons = back/forward, middle click = open aside, configurable; guard the webview’s own button handling. Plan in Input Layoutsrequired, planned026Rich editor typography: font size, body font, code font — settings under the Markdown extensiondone027macOS keybindings: Ctrl in a binding means Cmd on a Mac and only Cmd; Ctrl stays the text system’s (Emacs keys); keys::primary everywheredone (unverified on a Mac)028Export/import the phone’s vault (and open a real folder through the Storage Access Framework): private storage is lost on every uninstall and run-as only works on debug buildsopen029The Android app’s name and launcher icon come from a post-build patch that Gradle’s caches can defeat (an APK said “Mobile” with the template icon); verify the artefact, then move it into configurationpartly done030The UI in English, German and Chinese; themes (dark, light, follow system, user/extension themes)open — after Milestone 18 phase 4 (per-extension strings and settings)
Planned — not yet numbered
Requests that are agreed but have no spec number yet. Daniel numbers them when he writes the spec; until then they live here.


Components on the canvas (2026-10-14). Small Dioxus components drawn over the graph and flow renderer, for example a table node in a schema editor (Supabase-like), a node’s settings edited in place, or an Obsidian-like canvas of documents. They show only when zoomed in far enough, and only a few at a time. The shape:

a DOM layer above the GPU canvas and the label overlay, moved by one CSS transform per camera change, with components placed in canvas coordinates;
a node marked as embedded keeps its rectangle in the engine (wires, ports, drag, layout); only its label and symbol give way to the component;
below a screen size or off-screen, the component unmounts and the plain rectangle remains;
clicks pass through the layer except on components, and a card’s header drags its node;
2D only.

Items 1–3 implemented in WP-04/05 (2026-10-23): the engine reports a
frame-coalesced CSS-pixel camera mapping, and InNode.embed reserves a plain
rectangle without label, caption, icon or schematic ink. The new shared
packages/canvas-layer crate provides CanvasLayer, CanvasItem and
CanvasHeader: one camera transform, world-space placement, size/viewport
unmounting, component-only pointer handling and header drag callbacks. It
rejects 3D views. Graph and future canvas editors can use it without depending
on the flow extension.
Flow is the first user: its selected block’s parameter card follows pan,
zoom, fit and resize, and its header moves the document’s block with one undo
step. Undo/redo retain selections that still exist in the restored scope.
Flow limits automatic fit magnification so a single block leaves room for the
card; explicit zoom remains free. The card remains beside its schematic;
hosts replacing node content can use embed:true instead.
Acceptance is covered by native camera/embed/visibility tests,
graph-camera.mjs and the production-panel canvas-layer.mjs, alongside
graph/flow/subflow suites. The layer unmounts below 100 × 32 projected CSS
pixels or outside the viewport, leaving the engine node in place.
Item 4 remains open: an extension node-kind contribution would resolve a
host-side view factory returning a Dioxus Element plus world bounds and LOD
limits. The host wraps it in CanvasItem, supplies its camera and node-drag
callback, and marks the corresponding engine node embedded. The shared layer
does not depend on a registry or extension API; the contribution contract and
permissions can be added later without changing camera/placement plumbing.


Code editor at 60 FPS (2026-10-14): requirement CED-R22 in Code Editor Requirements, the gate in Rust Code Editor Roadmap. p95 frame interval ≤ 16.7 ms while typing, scrolling and selecting, in an ordinary file and the 3 MB one, web and desktop. The current Rust editor does not meet it yet.


A stripped-down static reader (2026-10-14, way later): a repository or a knowledge graph published as wiki-like pages, Quartz-like but with code navigation, Moonkale’s graph and in-browser SQL. It sits beside the full web version, not in place of it. Quartz stays for the vault until then. Notes in Publishing Sources (“Revisited 2026-10-14”).


Math in any delimiter, LaTeX or Typst (2026-10-14): $, $$, \(, \[ and their doubled-backslash forms all work. Each formula renders as LaTeX (KaTeX) or Typst math, whichever it is, and errors only when both fail. A command normalises a file or folder to one convention. Spec in Math Delimiters and Renderers, WP-36.


Shared work in a session (2026-10-14): several people and agents in one session (roles, agents with a sponsor, tasks, an approval inbox, attribution); concurrent edits on one graph, where the database guarantees each write and Moonkale adds awareness, conflicts, proposals and per-actor undo; comments on anything, with @agent mentions. In Shared Work, WP-48 to WP-50. Conversations already render Markdown.


Linked panels (2026-10-14): a node’s content and its context (the local graph, backlinks, rows, plots) form a link group that follows one subject. Each group has a tab colour plus a marker (never colour alone), and several groups can exist side by side, each with its own local graph. Plan in Linked Panels, WP-59.


Overview (2026-10-14): like GNOME’s Activities, Ctrl+Alt+Space (the Windows key isn’t available) shows every open tab across tiles and windows as a card with a schematic preview of its content, grouped by link group, with type-to-search that also reaches quick open. Plan in Overview, WP-60.

testing/Benchmarks.title: Benchmarks — what to measure, how, and against which budget
testing/Benchmarks.content:
Why (Daniel, 2026-10-14): a document of benchmarking tasks for Moonkale, covering performance on CPU and GPU, memory consumption, internet usage and load balancing. What lives in memory and what goes to the database is decided beside it, in ADR-0026 Memory and the store.
Today: benchmarks exist, but scattered:

bench.mjs (layout step time, 1 k to 100 k nodes);
bench-draw.mjs (draw time per frame, SwiftShader);
spec 018’s 3 MB typing latency (87 ms per key);
the code editor’s 60 FPS gate (CED-R22, Rust Code Editor Roadmap);
ratio bounds inside live-preview-long.mjs;
the 50 000-row scroll in table-grid.mjs.

None of them keeps its results over time. This page turns them into one catalogue, BM-nn.
Method

The reference machine is the development box: 8 cores, 30 GB RAM, an RTX 3080 (10 GB), NVMe, Linux on Wayland. Plus the phone (Galaxy S10e) for mobile budgets, and CI runners only for coarse regressions (they’re noisy and have no GPU).
A quiet machine. A benchmark takes the bench lock (flock ~/.cache/moonkale-slots/bench.lock, beside the build slots so a sandboxed agent that may write that one directory can take it) and refuses to run while builds or other agents’ browser suites are running (see Running Several Agents). Numbers from a busy machine are not recorded.
Medians over runs: a warm-up first, then N runs (N ≥ 5), recording median, p95 and max. Frame metrics use requestAnimationFrame intervals, latency uses performance.now() around the action, and memory uses RSS (native) and performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory (web, where available).
Results are kept in a database, not in logs: each run appends a row (benchmark, commit, platform, metric, value, timestamp) to ~/.cache/moonkale-bench/results.sqlite. Moonkale opens that file as a source, so the history is a table and, with the plot extension, a chart (Plotting Requirements). A release’s summary row goes into this page.
Budgets: a benchmark with a budget fails when over it. Where none is set, the first job is a baseline; the budget follows from it and from use.

The catalogue
CPU and latency

Order (proposal)

The method first: the bench lock, the results database, and a runner that records.
Move the existing benchmarks into it: BM-04, 09, 11, and the scroll part of BM-06.
The frame gates: BM-10 (codex’s WP-01), BM-11 on the real GPU, BM-13 and BM-14.
No growth: BM-25 catches leaks early and cheaply.
Network on the web build: BM-30 to 32.
Server load: BM-50 to 54, before a shared server is offered to anyone.

Work package: WP-55 in Work Packages.
WP-69 development profiles — 2026-10-17
Development builds optimize the Tree-sitter runtime and dioxus-code syntax-query dependency at level 2, and the code-view crate at level 1. The standalone native fixture mirrors these overrides because it has its own workspace. This is a developer-experience change: parsing and preview indexing remain responsive while exercising ordinary development builds. It trades some compilation time and precise debug stepping for faster input-path work. Release and graph-wasm profiles are unchanged.
These overrides are a separate proposal from the code fix in P-211 Preview row queries and folding repeated full text work. Validate live-preview-long with the code changes and the original development profile first; record the same code with these overrides separately. A compiler-profile improvement must not stand in for fixing repeated document scans or parsing. The per-run medians, p95s, build variants and retained logs are in the WP-69 handoff and commit requests.
On the final WP-69 code, the fresh-fixture Firefox run measured Preview median/p95 82.84/86.14 ms against Source 72.92/76.20 ms with the original profile. With the overrides, the same suite measured 73.38/77.76 ms against 68.70/70.66 ms. Both pass the unchanged bound; the overrides are retained solely as a separate development-experience improvement. These are local development-build results, not release or physical-device acceptance.

testing/How-to-Write-Tests.title: How to Write Tests
testing/How-to-Write-Tests.content:
Checked 2026-10-01 
                  
                

The recipes for plain #[test], integration tests in tests/, VirtualDom component tests and the Playwright suites match what the repository does. proptest, insta, nextest, FakeSource and TestHost are recommendations, not in use — no crate depends on them yet. Where the real tests are: Testing Strategy.


Concrete recipes for each layer, in the order you’ll meet them. Strategy and rationale: Testing Strategy. All snippets target Dioxus 0.7.10 (APIs checked: VirtualDom::rebuild_in_place, dioxus_ssr::render).
0. Where tests live and how to run them
packages/core/src/graph/node.rs      # #[cfg(test)] mod tests { … }   ← unit tests next to the code
packages/core/tests/transactions.rs  # integration tests: use the crate as a consumer would
packages/shell/tests/workbench.rs       # component tests (render to string)
packages/server/tests/server_fns.rs     # server-function tests
packages/web/tests/e2e/…             # scripts driving a real browser
cargo test -p moonkale-core                 # one crate
cargo test --workspace --exclude web        # all native tests
cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude web # same, parallel processes (install: cargo install cargo-nextest)
cargo test -p moonkale-core -- ids::        # filter by name
cargo insta review                          # accept/reject snapshot changes
1. Unit tests for pure logic (core, lift, extract)
The bulk of the suite. No async, no I/O.
// packages/core/src/id.rs
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
 
    #[test]
    fn derived_ids_are_deterministic() {
        let src = SourceId::new("folder-1");
        assert_eq!(NodeId::derive(&src, "src/main.rs"), NodeId::derive(&src, "src/main.rs"));
        assert_ne!(NodeId::derive(&src, "src/main.rs"), NodeId::derive(&src, "src/lib.rs"));
    }
}
Property tests for invariants (proptest):
proptest! {
    #[test]
    fn apply_then_undo_is_identity(ops in arb_transaction()) {
        let mut g = Graph::default();
        let applied = g.apply(&ops).unwrap();
        g.undo(&applied).unwrap();
        prop_assert_eq!(g, Graph::default());
    }
}
Snapshot tests for structures (insta) — e.g. the lifted schema graph of a SQLite file:
#[test]
fn sqlite_schema_lifts_to_graph() {
    let schema = introspect_sqlite("tests/fixtures/chinook.sqlite");
    insta::assert_yaml_snapshot!(lift::schema_graph(&schema));
}
First run writes snapshots/…snap.new; cargo insta review accepts it; later runs diff against it.
2. Component tests (render rsx! without a browser)
Dioxus components are functions; you can build a VirtualDom, run one render, and serialise it with dioxus-ssr. This tests structure, conditional rendering and props — not clicks.
# packages/shell/Cargo.toml
[dev-dependencies]
dioxus-ssr = "0.7"
insta = { version = "1", features = ["yaml"] }
// packages/shell/tests/workbench.rs
use dioxus::prelude::*;
use ui::EditorWorkbench;
 
#[test]
fn workbench_renders_all_panels() {
    let mut dom = VirtualDom::new(EditorWorkbench);
    dom.rebuild_in_place();
    let html = dioxus_ssr::render(&dom);
 
    for title in ["Explorer", "Search", "main.rs", "lib.rs", "Terminal", "Problems", "Outline"] {
        assert!(html.contains(title), "missing panel {title}");
    }
    assert!(html.contains("wb-status-bar"));
}
With props: VirtualDom::new_with_props(SourceFile, SourceFileProps { name: "lib.rs".into() }).
Testing state changes without a browser: drive the signal, not the DOM.
#[test]
fn search_shows_hint_when_empty() {
    let mut dom = VirtualDom::new(Search);
    dom.rebuild_in_place();
    assert!(dioxus_ssr::render(&dom).contains("Type to search"));
}
For “type into the input and see results”, the logic (query → results) should be a plain function you unit-test; the component test only checks both branches render. If you find yourself needing to click, that’s an E2E test.
Snapshot the HTML for shells and layouts (insta::assert_snapshot!(html)) — a changed snapshot is a cheap review of “did I mean to change the DOM?“.
3. Server-function tests (api)
Server functions are ordinary async fns on the server side. With the server feature on, call them directly:
# packages/server/Cargo.toml
[dev-dependencies]
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
// packages/server/tests/server_fns.rs
#[tokio::test]
async fn echo_round_trips() {
    let out = api::echo("hi".to_string()).await.unwrap();
    assert_eq!(out, "hi");
}
Run with cargo test -p api --features server. This tests the function body, auth checks you put in it, and its interaction with real sources — use a tempdir SQLite/DuckDB and a FakeSource.
For the wire (serialisation, routing, errors as seen by a client), start the server and use reqwest:
#[tokio::test]
async fn query_endpoint_rejects_unauthenticated() {
    let base = test_server::spawn().await;              // helper: binds api on a free port
    let res = reqwest::Client::new().post(format!("{base}/api/query")).json(&…).send().await.unwrap();
    assert_eq!(res.status(), 401);
}
Keep these few; they’re slower and mostly guard auth/CORS/error mapping.
4. Integration tests for sources (real engines, temp files)
// packages/sources/sql/tests/sqlite.rs
#[tokio::test]
async fn foreign_keys_become_edges() {
    let dir = tempfile::tempdir().unwrap();
    let db = dir.path().join("t.sqlite");
    seed_sqlite(&db, "CREATE TABLE a(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE b(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, a_id REFERENCES a(id)); …");
 
    let src = SqliteSource::open(&db).await.unwrap();
    let view = src.query(Query::neighbours(row_id("b", 1), Direction::Out)).await.unwrap();
 
    assert_eq!(view.edges().filter(|e| e.kind == EdgeKind::ForeignKey).count(), 1);
}

Embedded engines (SQLite, DuckDB, lbug) → tempdir, no infra.
Networked engines (Postgres, Redis, Falkor, TypeDB) → testcontainers starts Docker containers per test module; mark #[ignore] so cargo test stays infra-free and run them with --ignored in CI.
lbug/duckdb link C++: use cargo nextest so a crash in one test doesn’t kill the whole binary.

5. Extension tests
ext-api will ship a TestHost:
#[test]
fn greet_increments_counter() {
    let host = TestHost::new().with_source(FakeSource::from_nodes([...]));
    let mut ext = Hello::default();
    ext.activate(host.handle()).unwrap();
    let out = ext.command("hello.greet", json!({"name": "x"})).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(out["message"], "Hello, x!");
    assert_eq!(host.recorded_calls().len(), 1);   // set_status
}
Same test runs for a static build and (via the wasm harness) for the component build — the point of one API.
6. Browser tests for wasm-only code
For code that only makes sense in a browser (the interop transport, OPFS backend):
[dev-dependencies]
wasm-bindgen-test = "0.3"
#![cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")]
use wasm_bindgen_test::*;
wasm_bindgen_test_configure!(run_in_browser);
 
#[wasm_bindgen_test]
async fn eval_round_trip() { /* mount, apply, expect CustomEvent */ }
Run: wasm-pack test --headless --firefox packages/editors/code (Firefox is installed on the dev box). The JS bundles themselves get vitest unit tests inside packages/js/<pkg>/.
7. End-to-end
What we already did for the dummy UI, scripted:
(cd packages/web && dx serve --port 8080 &) ; until curl -sf localhost:8080 >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
firefox --headless --profile /tmp/ff --window-size=1400,900 --screenshot /tmp/shot.png http://127.0.0.1:8080/
Assert on the DOM (dump document.body.innerHTML via a tiny Playwright script) or compare screenshots against a baseline with a tolerance. Start with 2–3 flows: app boots, a panel can be docked, a file opens. Add a WebKitGTK desktop E2E only when the graph surface work starts (ADR-0011 Desktop graph surface strategy).
The desktop app on a private display
tools/headless.sh (2026-10-15) gives each worktree its own headless Wayland display: a sway with no screen. The desktop app runs there and is clicked, typed into and screenshotted, and nothing appears on the user’s screen. Several agents can run one each at once.
tools/headless.sh start                       # sway + input; prints WAYLAND_DISPLAY
tools/headless.sh run MOONKALE_CONFIG_DIR=$PWD/target/headless/cfg \
    target/dx/moonkale/release/linux/app/moonkale
tools/headless.sh click 200 128               # left; or: click X Y right|middle
tools/headless.sh type "/path/to/folder"      # printable ASCII, US keymap
tools/headless.sh key Return ctrl+a ctrl+shift+p
tools/headless.sh hold right 5               # compositor key repeat; maximum 10 seconds
tools/headless.sh wheel vertical .25 70 .08   # pixel delta, count, gap in seconds
tools/headless.sh move 300 400                # absolute output coordinates
tools/headless.sh press                      # left button; move, then release to drag
tools/headless.sh release
tools/headless.sh shot target/headless/shot.png
tools/headless.sh stop                        # the apps it started, the input helper, sway

Tools: sway, grim, xkbcli (libxkbcommon) and Python 3, all in nix develop.
Input comes from tools/headless-input.py, which keeps one virtual pointer and one keyboard attached. It replaced wlrctl and wtype: each of their calls adds a device and removes it right away, and the app lost clicks and dropped letters at random.
Rendering:

Apps get Mesa’s software GL by default. With the NVIDIA driver, WebKit’s web process crashes in libnvidia-eglcore on a headless sway once a pointer or a screen capture is involved, which is also why wayvnc was dropped.
HEADLESS_GPU=1 opts out of software GL.
HEADLESS_GL_THREADS=0..32 optionally controls Mesa’s LP_NUM_THREADS for profiling (0 disables render worker threads); unset keeps Mesa’s default. The desktop report records this override. See Mesa environment variables.
The graph canvas under software GL is not verified yet.


Typing speed is about human speed (HEADLESS_KEY_GAP, 30 ms between key events). Faster typing loses keys in the app’s controlled inputs.
State: PIDs, logs, the input socket, sway’s own runtime dir with its Wayland socket (run/) and the apps’ private cache, data and config homes (home/, kept between runs so shader caches stay warm) are in target/headless/ (or $HEADLESS_DIR), so nothing lands in /run/user and a sandbox that can write only the worktree can still run it. Logs: moonkale.log, sway.log.
Bounded gestures: wheel accepts vertical/horizontal pixel deltas in [-1000, 1000], 1–200 events, gaps of 0.01–1 second and at most 15 seconds total. Hold accepts a named key or printable unshifted key, for at most 10 seconds; it releases the key in a finally block. Motion is bounded by the configured output (maximum 16384 pixels per axis).
Desktop frame harness: packages/web/tests/e2e/editor-fps-desktop.py --binary <release-fixture> --corpus <directory> --report <new-json-path> drives all 21 production-panel cases on a private 1500×1100 display, verifies the selected case and observed interaction, writes raw/summary JSON and stops its display even on failure. It uses compositor input, including key repeat and small pixel wheel deltas; the recorder observes trusted WebView events. Its fixed coordinates are specific to this fixture. Software GL results measure CPU-side Rust/DOM/layout costs and do not establish hardware GPU compositing performance. A pass is necessary, not sufficient: Daniel’s real-desktop check is the final acceptance.
Timing precision: the desktop recorder retains both callback-entry and rAF clocks. GTK WebKit quantizes both to 1 ms here; the report labels the calibrated vsync fallback separately from the original strict interval gate (ADR-0023). Acquire ~/.cache/moonkale-slots/bench.lock and both heavy slots for measurements; the idle baseline must contain at least 30 frames and have a p95 no slower than 17 ms. Software GL also includes CPU painting/compositing costs, not just editor layout.
Still for Daniel: real keyboard, IME and pointer behaviour on his own KDE session.

8. How I’d go about it, day to day

Write the fake first. Before the first real Source, write FakeSource (in-memory nodes/edges, records calls). Every editor and the shell test against it; real sources get integration tests that prove they behave like the fake.
One test per rule in the vault. Lifting rules in Data Sources, id determinism in Graph-Native Model, permission checks in Host API Reference — each bullet is a test name.
Snapshot the shell, assert the logic. Component snapshots catch accidental DOM changes; put decisions in plain functions and unit-test those.
Reproduce bugs as tests. Every P-nnn in Problem Log that has a code fix gets a regression test named after it.
Keep the fast suite under a minute. Move anything slower to #[ignore] + CI.
Platform gates are tests too. cargo check -p web --target wasm32-unknown-unknown is the test that says “no native crate leaked”; wire it into cargo xtask check so it isn’t forgotten.

Desktop FPS preflight samples aggregate /proc/stat activity before each mode and gesture. It requires two consecutive samples at or below 10% active CPU within six attempts; all samples are retained in the summary. Settling occurs before input, never by discarding a failed gesture. Hold the bench lock and both heavy slots throughout the run.
8. Parser fuzzing and dependency gates (WP-47)
fuzz/ is a standalone cargo-fuzz crate with its own workspace and lockfile. It
includes the actual production source files instead of copying parser code or
compiling the Dioxus UI. Ordinary cargo test --workspace needs no nightly or
libFuzzer build. Check its existing parser regressions on stable:
CARGO_TARGET_DIR="$PWD/target/agent" cargo test --manifest-path fuzz/Cargo.toml --locked --lib
cargo fmt --manifest-path fuzz/Cargo.toml --check
Install cargo-fuzz 0.13.2 with cargo install cargo-fuzz --version 0.13.2 --locked.
Use a nightly with its rust-src component if building the standard library (CI
pins nightly-2026-09-29). Run heavy commands through your slot wrapper and keep
CARGO_TARGET_DIR absolute and inside your own worktree:
CARGO_TARGET_DIR="$PWD/target/agent" cargo +nightly fuzz run math_delimiters -- -max_total_time=60 -max_len=65536 -rss_limit_mb=2048 -timeout=10
CARGO_TARGET_DIR="$PWD/target/agent" cargo +nightly fuzz run flow_format -- -max_total_time=60 -max_len=65536 -rss_limit_mb=2048 -timeout=10
math_delimiters exercises the existing Markdown display-math range parser,
checking ordered UTF-8 ranges and the 16 KiB TeX bound. WP-36’s planned delimiter
normaliser is not built on this branch and must get its own target when added.
flow_format exercises Flow::parse and successful JSON serialization/reparsing.
The harness limits are smoke-test budgets, not proof that the production parsers
have sufficient bounds. Seed corpora include Unicode and code/metadata exclusions
and an empty/subflow document. Normal parser tests compile in the standalone crate
too. The new libFuzzer harness dependency is isolated to that crate; its exact
version matches the existing production lockfile’s transitive libfuzzer-sys.
CI runs separate non-blocking jobs. Crashes land in fuzz/artifacts/<target>/
and are uploaded even after failure. Reproduce with
cargo +nightly fuzz run <target> fuzz/artifacts/<target>/<crash-file>. Reduce with
cargo +nightly fuzz tmin <target> <crash-file>. Before a fix, add the minimized
input and assertion as a normal #[test] in
packages/code-view/src/native_math_parser.rs or packages/ext-api/src/flow.rs;
verify it fails before and passes after the fix. Do not commit generated corpora,
coverage, targets or crash dumps containing private source. Commit only reviewed
seeds/regression inputs. The initial local 60-second runs found no crash. CI subsequently found P-212:
p-212-crash.md is the original 128-byte input; the other three P-212 seeds are
nine-byte minimized/substituted inputs. They also feed stable production tests
(cargo test -p moonkale-code-view --lib and
cargo test -p moonkale-editor-agent --lib). The production guard bypasses NUL,
vertical tab and form feed before parsing on all profiles; unwind builds also
catch failed complete parse operations. Do not remove the control guard after a
native-only catch test passes: the wasm release uses panic=abort.
Dependency checks: python3 tools/check-security.py rust requires cargo-deny
0.20.2 and cargo-audit 0.22.2. --db-root <writable-directory> relocates the two
RustSec caches without changing deny.toml. python3 tools/check-security.py js
audits all checked-in JS lockfiles without installs or scripts (npm registry
access required). python3 tools/check-vendored.py and
python3 tools/test-security.py run offline. New findings fail; existing dated
exceptions and their limitations are in Security. To update vendored bytes,
verify upstream/version and documented local patches first, then change the
reviewed SHA-256 entries in tools/vendored-assets.json explicitly; CI never
fetches or silently regenerates them.
Platform CI (WP-26, 2026-10-17)
.github/workflows/ci.yml keeps the full workspace, clippy, wasm check and
browser suites on Ubuntu. The portable matrix adds windows-latest and
macos-14 (Apple silicon), initially advisory, with a 45-minute timeout
per OS and separate Rust caches. It runs core, project-fs, index, ext-api,
LLM and Unison tests, plus remote library tests, then checks the default
extension distribution. These defaults match the desktop release’s extension
selection (no Julia); LadybugDB is enabled only by desktop’s Linux target table
(P-144). This checks the distribution, not the desktop binary, installers or UI.
Portable filesystem tests retain forward-slash native keys (the source API’s
format), canonicalize paths used by content-open instrumentation, use temporary
folders and write fixture bytes explicitly, so checkout
CRLF conversion cannot alter them. General rename tests use distinct basenames
for case-insensitive volumes. Plain relative-path jail validation runs everywhere;
Unix symlink fixtures require no Windows privilege setup and remain Unix-only.
The FIFO fixture uses the Linux/Android-only rustix dependency. Watcher tests
exercise native recursive watching on Windows/macOS. Remote library tests cover
its platform branches without the Unix shell/server integration shim; the
PTY handshake fixture uses Unix sleep and stays Unix-only. Unison’s
existing Unix symlink fixture remains gated; its other unit tests run on both. The UCM integration fixture skips when UCM is
absent; these jobs do not install it.
The first GitHub runs still need review: Linux validation cannot establish native
Windows/macOS success. Once both OS jobs are green, remove continue-on-error: true from portable and remove (advisory) from its name; branch protection
must also require both matrix checks if desired. Intel macOS remains release-only.
WP-07 adds the standalone egraph fuzz target and its reviewed saturation seed.
Run cargo +nightly fuzz run egraph -- -max_total_time=60 -max_len=65536 -rss_limit_mb=2048 -timeout=10 through the heavy-slot wrapper from the repository
root, with a worktree-local CARGO_TARGET_DIR. It exercises the production
bounded parser, incoming rewrite walk and aggregate collapse/expand delta path.
It is not yet part of the two-target nightly matrix.

testing/Testing-Strategy.title: Testing Strategy
testing/Testing-Strategy.content:
As practised (checked 2026-10-01) 
                  
                


129 Rust tests: unit tests next to the code, integration tests in tests/ against real SQLite/DuckDB/Turso/redb/RocksDB/HelixDB/LadybugDB files in temp dirs, server-function tests, and component tests with a VirtualDom harness (shell/tests/remote_dialog.rs, shell/tests/server_dialog.rs).
47 browser suites (Playwright, packages/web/tests/e2e/*.mjs, run-all.sh) against dx serve of the web build, Chromium and Firefox; two Android suites over the WebView’s DevTools socket. Setup and rules: packages/web/tests/e2e/README.md.
Not used (despite the tables below): proptest, insta, cargo nextest, testcontainers, wasm-bindgen-test, vitest, a TestHost/FakeSource test utility. The bundles have one unit test (packages/js/milkdown, npm test).
CI (since 2026-10-01, .github/workflows/ci.yml, Milestone 18 - Implementation Log): rustfmt, the layering rules (tools/check-deps.py), cargo test --workspace, clippy -D warnings, a wasm32 check of the web client, and six browser suites (files rich stores palette shell wiki) against dx serve. The other 41 suites run locally with run-all.sh.



A fullstack Dioxus workspace has five different kinds of code, and each is tested differently. Knowing which kind you’re looking at tells you which tool to reach for. The companion note How to Write Tests is the hands-on walkthrough.
The pyramid, mapped to this repo
flowchart TB
  E2E["E2E: real app in a real browser/webview<br/>few, slow, catch integration + platform bugs"]
  COMP["Component tests: render rsx! to a string, assert<br/>many, fast, no browser"]
  SRV["Server-function tests: call the async fn in a tokio test<br/>+ HTTP tests against a running api"]
  INT["Integration: a Source against a real SQLite/DuckDB/lbug file in a tempdir"]
  UNIT["Unit: core model, lifting rules, query IR, when-clauses, link resolution<br/>most tests live here; plain #[test]"]
  E2E --- COMP --- SRV --- INT --- UNIT






















































kind of codewheretest withruns onPure logic (model, parsers, lifting, layouts)core, sources::lift, index::extract, editor-graph::layout#[test], proptest for invariants, insta snapshots for structurescargo test native, fastComponents (rsx!)ui, editors/*build a VirtualDom, rebuild_in_place(), dioxus_ssr::render → assert on the HTML string; insta for snapshotsnative, no browserServer functionsapicall them as normal async fns under #[tokio::test] with the server feature; HTTP-level tests with reqwest against dx serve/a test servernativeSources / driverssources-*, project-fsintegration tests in tests/ with a tempdir DB; containers (testcontainers) for Postgres/Redis/Falkornative, some need DockerBrowser-only behaviour (interop, wasm)packages/js, wasm pathswasm-bindgen-test in headless Firefox/Chrome; JS unit tests with vitest for the bundleswasmWhole appweb, desktopE2E: headless Firefox screenshot/DOM checks (what we did for the dummy UI); Playwright laterbrowserExtensionsanyTestHost from ext-api (in-memory sources, recorded calls)native
Principles

Test at the seam you designed. The traits in this project (Source, CodeEditorBackend, Extension, Layout) exist to be swapped — so they are also where fakes go. A FakeSource in core test utils is the single most valuable test fixture in the repo.
Push logic down the pyramid. If a component test needs a database, the logic is in the wrong layer. Components should be thin over signals; test the signal logic with plain functions.
Snapshot what is structural, assert what is semantic. insta snapshots for rendered HTML and lifted graphs; explicit asserts for “the FK became an edge from A to B”.
Property tests for the model. Transaction apply/undo round-trips, deterministic ids (derive(a) == derive(a)), WhenClause parse/print, layout stability under permutation.
Every platform-gated module gets a compile test. cargo check -p web --target wasm32-unknown-unknown in CI proves no native crate leaked in (Platform Matrix).
E2E is for integration and platform bugs only. Keep them few; they found both CSS bugs in the dummy UI (P-002 Dioxus mount point and full-height layout, P-003 dioxus-workbench theme variables) that no unit test could.

Tooling

cargo nextest for parallel, per-test-process runs (a panicking test can’t take the others down; matters with C++ drivers).
cargo test --workspace --exclude web for the native suite; a separate wasm job.
cargo clippy --workspace — the repo’s clippy.toml already bans holding signal guards across .await; keep it.
cargo fmt --check.
CI matrix (planned): linux-native, linux-wasm-check, linux-webkitgtk-e2e, macos-native.

What we test first (Phase 1)

core: ids, PropertyMap, Transaction apply/undo, WhenClause.
project-fs: tree building with .gitignore, patch application atomicity, watch coalescing (tempdir + notify).
ui: the workbench shell renders the registry’s panels (component snapshot).
api: echo (exists) and, once real, query/fetch/apply over a FakeSource.
One E2E: open the web build, assert the workbench and one panel exist.
